u2-1.title: Triads: minor and major
u2-1.goal: Hear root, third and fifth as one harmony.
u2-1.text:
Em contains E–G–B; E major contains E–G#–B: only the third changes. Moving a chord tone to another octave preserves the chord. Play each tone separately and sing the third above the bass.

Pick E bass first, then the upper three strings with a short controlled stroke. Keep unused strings muted. G3 and G#3 are on D frets 5 and 6; B3 and E4 remain fretted. Let the notes ring together after the spread attack.

ku2-1.title: Triads: minor and major
ku2-1.goal: Hear root, third and fifth as one harmony.
ku2-1.text:
Em contains E–G–B; E major contains E–G#–B: only the third changes. Moving a chord tone to another octave preserves the chord. Play each tone separately and sing the third above the bass.

Left E3; right G4–B4–E5 or G#4–B4–E5. Use right 1–2–5; only the thumb moves a semitone.

u2-2.title: Inversion and bass note
u2-2.goal: Distinguish the lowest note from the upper voicing.
u2-2.text:
Em over E is root position, over G first inversion, over B second inversion. The lowest sounding note determines the inversion, not the shape above it. The melody can retain E as a common tone.

Keep G3–B3–E4 above. Bass: open E2, G2 at E-string fret 3, B2 at A-string fret 2. Mute each previous bass at the change.

ku2-2.title: Inversion and bass note
ku2-2.goal: Distinguish the lowest note from the upper voicing.
ku2-2.text:
Em over E is root position, over G first inversion, over B second inversion. The lowest sounding note determines the inversion, not the shape above it. The melody can retain E as a common tone.

Retain the same right-hand chord; rehearse the written bass separately. Name the bass note and then the inversion at each change.

u2-3.title: Thirds with a melodic line
u2-3.goal: Deliberately bring out the upper voice of a dyad.
u2-3.text:
E–G and A–C are minor thirds; G–B is major. Diatonic parallel thirds therefore change size. Read the upper line as the melody first, then add the lower line. Coordinate their releases.

For E3–G3 use A fret 7 and D fret 5. Then G3–B3 on D/G, A3–C4 on G/C. Move the hand with each change.

ku2-3.title: Thirds with a melodic line
ku2-3.goal: Deliberately bring out the upper voice of a dyad.
ku2-3.text:
E–G and A–C are minor thirds; G–B is major. Diatonic parallel thirds therefore change size. Read the upper line as the melody first, then add the lower line. Coordinate their releases.

Right-hand thirds with 1–3 or 2–4; move the whole hand between positions. Quiet left E3 each bar. Also play the top line alone.

u2-4.title: Arpeggio above a bass
u2-4.goal: Play broken triads with a clear upper voice.
u2-4.text:
An arpeggio distributes chord tones in time. Here each written eighth ends at the next melodic note; only the bass sustains. Longer overlap is a later artistic choice, not a substitute for controlled releases.

The pick plays both bass and upper figure. At a shared entry, place bass on the pulse and the upper note immediately after it. Continue the written eighths with small string crossings while the bass rings. Bring out the top note without reattacking the bass.

ku2-4.title: Arpeggio above a bass
ku2-4.goal: Play broken triads with a clear upper voice.
ku2-4.text:
An arpeggio distributes chord tones in time. Here each written eighth ends at the next melodic note; only the bass sustains. Longer overlap is a later artistic choice, not a substitute for controlled releases.

Prepare the right-hand triad, starting with 1–3–5–3. Left hand only at bar starts. Loop one bar before adding chord changes.

u2-6.title: Power chords and muting
u2-6.goal: Play fifths without thirds cleanly and in time.
u2-6.text:
E5 means E and B, not a five-note chord. Without a third it is not explicitly major or minor. In P4 the fifth is one string higher and two frets up. Muting determines clarity under gain.

E5: open E/A fret 2; A5: open A/D fret 2; B5: A fret 2/D fret 4. Strike only those strings. Use both hands to stop rests.

u2-rhythm.title: Short chords and offbeats
u2-rhythm.goal: Enter between clicks and release on time.
u2-rhythm.text:
Here the eighth rest falls on the beat and the chord on the offbeat. Keep counting while you play nothing on the click. A short chord needs a defined release; the next rest is not an extra attack.

Use a short pick stroke across the upper three strings on the offbeat. Release fretting pressure at note-off and control open bass strings. Pick the bass separately on its written beat. Do not fill the eighth rest before the chord with an attack.

ku2-rhythm.title: Short chords and offbeats
ku2-rhythm.goal: Enter between clicks and release on time.
ku2-rhythm.text:
Here the eighth rest falls on the beat and the chord on the offbeat. Keep counting while you play nothing on the click. A short chord needs a defined release; the next rest is not an extra attack.

Right-hand chords are short while the left holds. No sustain pedal. Release with small movements rather than lifting the whole hand high.

u2-5.title: Hear a triad, build a phrase
u2-5.goal: Find chord tones in an original melody.
u2-5.text:
A melody can imply a chord without playing all its notes together. Listen first to the upper closing notes. Sing them away from the instrument, then add bass. More notes do not automatically create more coherence.

Play the upper line first on D/G/C strings. Add bass only at written bar starts. E can remain an audible reference through Em–C.

ku2-5.title: Hear a triad, build a phrase
ku2-5.goal: Find chord tones in an original melody.
ku2-5.text:
A melody can imply a chord without playing all its notes together. Listen first to the upper closing notes. Sing them away from the instrument, then add bass. More notes do not automatically create more coherence.

Sing and play the right-hand melody alone first. Name left-hand bass notes before combining. Write down your fingering and keep it consistent.

u3-1.title: Lamento: a descending bass
u3-1.goal: Combine a slow descending bass with a singing upper voice.
u3-1.text:
E–D–C–B is a descending bass model. Its effect also depends on tempo, duration and upper voice; the notes alone do not guarantee sadness. Read bass and melody separately and compare their intervals at each bar start.

Play E3–D3–C3–B2 bass entirely on A at frets 7–5–3–2. Melody mainly on D. Move the hand down with the bass without shortening the upper line.

ku3-1.title: Lamento: a descending bass
ku3-1.goal: Combine a slow descending bass with a singing upper voice.
ku3-1.text:
E–D–C–B is a descending bass model. Its effect also depends on tempo, duration and upper voice; the notes alone do not guarantee sadness. Read bass and melody separately and compare their intervals at each bar start.

Try left 1–2–3–4 for the slow descending bass. Sing the right-hand line separately. Combine only when the left-hand motion no longer requires searching.

u3-2.title: A circle-of-fifths path
u3-2.goal: Follow common tones through several chords.
u3-2.text:
Em–Am–D–G–C–F#dim–B–Em links roots by descending fifths or ascending fourths, with a diminished fifth from C down to F# (an augmented fourth upward). B major contains D# and leads back to Em here. Hear chord tones rather than recalling shapes alone.

Connect upper triads without bass first. Retain common tones only when their fingering allows the next shape. Mute the old string at each bass change.

ku3-2.title: A circle-of-fifths path
ku3-2.goal: Follow common tones through several chords.
ku3-2.text:
Em–Am–D–G–C–F#dim–B–Em links roots by descending fifths or ascending fourths, with a diminished fifth from C down to F# (an augmented fourth upward). B major contains D# and leads back to Em here. Hear chord tones rather than recalling shapes alone.

Use compact right-hand voicings and left-hand roots. Look at a target before moving. The right hand should not copy every bass leap.

u3-reading.title: Syncopation and tied entries
u3-reading.goal: Sustain an accented subdivision across the next beat.
u3-reading.text:
A syncopation begins between beats and continues across a stronger beat. The tie does not create a second attack. Count eighths, mark quarters with your foot and count through rests.

Melody is on D/G, with picked E bass. Pick each rhythm separately first while the foot keeps quarters. Briefly spread shared entries bass–melody. Sustain tied syncopated melody notes through the following bass attack.

ku3-reading.title: Syncopation and tied entries
ku3-reading.goal: Sustain an accented subdivision across the next beat.
ku3-reading.text:
A syncopation begins between beats and continues across a stronger beat. The tie does not create a second attack. Count eighths, mark quarters with your foot and count through rests.

Hold long E3 notes on the left; rehearse the right-hand rhythm on one key. Check whether a new left-hand attack accidentally retriggers the right.

u3-4.title: Sixteenths and precise rests
u3-4.goal: Read four subdivisions per quarter without accelerating.
u3-4.text:
Sixteenths have two flags or beams. Four fill a quarter. Count “1 e and a” or four even syllables. A sixteenth rest occupies one of those slots; it does not shorten the bar.

Keep picking movements small and loose. Continue the motion internally through rests while muting the string. Start on one pitch, then add the written notes.

ku3-4.title: Sixteenths and precise rests
ku3-4.goal: Read four subdivisions per quarter without accelerating.
ku3-4.text:
Sixteenths have two flags or beams. Four fill a quarter. Count “1 e and a” or four even syllables. A sixteenth rest occupies one of those slots; it does not shorten the bar.

Begin on one right-hand key with alternating fingers, then use the written pitches. Release the key for rests. Keep the left hand independent of the fast subdivisions.

u3-3.title: Separate bass and melody by ear
u3-3.goal: Reduce a two-voice idea to its essential lines.
u3-3.text:
Transcribe the lowest entries first, then the highest. Write rhythm before pitch. The preview provides a fixed reference: do not silently alter what you heard to fit easier shapes.

Bass on E/A, melody on D/G. Listen away from the instrument, write the bass path and verify it alone before adding melody.

ku3-3.title: Separate bass and melody by ear
ku3-3.goal: Reduce a two-voice idea to its essential lines.
ku3-3.text:
Transcribe the lowest entries first, then the highest. Write rhythm before pitch. The preview provides a fixed reference: do not silently alter what you heard to fit easier shapes.

Reconstruct the heard bass with the left hand alone. Sing and find the right-hand melody. Combine only once both lines match.

u3-6.title: Chromatic bass, calm melody
u3-6.goal: Lead semitone bass steps without clipping the upper voice.
u3-6.text:
E–Eb–D–Db–C–B adds chromatic steps to the diatonic descent. Read repeated letter names with changing accidentals carefully. Let audible voice motion create tension rather than adding gain.

Bass entirely on A: frets 7–6–5–4–3–2. Melody on D. End each old bass while retaining the upper note for its written duration.

u3-5.title: Repeats and two endings
u3-5.goal: Play repeats and alternate endings without losing the form.
u3-5.text:
Play the section between repeat signs twice. Use ending 1 on the first pass and ending 2 on the second. The expanded order below the score is a checking aid; afterwards follow the signs alone.

Keep the repeated E bass steady. The first ending stays open on B, the second lands on E. Do not insert a fretting pause at the repeat.

ku3-5.title: Repeats and two endings
ku3-5.goal: Play repeats and alternate endings without losing the form.
ku3-5.text:
Play the section between repeat signs twice. Use ending 1 on the first pass and ending 2 on the second. The expanded order below the score is a checking aid; afterwards follow the signs alone.

Move both hands together at the repeat. Read the two endings separately first, then play the complete order.

u4-1.title: Leading tone and harmonic minor
u4-1.goal: Hear and read D# as a directed approach to E.
u4-1.text:
E harmonic minor is E F# G A B C D#. D#–E is a semitone; C–D# is an augmented second spanning three semitones. The leading tone has direction within a cadence, though other continuations are possible outside it.

Play the upper line on D/G/C. D#4 is C-string fret 3, E4 fret 4. Hear the semitone before moving the finger.

ku4-1.title: Leading tone and harmonic minor
ku4-1.goal: Hear and read D# as a directed approach to E.
ku4-1.text:
E harmonic minor is E F# G A B C D#. D#–E is a semitone; C–D# is an augmented second spanning three semitones. The leading tone has direction within a cadence, though other continuations are possible outside it.

Try right 1–2–3–1–2–3–4–5 for E4–E5. Sing C5–D#5 separately before inserting it in the line. Rehearse bass alone first.

u4-3.title: Cadence: tension and arrival
u4-3.goal: Shape Am–B7–Em as preparation, dominant and arrival.
u4-3.text:
In E minor, Am is iv, B7 is V7 and Em is i. B7 contains B–D#–F#–A. Here D# moves to E and A to G. Hear these motions individually; louder playing does not replace voice leading.

For B7 use F#3–A3–D#4 over B2. Slowly connect the semitone/whole-tone motions to Em. Avoid lifting every finger hurriedly at once.

ku4-3.title: Cadence: tension and arrival
ku4-3.goal: Shape Am–B7–Em as preparation, dominant and arrival.
ku4-3.text:
In E minor, Am is iv, B7 is V7 and Em is i. B7 contains B–D#–F#–A. Here D# moves to E and A to G. Hear these motions individually; louder playing does not replace voice leading.

Play the two resolutions as a right-hand dyad over left B–E first. Add the third right-hand chord tone and coordinate the timing.

u4-chords.title: Sixths, sevenths and chord symbols
u4-chords.goal: Distinguish Em, Em7, Em6, Cmaj7 and B7 by ear.
u4-chords.text:
Em7 adds D, Em6 adds C#. Cmaj7 contains C–E–G–B; B7 contains B–D#–F#–A. “maj7” means a major seventh; “7” uses a minor seventh. A symbol specifies tones, not register or duration.

Check the P4 voicings one note at a time. In Em7 use D4 at G fret 7 and E4 at C fret 4. Keep bass and top voice audible through the change.

ku4-chords.title: Sixths, sevenths and chord symbols
ku4-chords.goal: Distinguish Em, Em7, Em6, Cmaj7 and B7 by ear.
ku4-chords.text:
Em7 adds D, Em6 adds C#. Cmaj7 contains C–E–G–B; B7 contains B–D#–F#–A. “maj7” means a major seventh; “7” uses a minor seventh. A symbol specifies tones, not register or duration.

Left plays the root, right the other three tones. Name each right-hand pitch before playing. Fingering may change between chords; keep the top line connected.

u4-2.title: A diminished seventh in motion
u4-2.goal: Lead D#–F#–A–C as four voices into Em.
u4-2.text:
D#dim7 stacks minor thirds: D#–F#–A–C. Steps of three semitones give 3+3+3 to the diminished seventh C. The symmetry allows different interpretations; here resolution to Em establishes the role. Play each voice’s destination separately.

Bass D#3 is on A fret 6, with F#3 on D4, C4 on G5 and A4 on F4. Spread the chord low to high with the pick. Deliberately mute the C string and skip it or brush it silently; it is not part of this chord. Check every sounding string slowly first.

ku4-2.title: A diminished seventh in motion
ku4-2.goal: Lead D#–F#–A–C as four voices into Em.
ku4-2.text:
D#dim7 stacks minor thirds: D#–F#–A–C. Steps of three semitones give 3+3+3 to the diminished seventh C. The symmetry allows different interpretations; here resolution to Em establishes the role. Play each voice’s destination separately.

Left D#3, right F#4–A4–C5; then left E3 with right G4–B4–E5. Play individual resolutions before the complete four-voice sonorities.

u4-4.title: Lead the inner voices
u4-4.goal: Combine a retained top note with moving inner voices.
u4-4.text:
Across D7–G, D can remain on top while F# moves to G and C to B. Not every voice must move at each chord change. Hear the inner line alone, then within the full sonority.

Hold D4 at C fret 2 as a common top note. For D7–G move F#3/G3 on D and C4/B3 on G. Mute the D3 bass when moving to G2.

ku4-4.title: Lead the inner voices
ku4-4.goal: Combine a retained top note with moving inner voices.
ku4-4.text:
Across D7–G, D can remain on top while F# moves to G and C to B. Not every voice must move at each chord change. Hear the inner line alone, then within the full sonority.

Retain the upper right-hand finger on D5 while the lower fingers move. Prepare left D–G separately; do not hide unclear transitions with sustain pedal.

u4-6.title: Fifth/sixth changes in a riff
u4-6.goal: Play a bass riff with precise upper-interval changes.
u4-6.text:
E–B is a fifth and E–C# a major sixth: seven and nine semitones. These dyads are not complete E6 chords because the third is absent. Use straight eighths first; shuffle follows in phase 5.

Open E plus A frets 2/4; then open A plus D frets 2/4. Change the upper finger while retaining the root reference. Mute unused strings consistently.

u4-5.title: Make a cadence your own
u4-5.goal: Combine modal colour and a functional ending in one form.
u4-5.text:
A long E-pedal passage can remain open; Am–B7–Em then focuses the direction. Decide where the ending starts. Reserving D# for that point makes its contrast with D easier to hear.

First half: open E and single melody. Then use the familiar compact chords. Do not add a fretting pause at the transition.

ku4-5.title: Make a cadence your own
ku4-5.goal: Combine modal colour and a functional ending in one form.
ku4-5.text:
A long E-pedal passage can remain open; Am–B7–Em then focuses the direction. Decide where the ending starts. Reserving D# for that point makes its contrast with D easier to hear.

Left starts with E3, then the cadence roots. Right changes from a single melody to triads without a sudden jump in level.

u5-1.title: Sequence: move a motif
u5-1.goal: Move a motif by scale steps while preserving its identity.
u5-1.text:
A diatonic sequence preserves directions and scale-step distances, not necessarily semitone sizes. This example moves the same four-note motif within E Aeolian. Sing each new starting note first.

Read in the D/G window first. Use the C string for C4; open E bass remains. Do not mask the position change with a louder bass attack.

ku5-1.title: Sequence: move a motif
ku5-1.goal: Move a motif by scale steps while preserving its identity.
ku5-1.text:
A diatonic sequence preserves directions and scale-step distances, not necessarily semitone sizes. This example moves the same four-note motif within E Aeolian. Sing each new starting note first.

Check the new right-hand five-note space before each move. Adapt fingering to the motif instead of forcing the same fingers regardless of black keys.

u5-2.title: Three layers: bass, figure, melody
u5-2.goal: Hold a melody while the inner voice continues.
u5-2.text:
Three layers have separate roles: bass anchors harmony, inner quarters provide motion, long top notes form the melody. Practise each pair before combining all three. Do not reattack melody with every inner note.

Briefly spread the shared entry bass–inner voice–melody with the pick. Hold the top string while picking the inner quarters. Reattack only voices due to enter. Later, a prepared left-hand hammer-on from silence can start an inner voice together with a picked attack; first secure the technique in the phase 5 legato unit.

ku5-2.title: Three layers: bass, figure, melody
ku5-2.goal: Hold a melody while the inner voice continues.
ku5-2.text:
Three layers have separate roles: bass anchors harmony, inner quarters provide motion, long top notes form the melody. Practise each pair before combining all three. Do not reattack melody with every inner note.

Left plays bass. Right holds the top with 5 while 1/2/3 move inside. Practise upper and inner voices with the right hand alone before adding left.

u5-groove.title: Triplets against straight eighths
u5-groove.goal: Alternate two and three subdivisions at a fixed quarter pulse.
u5-groove.text:
A bracketed 3 means three written eighths in the time of two ordinary eighths. Both groups fill one quarter. Count two, then three even syllables per quarter without changing the quarter-note tempo.

Start triplets on E3 with small alternate-picking movements. Continuous alternate picking reverses the starting stroke on the next quarter; that is intentional.

ku5-groove.title: Triplets against straight eighths
ku5-groove.goal: Alternate two and three subdivisions at a fixed quarter pulse.
ku5-groove.text:
A bracketed 3 means three written eighths in the time of two ordinary eighths. Both groups fill one quarter. Count two, then three even syllables per quarter without changing the quarter-note tempo.

Start with right 1–2–3 for each quarter while left plays steady bar starts. Relax after groups without inserting a pause.

u5-4.title: 12/8: four large pulses
u5-4.goal: Read and accompany twelve eighths as four groups of three.
u5-4.text:
12/8 contains twelve eighths, grouped here as 3+3+3+3. Tempo refers to the dotted quarter: four pulses per bar. These eighths are ordinary notes in the meter, not separately marked triplets.

Pick the bass on pulses 1 and 3 and play the upper eighth-note figure between them. Briefly spread shared entries low to high. Preserve the regular eighth spacing afterwards and accent group starts only lightly.

ku5-4.title: 12/8: four large pulses
ku5-4.goal: Read and accompany twelve eighths as four groups of three.
ku5-4.text:
12/8 contains twelve eighths, grouped here as 3+3+3+3. Tempo refers to the dotted quarter: four pulses per bar. These eighths are ordinary notes in the meter, not separately marked triplets.

Hold each left dotted half for two large pulses. Read right-hand groups of three. Play only each group’s first note before filling in the others.

u5-6.title: Legato: hammer-on and pull-off
u5-6.goal: Reduce picked attacks without losing rhythm or level.
u5-6.text:
A slur connects different pitches; unlike a tie, it does not merge repeated pitches. Pick the first note, then create the next with a hammer-on or pull-off. Preview demonstrates pitches and rhythm, not the physical technique’s timbre.

D string: E3 fret 2 with 1, F#3 fret 4 with 3, G3 fret 5 with 4. Prepare the target finger before a pull-off and release the string with control rather than pulling far away.

Only after ordinary hammer-ons and pull-offs are even at low gain: introduce left-hand tapping as a hammer-on from silence. Do not pick the D string first. Tap E3 at fret 2 with finger 1 using a short precise movement, then mute it cleanly. Avoid excess force; aim for a clear note and silent neighbouring strings. Then align the left-hand attack with a picked E2. The right hand keeps the pick.

u5-3.title: Sequence over changing bass
u5-3.goal: Control motif contour and harmonic rhythm together.
u5-3.text:
The figure repeats its rhythm while bass changes every bar: one chord per bar is the harmonic rhythm. Check strong-beat notes first; they should clarify each harmony.

Read the melody ahead of each bass change. Pick the new bass first, immediately followed by the upper note written at the same onset. Continue the figure without accidentally muting the bass. End the old bass at the next change.

ku5-3.title: Sequence over changing bass
ku5-3.goal: Control motif contour and harmonic rhythm together.
ku5-3.text:
The figure repeats its rhythm while bass changes every bar: one chord per bar is the harmonic rhythm. Check strong-beat notes first; they should clarify each harmony.

Left plays root, fifth, octave, fifth in quarters; the diminished chord uses a diminished fifth. Start with 5–2–1–2, allowing the hand to move. Read the right-hand figure separately before combining both moving lines.

u5-5.title: Compare shuffle and swing deliberately
u5-5.goal: Hear ternary phrasing and read it in ordinary eighth notation.
u5-5.text:
Shuffle can be practised as long and short triplet portions. Swing often uses ordinary eighths plus a performance indication. Preview uses 2:1 as a study model; real swing ratios vary with tempo and style. There is no universal swing percentage.

Play long–short on the right while retaining bass once per bar. Use smaller movements at faster tempos; do not swallow short notes. Check the rhythm without gain too.

ku5-5.title: Compare shuffle and swing deliberately
ku5-5.goal: Hear ternary phrasing and read it in ordinary eighth notation.
ku5-5.text:
Shuffle can be practised as long and short triplet portions. Swing often uses ordinary eighths plus a performance indication. Preview uses 2:1 as a study model; real swing ratios vary with tempo and style. There is no universal swing percentage.

Right plays long–short while left stays unchanged. Start with alternating E4–G4 before the full phrase. Avoid locking the hand and arm on every long note.

u6-1.title: Fourth-based sonorities
u6-1.goal: Balance fourth-based sonorities above a clear bass reference.
u6-1.text:
E–A–D stacks two perfect fourths, five semitones each. Without a third, major/minor identity is ambiguous. Bass changes the interpretation. Compare the same upper sonority over E and A before assigning a fixed chord label.

E3–A3–D4 lie on D/G/C at fret 2. A small barre is possible; check each string separately. Briefly spread the bass and upper quartal voicing with the pick. Mute A when using E bass, then let the intended bass sustain.

ku6-1.title: Fourth-based sonorities
ku6-1.goal: Balance fourth-based sonorities above a clear bass reference.
ku6-1.text:
E–A–D stacks two perfect fourths, five semitones each. Without a third, major/minor identity is ambiguous. Bass changes the interpretation. Compare the same upper sonority over E and A before assigning a fixed chord label.

Try right 1–2–5 for E4–A4–D5. With a smaller hand prepare notes consecutively, then sound together only in a comfortably reachable voicing.

u6-2.title: C Lydian: the raised fourth
u6-2.goal: Deliberately compare F# and F above C.
u6-2.text:
C Lydian is C D E F# G A B. Only F changes to F# compared with C major. Make C audible as reference; the same notes over E produce another modal effect. The raised fourth is a colour, not a compulsory resolution rule.

C3 bass at A fret 3. Melody on D/G/C; F#3 at D fret 4. Keep C bass deliberately quieter than the upper phrase.

ku6-2.title: C Lydian: the raised fourth
ku6-2.goal: Deliberately compare F# and F above C.
ku6-2.text:
C Lydian is C D E F# G A B. Only F changes to F# compared with C major. Make C audible as reference; the same notes over E produce another modal effect. The raised fourth is a colour, not a compulsory resolution rule.

Left C3; right reads within C4–B4. Prepare a finger for F# and avoid lifting the hand high when returning to white keys.

u6-3.title: Register changes without a new idea
u6-3.goal: Play a recognisable motif in two octaves.
u6-3.text:
Octave transposition changes register, not note names or rhythm. It still changes presence and density. First check that the higher motif retains its durations and accents.

First phrase on D/G, second on C/F. Look at the target before attacking; bass remains open E. Decide the return fingering too.

ku6-3.title: Register changes without a new idea
ku6-3.goal: Play a recognisable motif in two octaves.
ku6-3.text:
Octave transposition changes register, not note names or rhythm. It still changes presence and density. First check that the higher motif retains its durations and accents.

Move the right hand an octave while retaining left bass. Release the old shape and prepare at the target. The higher version stays below C6.

u6-4.title: Density and release as musical controls
u6-4.goal: Shape two distinct textures from the same pitches.
u6-4.text:
Density comes from simultaneous voices and their decay. More reverb or gain can conceal lines. Shape it first through playing: long bass, short middle, clear melody. Only then compare sounds at similar levels.

Pick only: briefly spread the shared bar opening from bass through inner voice to melody. Let bass and melody ring afterwards; pick only the subsequent inner quarters. Mute the inner voice with the fretting hand at its written release without stopping the melody string. Keep the inner voice completely silent in bar two. Start with low gain, then use your usual amp sound. This version does not require tapping.

ku6-4.title: Density and release as musical controls
ku6-4.goal: Shape two distinct textures from the same pitches.
ku6-4.text:
Density comes from simultaneous voices and their decay. More reverb or gain can conceal lines. Shape it first through playing: long bass, short middle, clear melody. Only then compare sounds at similar levels.

Begin without sustain. On synth choose release short enough to reveal rests; on piano control the same endings with fingers.

u6-5.title: Chromatic approaches
u6-5.goal: Reach a chord tone deliberately from a neighbouring pitch.
u6-5.text:
A chromatic neighbour lies a semitone from its target and need not belong to the home scale. Its role depends on destination and accent. Play the target alone first, then approach it briefly from below.

A#3–B3 on G frets 3–4; G#3–A3 on G 1–2. Prepare the target finger close to the fret. Avoid large searching motions.

ku6-5.title: Chromatic approaches
ku6-5.goal: Reach a chord tone deliberately from a neighbouring pitch.
ku6-5.text:
A chromatic neighbour lies a semitone from its target and need not belong to the home scale. Its role depends on destination and accent. Play the target alone first, then approach it briefly from below.

Prepare black neighbour and white target as a small movement. Hear the right-hand destination while holding the chord root on the left.

u6-7.title: Natural harmonics
u6-7.goal: Produce clear octave harmonics and use them as a texture change.
u6-7.text:
A light touch above fret twelve suppresses parts of the string’s vibration; the harmonic sounds one octave above the open string. Diamond heads here show sounding harmonic pitches. Preview plays their pitches without imitating the timbre.

Touch directly above fret twelve rather than pressing between frets. Pick, release the touching finger and mute other strings. E/A/D/G/C/F produce E3/A3/D4/G4/C5/F5.

u6-6.title: Dark reference, bright contrast
u6-6.goal: Distinguish E Aeolian and C Lydian through bass and phrasing.
u6-6.text:
The modes share pitch classes but have different centres, E or C. Changing bass alone may not suffice; give the new centre time and a suitable phrase ending. Make the return audible as a return.

Use open E bass and C at A fret 3. In the contrast hold F#3 deliberately over C. Prepare returning bass and first melody note separately.

ku6-6.title: Dark reference, bright contrast
ku6-6.goal: Distinguish E Aeolian and C Lydian through bass and phrasing.
ku6-6.text:
The modes share pitch classes but have different centres, E or C. Changing bass alone may not suffice; give the new centre time and a suitable phrase ending. Make the return audible as a return.

Left E3 and C3; right retains the same pitch collection. Rest on C or E in the C section, then confirm E as centre for longer on the return.

u7-1.title: Three against two
u7-1.goal: Distribute three upper entries evenly against two bass pulses.
u7-1.text:
Three quarter-note triplets occupy two ordinary quarters. Subdivide their shared span into six: upper entries on 1,3,5 and lower on 1,4. Eventually remove the counting aid while preserving the shared start.

Pick each voice separately first. Then pick bass quarters while the left hand produces upper notes using prepared hammer-ons from silence and suitable pull-offs. A note on a new string needs a fresh left-hand attack on that string; a pull-off on the previous string cannot create it. Both hands meet at shared entries. This is an advanced application of the legato unit; slow down rather than altering the 3:2 rhythm.

ku7-1.title: Three against two
ku7-1.goal: Distribute three upper entries evenly against two bass pulses.
ku7-1.text:
Three quarter-note triplets occupy two ordinary quarters. Subdivide their shared span into six: upper entries on 1,3,5 and lower on 1,4. Eventually remove the counting aid while preserving the shared start.

Left plays quarters, right quarter-note triplets. Tap on your thighs first, then use one key each. Hands share the start, not every attack.

u7-2.title: 3+3+2 within 4/4
u7-2.goal: Displace accents without restarting the measure.
u7-2.text:
Eight eighths can be accented 3+3+2 while remaining one 4/4 bar. Accents fall on beat 1, the offbeat after 2, and beat 4. Bass and drums retain the regular meter against the melodic grouping.

Create accents with attack, not extra duration. E bass on beats 1 and 3. Do not rush the last group of two.

ku7-2.title: 3+3+2 within 4/4
ku7-2.goal: Displace accents without restarting the measure.
ku7-2.text:
Eight eighths can be accented 3+3+2 while remaining one 4/4 bar. Accents fall on beat 1, the offbeat after 2, and beat 4. Bass and drums retain the regular meter against the melodic grouping.

Left plays halves, right even eighths with three accents. If the patch ignores velocity, clarify accents by slightly shortening unaccented notes.

u7-3.title: Grouped 7/8 and 5/8
u7-3.goal: Hear odd meters as recurring groups.
u7-3.text:
Here 7/8 is grouped 2+2+3: count “1-2, 1-2, 1-2-3”. Follow with 5/8 grouped 2+3. Tempo counts eighths, not quarters: at 120 eighths per minute each eighth lasts half a second.

Pick the bass at group starts and the upper eighth-note line. Briefly spread shared entries bass–melody, then keep following eighths on their grid. Later the left hand can attack the shared melody entry while the pick plays bass. Combine rhythm first, then pitches.

ku7-3.title: Grouped 7/8 and 5/8
ku7-3.goal: Hear odd meters as recurring groups.
ku7-3.text:
Here 7/8 is grouped 2+2+3: count “1-2, 1-2, 1-2-3”. Follow with 5/8 grouped 2+3. Tempo counts eighths, not quarters: at 120 eighths per minute each eighth lasts half a second.

Left holds quarter, quarter, dotted quarter group durations. Right plays eighths. Count the complete final group of three before the next beat 1.

u7-4.title: Minor pentatonic with target notes
u7-4.goal: Shape a phrase with a clear destination from five pitches.
u7-4.text:
E minor pentatonic: E G A B D, degrees 1 b3 4 5 b7. F# and C are omitted from E Aeolian. Fewer notes do not replace phrasing: repetition, silence and a target make the statement.

D string E3/G3, G string A3/B3, C string D4/E4. Do not import a standard-tuning box. Sing the target before crossing to the higher string.

ku7-4.title: Minor pentatonic with target notes
ku7-4.goal: Shape a phrase with a clear destination from five pitches.
ku7-4.text:
E minor pentatonic: E G A B D, degrees 1 b3 4 5 b7. F# and C are omitted from E Aeolian. Fewer notes do not replace phrasing: repetition, silence and a target make the statement.

Organise E4–E5 in two small groups. Try 1–2–3–1–2–3 for E–G–A–B–D–E ascending. Left plays E3, then the written changes.

u7-solo.title: Solo, segno and coda
u7-solo.goal: Leave a solo section and land its return reliably.
u7-solo.text:
D.S. means return to the segno. Ignore “to coda” on the first pass; after returning, jump from that point to the coda sign. This example follows 1–2–3–4–2–3–5–6. Count the form before playing. The first bar is written as a count-in: melody enters on beat 4 as a pickup to bar 2. Abbreviated pickup notation omits the preceding rests; the following full measure still begins on beat 1.

Read the melody on the first visit; replace it with an equally long original motif on the second. Retain the bass rhythm and ending.

ku7-solo.title: Solo, segno and coda
ku7-solo.goal: Leave a solo section and land its return reliably.
ku7-solo.text:
D.S. means return to the segno. Ignore “to coda” on the first pass; after returning, jump from that point to the coda sign. This example follows 1–2–3–4–2–3–5–6. Count the form before playing. The first bar is written as a count-in: melody enters on beat 4 as a pickup to bar 2. Abbreviated pickup notation omits the preceding rests; the following full measure still begins on beat 1.

Vary the right-hand solo while retaining the left. Prepare the right-hand coda position without stopping the left.

u7-6.title: Bending towards a heard target
u7-6.goal: Bend a whole tone, hold the target and stop cleanly.
u7-6.text:
A whole tone is two semitones. Hear normally fretted B4 first, then bend A4 to exactly that pitch. The arrow shows the destination. Check intonation before adding vibrato at the target.

High F string: B4 at fret 6, A4 at fret 4. Bend A with the ring finger supported by other fingers. Mute before releasing to avoid an unintended descending note.

u7-5.title: Tempo and longer performances
u7-5.goal: Stabilise eighths, chord accompaniment and long forms at the repertoire’s written tempo.
u7-5.text:
Tempo is a separate skill. A clean slow pass does not guarantee a fast one. Start at a secure tempo, increase in small steps and note the first specific unstable spot. Practise it briefly, then restore the context.

Use small attacks, fixed string choices and prepared changes. Reduce movement at higher tempos rather than increasing fretting pressure.

ku7-5.title: Tempo and longer performances
ku7-5.goal: Stabilise eighths, chord accompaniment and long forms at the repertoire’s written tempo.
ku7-5.text:
Tempo is a separate skill. A clean slow pass does not guarantee a fast one. Start at a secure tempo, increase in small steps and note the first specific unstable spot. Practise it briefly, then restore the context.

Set fingering before the tempo series. Begin arm movements for jumps while the last note still sounds. Playing louder is not a tempo aid.

u8-1.title: Form: return and contrast
u8-1.goal: Organise a longer statement from familiar motifs.
u8-1.text:
The model has four four-bar sections: A, varied A, contrasting B, returning A. Retained rhythm and motif opening make the return recognisable. Plan section boundaries before adding more notes.

Mark string changes at section boundaries. Play bass and melody separately through all sixteen bars before combining.

ku8-1.title: Form: return and contrast
ku8-1.goal: Organise a longer statement from familiar motifs.
ku8-1.text:
The model has four four-bar sections: A, varied A, contrasting B, returning A. Retained rhythm and motif opening make the return recognisable. Plan section boundaries before adding more notes.

Learn the left-hand bass as its own form. Know each section’s right-hand opening from memory; this supports recovery without replacing reading.

u8-2.title: Solo arrangement in three layers
u8-2.goal: Combine melody, figuration and bass into a playable arrangement.
u8-2.text:
Begin with a singable melody. Add bass, then inner voices only where hands and ears have room. A written rest is a musical choice. The example moves from two to three layers.

For each held note check which string remains free for the next. If two voices need the same string, change position or notate a deliberate release.

ku8-2.title: Solo arrangement in three layers
ku8-2.goal: Combine melody, figuration and bass into a playable arrangement.
ku8-2.text:
Begin with a singable melody. Add bass, then inner voices only where hands and ears have room. A written rest is a musical choice. The example moves from two to three layers.

Where practical, right 4/5 retain the top while 1/2/3 handle the middle. Do not force an octave stretch: revoice or omit an inner note and notate that decision.

u8-3.title: Carry a motif into another key
u8-3.goal: Transpose an idea by pitch relationships rather than shape memory.
u8-3.text:
E to A is a perfect fourth, five semitones upward. E–G–B becomes A–C–E while intervals and durations stay the same. Open strings and fingering still require a fresh check.

Open E bass becomes open A. Redistribute melody over G/C; do not treat an open note as a movable fret.

ku8-3.title: Carry a motif into another key
ku8-3.goal: Transpose an idea by pitch relationships rather than shape memory.
ku8-3.text:
E to A is a perfect fourth, five semitones upward. E–G–B becomes A–C–E while intervals and durations stay the same. Open strings and fingering still require a fresh check.

Right E4–G4–B4 becomes A4–C5–E5. Transpose left bass accordingly. Name pitches before placing the hands.

u8-4.title: Score, silence and D.C. al Fine
u8-4.goal: Create a readable score including a return and silence.
u8-4.text:
D.C. al Fine means return to the beginning and stop on reaching Fine again. Ignore Fine on the first visit. Here four sounding bars lead to two silent bars and the return: 1–2–3–4–5–6–1–2–3–4. In a multi-measure rest, the number above the rest bar gives the number of silent measures. Both bars remain written out here to check the counting.

Mute all strings through the silent bars while counting internally. Prepare the restart in time. Avoid creating an accidental count-in with string noise.

ku8-4.title: Score, silence and D.C. al Fine
ku8-4.goal: Create a readable score including a return and silence.
ku8-4.text:
D.C. al Fine means return to the beginning and stop on reaching Fine again. Ignore Fine on the first visit. Here four sounding bars lead to two silent bars and the return: 1–2–3–4–5–6–1–2–3–4. In a multi-measure rest, the number above the rest bar gives the number of silent measures. Both bars remain written out here to check the counting.

Release keys and pedal completely during silent bars. Prepare the next position quietly; long synth release must not obscure the written silence.

u8-5.title: A performance starts before the first note
u8-5.goal: Present a short form without trial starts.
u8-5.text:
Before starting, hear the tonic internally, choose tempo and know the first entry and ending. After an error keep pulse and aim for the next secure landmark. Practise starting mid-piece so every error does not force a restart.

Check tuning, set the intended level and prepare the opening shape. Play clean first, then with your tone at a comparable level.

ku8-5.title: A performance starts before the first note
ku8-5.goal: Present a short form without trial starts.
ku8-5.text:
Before starting, hear the tonic internally, choose tempo and know the first entry and ending. After an error keep pulse and aim for the next secure landmark. Practise starting mid-piece so every error does not force a restart.

At an unfamiliar piano briefly check register and pedal response. Choose a secure key and start with a simple bass-and-melody form without hunting for sounds.

u8-7.title: Self-sufficient guitar transitions
u8-7.goal: Connect harmonic, pedal, figure and chord without breaking flow.
u8-7.text:
A solo arrangement does not need every voice continuously. Transitions matter: a decaying note can prepare movement, a rest can articulate a texture change. Put every deliberate interruption in the score.

Play the E-string harmonic above fret twelve, then move to the low position. Use the written rest for travel. In the three-layer section hold the top string and mute inner voices selectively.

u8-6.title: Final project: an original solo piece
u8-6.goal: Read, shape and develop a complete notated form.
u8-6.text:
The 32-bar model combines motif, contrast, three layers, triplets and cadence. It is a working example, not a substitute for your own piece. Check four bars, then eight, then the whole form. Completion requires audible shaping and repeatable decisions.

Check bass muting, held melody, free strings for inner voices and position changes. Note essential finger/position cues; do not replace rhythm reading with tablature.

ku8-6.title: Final project: an original solo piece
ku8-6.goal: Read, shape and develop a complete notated form.
ku8-6.text:
The 32-bar model combines motif, contrast, three layers, triplets and cadence. It is a working example, not a substitute for your own piece. Check four bars, then eight, then the whole form. Completion requires audible shaping and repeatable decisions.

Check balance, readable hand positions and deliberate releases. Left plays a broken bass figure in the triplet section; prepare hands separately. Make at least one recording with piano-like decay; another may use your synth tone.

u2-pulse.title: Eighth-note power chords: pulse and hook
u2-pulse.goal: Play repeated eighths with chord changes, open accents and muting as a riff.
u2-pulse.text:
Eighth-note power chords also drive slow music. At ♩ = 70, two attacks together last one quarter; eight fill a 4/4 bar. Here the E5–G5 change and the answer on A5 create direction.

Start with alternate picking across exactly two strings. Then compare downstrokes at a tempo that keeps the hand relaxed. Use light palm muting on repeated attacks; marked accents and the ending may ring openly. This is a sound choice for this riff. Preview demonstrates pitches and rhythm; assess palm muting and pick direction on the instrument.

e2-pulse-1.title: Black Lantern · eighth-note riff
e2-pulse-1.instructions: Four bars A–B–A–C. Six E5 eighths lead to two G5 eighths; A5 answers the motif. Bar 3 returns, B5–A5–E5 closes. Play G5 on E fret 3/A fret 5. Sing the root motion, then play both strings. Start at 70, later 90 and 110 quarters per minute. Keep each chord change inside the same pulse.
checklist: Recognisable hook on its return?
Even eighths through changes; unused strings silent?
Audible accents and complete final rest?
e2-pulse-1.position: P4 · E/A and A/D strings · frets 0–5.

e2-pulse-2.title: Black Lantern · a gap in the answer
e2-pulse-2.instructions: In bar 2 an eighth rest replaces the first A5 attack. Play the written variant; mute both strings in the gap and enter on the “and” after 1. Keep the remaining attacks as in the original. Compare the delayed answer.
checklist: Unchanged bar length despite the gap?
Offbeat entry followed by steady eighths?

e2-pulse-3.title: Write an eighth-note riff
e2-pulse-3.instructions: Write eight bars using E5, G5 and A5: two hook, two answer, two return, two ending. Include eight consecutive eighths in one bar and a fully muted eighth rest in another. Change the final turn for the ending. Play and record the whole form; read it again on another day.
checklist: Hook recognisable from rhythm alone?
Changes and rests at the same pulse?
Form notated and read again?

u3-riff.title: Sixteenth-note power chords and gallop
u3-riff.goal: Control continuous sixteenths and eighth–sixteenth–sixteenth across two strings.
u3-riff.text:
A slow pulse can carry a dense riff: four sixteenths per quarter, hence 4 × 4 = 16 attacks per 4/4 bar. Alternate picking begins each quarter downwards. The eighth–sixteenth–sixteenth gallop also lasts one quarter: 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 1.

Mute unused strings and keep movements small. An accent changes loudness, not speed. Start with one quarter beat, then two bars, then the complete form. Chord changes and complete note endings belong to the task. Move from 50 to 60 and 72 after two clean passes; higher tempos follow in phase 7.

e3-riff-1.title: Iron Current · sixteenth-note riff
e3-riff-1.instructions: E5 drives bar 1; G5–A5 answers, then E5 returns. B5–E5 and the final rest close the phrase. Alternate pick across both strings, downstroke on the first sixteenth of each quarter. Sing the root path and ending first. Check with little gain, then your chosen sound.
checklist: Even sixteenths through the G5–A5 change?
Accents without rushing?
Longer ending and silent rest?

e3-riff-2.title: Iron Current · gallop
e3-riff-2.instructions: Play the written eighth–sixteenth–sixteenth version at the same quarter pulse. A continuous sixteenth motion gives down–down–up attacks; the free upstroke after the eighth misses the strings. Then compare down–up–down as a three-attack cycle: the next quarter begins upwards. Choose deliberately and retain the rhythm.
checklist: Long eighth lasts exactly two sixteenths?
Stable chord changes and next quarter entry?

e3-riff-3.title: Write a dense riff
e3-riff-3.instructions: Write eight bars: two sixteenth-note riff, two gallop answer, two return, two ending with a rest. Use E5, G5, A5 and B5. Include one bar of continuous sixteenths. Choose accents for the hook. Mark pick direction at a difficult change, record the complete form and read it again later.
checklist: Audible difference between motif and answer?
Precise muting and changes at unchanged tempo?
Notated, recorded and read again?

u4-strum.title: Strum chords and read rhythm charts
u4-strum.goal: Play rhythmic major/minor and seventh-chord changes; read rhythmic slashes and bar repeats.
u4-strum.text:
Chord symbols specify pitch content and harmony. Rhythmic slashes with stems specify attacks and durations; their height is not a pitch. A bar-repeat sign repeats the preceding bar. A slash inside a chord symbol, such as Gm/Bb, instead specifies a bass note.

This piece is in G minor with Bb and Eb. Three strings suffice for Gm and Eb; D7(no5) omits the fifth A and contains D, F# and C. The top line D–Bb–C–D belongs to the hook. P4 fingerings replace standard-tuning shapes while harmony and rhythm transfer. Place individual fingers first, then assess a partial barre where two notes share a fret. A full six-string barre is not required for these voicings.

e4-strum-1.title: Violet Gate · chord accompaniment
e4-strum-1.instructions: Eight bars: Gm opens twice, Eb–D7 answers, Gm returns, F–Gm closes. Read the written voicings. String/fret locations from low to high: Gm D5/G3/C2; Eb A6/D5/G3; D7(no5) A5/D4/G5; F D3/G2/C0. Numbers are frets. Strike only the three written strings. Begin with downstrokes, then alternate strum on a continuous eighth-note grid.
checklist: Major/minor and D7 understood from written pitches?
Chord changes without an extra pause?
Audible top line and phrase ending?

e4-strum-2.title: Violet Gate · rhythmic slashes
e4-strum-2.instructions: Play the same music from rhythm notation and chord symbols. Bar 2 repeats bar 1; bar 6 repeats bar 5. Reconstruct the voicings read earlier; preview plays these positions. Later choose other suitable voicings. Keep counting through every repeated bar and retain the final rest.
checklist: Bar repeats without losing a bar?
Rhythm read without written pitches?
Voicing deliberately chosen?

e4-strum-3.title: Write chord accompaniment
e4-strum-3.instructions: Write eight bars in G minor or another key. A hook returns and an answer leads to the ending. Use minor, major and a dominant seventh chord; include at least two changes within a bar. Write voicings first, then a second version with chord symbols, rhythmic slashes and a bar-repeat sign. Play and compare both versions.
checklist: Same harmony and rhythm from both notations?
Strings and position changes checked on the instrument?
Audible hook and ending?

ku5-comping.title: Left-hand chord pulses under a melody
ku5-comping.goal: Combine repeated left-hand chords with an independent right-hand melody; compare straight and swung rhythms.
ku5-comping.text:
Left-hand accompaniment can do more than hold bass notes. Here three chord tones play quarters while the right hand plays quarters, eighths and long notes. E7 omits its fifth B; the third G# and seventh D lead to Am.

Learn the left-hand progression alone with relaxed repeated attacks. Sing the right-hand E–A–G–E hook. Combine two bars first; retain the right-hand half note while the left hand strikes again. Start without pedal. In the swing comparison the left-hand quarters stay even. Preview uses 2:1; later refine by recordings and style.

ke5-comping-1.title: Night Relay · melody over chord pulses
ke5-comping-1.instructions: Eight bars Am–F–Dm–E7–Am–F–E7–Am. Left-hand quarter-note chords become halves at the ending. The two-bar right-hand hook returns; the answer rises to B and C–B–A closes. Read both clefs and sing the melody over accompaniment. Play left more quietly without interrupting right-hand halves at left-hand attacks.
checklist: Even, relaxed repeated left-hand chords?
Independent right-hand durations and loudness?
Audible hook, answer and ending?

ke5-comping-2.title: Night Relay · swing and offbeats
ke5-comping-2.instructions: Play the written swing version at the same quarter pulse; left-hand quarters remain straight. Then move left-hand attacks in bars 1–7 to all four “ands”, each preceded by an eighth rest and played as a short eighth. Write and play this variant: right hand unchanged, bar 8 still closes with halves.
checklist: Long–short right-hand eighths; left-hand quarters unchanged?
Offbeats without shifting the right-hand melody?
Chord endings controlled without pedal?

ke5-comping-3.title: Write melody and accompaniment
ke5-comping-3.instructions: Compose eight bars with a returning two-bar hook. Alternate left-hand quarter chords and offbeats; include right-hand halves and eighths. Give one bar a melody rest and another an accompaniment rest. Use a seventh chord and an audible ending. Notate both hands, choose fingerings and record the complete form.
checklist: Accompaniment supports rather than covers the melody?
Independent rests in each hand?
Notated, recorded and read again later?

ui.schedule:
A, B, C: 45 minutes guitar + 15 minutes keyboard each. D: 15 minutes guitar + 45 minutes keyboard. This gives 3 × 45 + 15 = 150 guitar minutes and 3 × 15 + 45 = 90 keyboard minutes.

**45 minutes:** 5 recall · 10 one difficulty · 20 listening, playing and varying · 5 recording · 5 break/log. **15 minutes:** 3 recall · 8 application · 4 recording/log.

Work on one unit per instrument. First task already secure → move to application. Resolve unfamiliar movements without time pressure, then stabilise with a click. Increase tempo only while pulse and tone remain controlled.

**Move on:** meet the criteria on two practice days, including one attempt without aids. Isolate a difficult passage, then return to a whole phrase. Notation is the main view, position is above it, and aids can be enabled.

**Theory:** read one unit per week, check the listening example against the album, hear the notated example in the preview. No tasks, no marking.
ui.hardware:
Choose a MIDI output connected to the synthesizer or another drum sound source. A DIN MIDI input requires a suitable MIDI interface; USB MIDI can connect directly when supported by the device.

Enable drum-note reception on channel 10. The mapping used here is kick 36, snare 38, closed hi-hat 42, click/rim 37. Check these note numbers against your sound source’s mapping. Set sound and level there.

The website sends individual notes, not MIDI clock or transport commands. Stop any device sequencer separately. Score preview independently uses FluidR3 GM in the browser.

ui.fretboardLegend: String 1 (F4) at the top, string 6 (E2) at the bottom. Orange = root, green = other pitches. 0 means open string. Intervals refer to the root: b3 is the minor third. B = German H; Bb = German B. Scroll wide fretboards horizontally.
ui.diagramScroll: ↔ Scroll wide maps sideways; keyboard arrow keys also work when focused.

ui.creditsText:
Sounds and the audio engine are served locally. FluidR3 GM contains the samples and instrument definitions. The selection retains the original sample data, envelopes and loop points.

Preview demonstrates pitch, rhythm and dynamics. It does not fully reproduce guitar techniques or synthesizer parameters. Progress and mix settings stay in your browser.
ui.repertoireRoutingLead: The four parts retain their MIDI channels. Choose separate outputs when needed. The default output also serves course drums.

book.title: Music theory
book.lead: Music theory for P4 guitar and keyboard. Doom, gothic, progressive and baroque supply listening examples and ideas for shaping music.
book.intro:
This book covers sound and notation, scales and modes, chords and harmony, rhythm, texture, timbre and form. The five references guide style and taste: My Dying Bride (*Turn Loose the Swans*), Type O Negative (*October Rust*), Anathema (*Eternity*), Vivaldi (*Le quattro stagioni*) and Biber (*Harmonia artificioso-ariosa*). They do not restrict keys, tempos, forms or playing techniques. Major keys, swing, fast chord attacks and other sound worlds remain available.

Examples use P4 guitar E2 A2 D3 G3 C4 F4 and a C2–C6 keyboard model. Definitions, historical conventions, physical models and compositional choices are distinguished. A model explains particular conditions; it is not a universal law of sound.

Each chapter introduces concepts through original notated examples and audio preview. Preview plays the written pitches; it does not simulate distortion, filters, physical playing technique or room acoustics. Style examples are original models, not transcriptions of the reference works. Summaries and appendices provide reference material.

c01-octaves.title: Four E’s: every octave doubles the frequency

c01-series.title: The overtone series on E2, partials 1–8

c01-harmonics.title: Harmonics of the low E string: partials 2 to 6 at sounding pitch

c01-ratios.title: Seven intervals over E3 as frequency ratios

c01-beating.title: Fifth and major third: pure and tempered size in cents

c01-difference.title: Three intervals over E4 and their difference tones

c01-register.title: The same minor third in three registers and its inversion to the sixth

c01.title: The tone
c01.text:
This chapter connects pitch, partials and distortion. Calculations use A4 = 440 Hz and equal temperament. Ideal strings and simple nonlinear models explain relationships; they do not establish fixed register or gain rules. The preview plays tempered notes and does not simulate measurements of beating or distortion.

## 1.1 Vibration and frequency

A musical tone usually has an approximately periodic vibration and a perceptible pitch. Frequency counts cycles per second, in hertz (Hz). With A4 = 440 Hz, MIDI note n has f = 440 × 2^((n − 69)/12): E2 (40) ≈ 82.4 Hz and C4 (60) ≈ 261.6 Hz. An octave has the ratio 2:1. Other intervals also have simple ratio models, such as the just fifth at 3:2; the octave is not the only musical interval grounded in physics.

[[c01-octaves]]

The example shows four E's with their frequencies: E2 of the low string (82.4 Hz), E3 (164.8), E4 (329.6) and E5 (659.3). Every step doubles. All the E's on the guitar are multiples of 41.2 Hz, the E1 of the bass.

Perceived loudness depends on level, frequency and duration, among other factors. Timbre involves the spectrum and its evolution over time, including attack and decay. An ideal sine contains one frequency; many instrumental tones contain several partials.

## 1.2 The overtone series

In the ideal string model, partial frequencies are integer multiples of the fundamental: f, 2f, 3f … The fundamental is the first partial; the first overtone is the second partial. Stiffness can make real strings depart from this model. Above E2 ≈ 82.4 Hz, the first eight partials are approximately 82.4, 164.8, 247.2, 329.6, 412.0, 494.4, 576.8 and 659.2 Hz. The written names E2, E3, B3, E4, G#4, B4, D5, E5 are tempered approximations.

[[c01-series]]

Counted from the bottom, the series therefore contains the octave, the fifth, the major third and a minor seventh. The distances shrink upward: octave, fifth, fourth, major third, minor third, then seconds. The fifth partial lies 14 cents below tempered G♯4, the seventh 31 cents below tempered D5; the preview plays the tempered pitches.

On the guitar the partials can be heard in isolation: a string touched lightly above the twelfth fret and plucked gives the second partial, above the seventh fret the third, above the fifth fret the fourth, above the fourth fret the fifth. These harmonics are not special tones but components of every ordinary string tone, exposed by the touch.

[[c01-harmonics]]

The example writes the sounding harmonic pitches with diamond heads. Touching near fret 12 permits the even partials; near fret 7, multiples of the third; near fret 5, multiples of the fourth. The lowest remaining partial becomes the harmonic’s pitch. Suitable nodes for the fifth and sixth partials lie near frets 3.86 and 3.16. Touching does not isolate a perfectly pure sine.

Many partials overlap in a just fifth, helping to explain its fusion. A power chord can remain clear under distortion; clarity also depends on tuning, muting, level and the signal chain. A tone with few overtones is a counterexample to the claim that every low single note sounds full by itself.

## 1.3 Intervals as ratios

Just intervals can be described by frequency ratios: octave 2:1, fifth 3:2, fourth 4:3, major third 5:4, minor third 6:5, major sixth 5:3, minor sixth 8:5. Shared partials can encourage fusion. Roughness and musical consonance do not follow solely from the size of these integers: spectrum, register, loudness, voice leading and listening habits also matter.

[[c01-ratios]]

The example compares seven tempered dyads above E3. The just ratios are a reference model; the preview does not realize them. Classical counterpoint treats a fourth above the bass differently from a fourth between upper voices (chapters 5 and 20).

Equal temperament, in which guitar and keyboard are tuned, divides the octave into twelve equal semitones; each semitone corresponds to the frequency ratio 2^(1/12) ≈ 1.0595. The pure ratios are slightly missed. The deviation is measured in cents, hundredths of a semitone: the tempered fifth is 2 cents smaller than the pure one (700 against 702 cents), the tempered major third 14 cents larger (400 against 386), the tempered minor third 16 cents smaller (300 against 316).

[[c01-beating]]

The preview repeats the same tempered interval; it is not an audible comparison of just and tempered tuning. Beating occurs between nearby frequency components. For E4–G#4, the fifth partial of E and the fourth of G# are separated: 5 × 329.63 ≈ 1648.15 Hz and 4 × 415.30 ≈ 1661.22 Hz, a difference of ≈ 13.1 Hz. Their strength depends on the spectrum. Comparing tempered G#4 with the just third at 1.25 × 329.63 ≈ 412.04 Hz instead gives about 3.3 Hz; that is a different comparison.

## 1.4 Timbre

Timbre depends on partial amplitudes and their evolution over time. In an ideal sawtooth, the nth partial’s amplitude falls as 1/n; a symmetrical square lacks even harmonics, and a triangle’s odd harmonics fall as 1/n². String stiffness stretches the partials. Plucking near the bridge changes their distribution. Chapter 24 connects these models to synthesis.

## 1.5 The distorted tone

Nonlinear distortion can generate new spectral components. For two sine tones, possible intermodulation products are |mf1 ± nf2| with integer m and n. Which appear and how strong they are depends on the transfer curve. An ideally symmetrical curve lacks even-order products, including f2 − f1. Combination tones can also arise in hearing without a distortion effect in the signal path.

[[c01-difference]]

The example adds separately struck approximation notes beneath three tempered intervals. E4–B4: 493.88 − 329.63 ≈ 164.26 Hz, near E3. E4–G#4: 415.30 − 329.63 ≈ 85.68 Hz, closer to F2 than E2. E4–G4: 392.00 − 329.63 ≈ 62.37 Hz, near B1; B2 is written here an octave higher to stay within the 49 keys. In just tuning, the major third’s difference tone would be E2. For the minor third, 2f1 − f2 ≈ 267.26 Hz is near C4. B and C both belong to E minor, although these frequencies differ from the tempered notes. The preview does not generate these products through distortion.

[[c01-register]]

The final example places E–G in three octaves and inverts E4–G4 to G4–E5: a minor third becomes a major sixth. Halving the input frequencies also halves possible combination-tone frequencies. This says nothing about their level. A difference component below the usual audible range is not automatically audible beating of the original tones.

The course starts low distorted accompaniments with few notes and fifths, then compares thirds in different registers at matched loudness. This is a learning strategy. A low interval on two separately distorted tracks can behave differently from the same interval entering one shared distortion effect. There is no fixed pitch above which thirds become permissible, nor a universal gain advantage for sixths.

## 1.6 Summary

- Frequency and pitch are related; an octave doubles frequency.
- The fundamental is partial 1; overtone 1 is partial 2.
- Natural harmonics suppress particular vibration modes.
- Ratios, spectrum and context contribute to consonance and roughness.
- Just and tempered intervals differ; the preview plays tempered pitches.
- Intermodulation products depend on the transfer curve, and their levels do not follow solely from register.
- Judge register and gain using the actual sound.

c02-clefs.title: Middle C in both clefs, with the clef tones G4 and F3

c02-lines.title: Lines and spaces in the treble and the bass clef

c02-octnum.title: The five C’s of the keyboard: octave numbers

c02-strings.title: The open strings in standard tuning and in P4, at sounding pitch

c02-transposed.title: The low E string: written E3, sounding E2

c02-keysig.title: E Aeolian with key signature, E harmonic minor with accidentals

c02-enharm.title: Enharmonics: D♯ strives upward, E♭ strives downward

c02.title: Pitch notation
c02.text:
Notation is a coordinate script: height on the page is pitch, width is time. This chapter treats height, the next one time. Whoever already reads music will find here the rules that are usually applied tacitly in practice: octave numbers, transposed notation, scope of accidentals, enharmonics.

## 2.1 Staff and clef

Tones are written on five lines and in four spaces; higher tones sit higher. Which pitch a line means is fixed by the clef. The treble clef (G clef) curls around the second line from the bottom and makes it G4. The bass clef (F clef) places its two dots around the fourth line and makes it F3. Middle C4 lies between both staves on a ledger line: below the treble staff, above the bass staff.

[[c02-clefs]]

The example shows the same tone C4 first in the upper, then in the lower staff, each on its ledger line, and then the two clef tones: G4 on the line the treble clef curls around, F3 on the line between the dots of the bass clef. Whoever knows these three tones securely can count out every other.

[[c02-lines]]

The treble staff’s lines from bottom to top are E4 G4 B4 D5 F5 and its spaces F4 A4 C5 E5. The bass staff’s lines are G2 B2 D3 F3 A3 and its spaces A2 C3 E3 G3. The lowest lines G2 and E4 are 21 semitones apart: an octave plus a major sixth. E3 in the third bass space is an octave below E4.

Notes outside the staff use ledger lines. Sounding E2 lies on the seventh ledger line below the treble staff. Guitar notation writes it an octave higher as E3, in the space immediately below the third ledger line. Octave transposition reduces the number of ledger lines.

## 2.2 Octave numbers

Every C begins a new octave, and the octaves are numbered: C4 is middle C, C5 lies an octave above, C3 below. A tone keeps its octave number up to the next C: B3 lies immediately below C4. In the MIDI standard C4 is note 60; some instrument displays count differently, which does not change the pitch.

[[c02-octnum]]

The example shows the five C's of the 49-key keyboard: C2 on the second ledger line below the bass staff, C3 in the second space, C4 on the ledger line between the staves, C5 in the third space of the treble staff, C6 on the second ledger line above it. The range of the P4 guitar runs from E2 to F4 on open strings and up to about C6 in high positions; the keyboard runs from C2 to C6; the four-string bass from E1 to about G4.

## 2.3 Transposed notation

Guitar and bass are written an octave higher than they sound. A tone written as E3 in the treble staff sounds E2. This keeps the notes within the staff without constant ledger lines. The guitar's treble clef carries a small 8 beneath its curl; in many prints it is omitted. Every statement in this book about register means the sounding tone.

[[c02-transposed]]

The example shows E3 in the treble staff and E2 in the bass staff. The preview actually plays them an octave apart. When comparing written guitar pitch with sounding pitch, read the first representation mentally an octave lower. Course notation explicitly uses the octave-transposing guitar clef.

[[c02-strings]]

The open strings at sounding pitch: the first four strings E2 A2 D3 G3 are the same in standard tuning and in P4. Standard tuning puts B3 and E4 above them, P4 puts C4 and F4. The difference is a semitone on the two high strings; what it means for fingerings and intervals is shown in chapters 5 and 7.

## 2.4 Key signatures and accidentals

A sharp (♯) raises the tone by a semitone, a flat (♭) lowers it, a natural (♮) cancels either. Double sharp and double flat change by two semitones. Signs placed at the beginning of every staff form the key signature; they apply to the letter in question in all octaves until the signature changes. Signs before a single note are accidentals; they apply to that pitch in that octave up to the barline.

[[c02-keysig]]

The key signature of E minor is one sharp, F♯. In the first bars the scale is played with this F♯ without any sign before the note. From bar 3 D♯ appears as an accidental because it does not belong to the signature: E harmonic minor (chapter 6).

[[c02-accrule]]

The example shows the scope rule in detail. Bar 1: D♯ with a sharp, then D without a sharp needs a natural because the sharp would hold until the barline. Bar 2: the D♯ at the end is tied to the D♯ in the next bar; the tie carries the raising across the barline without it being repeated. Bar 4: after the barline D counts as the natural tone again and needs no sign; many prints place a natural there in parentheses as a reminder.

## 2.5 Enharmonics

G# and Ab designate the same pitch in equal temperament but different note names. Spelling follows key, interval and harmonic function. Sharps ascending and flats descending are one convention for chromatic lines. Counterexample: G# remains the third of E major even when the melody descends to F#.

[[c02-enharm]]

In the first bar the line B–C♯–D♯ leads upward to E; the sharps show the direction. In the second bar it falls E–E♭–D to B; the flat shows the direction. E♭ and D♯ are the same key but different tones in writing, and a reader hears the direction before playing. In E major G♯ is the third; in E minor there is no G♯, and an A♭ would be a foreign tone there with its own meaning. The chromatic bass E–E♭–D–D♭–C–B (chapter 16) is therefore written with flats, the leading tone D♯ with a sharp.

## 2.6 Note names

This book uses international naming: B is the tone called H in German, B♭ the tone called B in German. The seven natural tones are C D E F G A B. Semitones lie between E and F and between B and C; all other neighbours are whole tones. On the keyboard these are the places where two white keys follow each other without a black key between.

## 2.7 Summary

- A clef names a line: G4 in treble, F3 in bass.
- Octave numbers change at C; B3 lies immediately below C4.
- Guitar and bass are written an octave above their sounding pitches.
- Key signatures apply in all octaves; accidentals apply in their octave until the barline.
- A tie continues the same pitch without a new attack.
- Enharmonic spelling follows musical context.
- International B is German H; Bb is German B.

c02b-strings.title: The six open strings of the P4 guitar in guitar notation, with string number and note name

c02b-c4.title: The same C4 in five places: string and fret

c02b-unison.title: One tone on three strings: every lower string needs five frets more

c02b-octaves.title: Four octaves of E: two strings up and two frets up is the octave

c02b-positions.title: The same scale in first and in seventh position: same tones, other strings and frets

c02b-reading.title: Bass on the low strings, melody on the high ones: one position, four bars

c02b-keys49.title: The 49 keys from C2 to C6: middle C4 is the 25th key

c02b-hands.title: Left hand below C4, right hand above: the division of the 49 keys

c02b.title: Fretboard and keyboard: where the tones lie
c02b.text:
Reading notation becomes useful only when every note has a place on the instrument. This chapter answers the practical questions: which string is E2, where C4 lies, where to finger a note that the guitar has in several places, and with which C a 49-key keyboard begins. It builds on chapter 2 and supplies the basis for the scale patterns in chapter 9.

## 3.1 The six strings

The strings are counted from the highest to the lowest: string 1 is the thinnest, string 6 the thickest. In P4 tuning the open strings sound F4 (1), C4 (2), G3 (3), D3 (4), A2 (5) and E2 (6). The low E string is therefore E2, the same pitch as the lowest E key of the keyboard, and the four low strings E2 A2 D3 G3 are identical with standard tuning (chapter 8). Every fret raises by a semitone; the twelfth fret is the octave of the open string, the fifth fret of a string sounds like the next higher open string.

[[c02b-strings]]

The example is in guitar notation: the treble clef carries an 8, and everything sounds an octave lower than written (chapter 2). The number in the circle is the string, the letter beneath the note name. Examples explicitly notated for guitar follow this notation; note names with octave numbers in the text always mean the sounding tone.

## 3.2 Where C4 lies

On the keyboard every tone has exactly one key. On the guitar almost every tone has several places because the strings overlap: the open string 2 is C4, and the same C4 lies on string 3 at the fifth fret, on string 4 at the tenth, on string 5 at the fifteenth and on string 6 at the twentieth.

[[c02b-c4]]

Figures beneath the notes are frets. On the next lower string the same pitch lies five frets higher: 5 semitones of string spacing are offset by 5 frets. This holds between all adjacent P4 strings. Without retuning or pitch effects the lowest pitch is E2. On the high F4 string, C6 is at fret 19: 65 + 19 = MIDI 84. Fret 20 gives C#6.

[[c02b-unison]]

The example shows E3 on strings 4, 5 and 6 and A3 on strings 3, 4 and 5: frets 2, 7 and 12 in each case. Pitch stays the same. Timbre and decay can differ with string gauge, vibrating length and attack; this does not imply a fixed ranking of sustain lengths.

## 3.3 The geometry of the fretboard

Because all string distances are equal, the P4 fretboard is symmetrical: every figure can be moved to any pair of strings and keeps its intervals. Three rules suffice to find one's way everywhere. First: the same tone one string lower lies five frets higher. Second: the octave lies two strings higher and two frets higher (twice five plus two is twelve). Third: the fifth lies one string higher and two frets higher, the fourth one string higher at the same fret (chapter 5).

[[c02b-octaves]]

The octaves are E2 on open string 6, E3 on string 4 fret 2, E4 on string 2 fret 4 and E5 on string 1 fret 11. Two strings plus two frets give 5 + 5 + 2 = 12 semitones. For the final jump only one higher string remains: 5 + 7 = 12, hence seven frets higher.

A position is named after the index-finger fret. A comfortable basic window often spans four frets; extensions and shifts enlarge it. Four frets across six strings give 6 × 4 = 24 positions. The lowest and highest positions span 5 × 5 + 3 = 28 semitones: two octaves and a major third. The window is not a complete chromatic range; one pitch is missing between each adjacent string window.

## 3.4 Reading and fingering

Choose a fingering path for the whole phrase. Avoid unnecessary shifts and prepare necessary ones during a rest or a sufficiently long note. A low position with open strings may be convenient; a higher position may better suit timbre or articulation. Simultaneous bass and melody need separate strings. A long note must not be cut short by the next fingering on the same string.

[[c02b-positions]]

The example plays the same scale E3 to E4 twice: first in first position with frets up to 4, then in seventh position with frets 7 to 10. The tones are identical; the strings and frets differ, and the sound of the second version is thicker because it lies on lower strings. In this book the position stands above the bars, the string in a circle above the note, and where it helps orientation, the fret beneath.

[[c02b-reading]]

Here the bass uses open string 6 and string 5 at fret 3 (C3) and fret 2 (B2). The melody uses strings 3 and 2 up to fret 4. No simultaneous voices require the same string. This is essential for independent durations; fretted notes must also be reachable together.

## 3.5 The keyboard

Here we use a synthesizer with 49 keys in the sounding range C2–C6. Four octaves contain 4 × 12 = 48 semitone steps; including both endpoints gives 49 keys. C4 lies 24 steps above C2, hence at key 25. Octave switches and transposition can shift the sounding range; device labels may differ from the MIDI convention C4 = 60 used here.

[[c02b-keys49]]

Orientation on the keyboard comes from the black keys, which stand in groups of two and three: C is the white key left of the group of two, F the white key left of the group of three. Every tone has exactly one key; G♯ and A♭ are the same black key (chapter 2).

[[c02b-chromatic]]

The twelve tones of an octave: the seven natural tones lie on the white keys, the five tones with sharp or flat on the black ones, between C and D, D and E, F and G, G and A, A and B. Between E and F and between B and C there is no black key; there the semitone lies between two white keys (chapter 2).

## 3.6 Hands and registers

As a starting point, the left hand plays bass and the right melody. C4 is a reference, not a boundary for the hands: either can cross it, exchange voices or share a chord. Notation shows the roles; hand assignment follows reach and voice leading.

[[c02b-hands]]

The example distributes Em across registers. Synthesizer C2 lies four semitones below guitar E2: MIDI 40 − 36 = 4. Without transposition this keyboard ends at C6; it has no keys above that. A 24-fret P4 guitar reaches F6 because F4 + 24 semitones = F6. Its actual upper limit depends on fret count. Both instruments are constrained by hand span and polyphony.

## 3.7 Summary

- P4 low to high: E2 A2 D3 G3 C4 F4. String 6 is low E.
- The same pitch lies five frets higher on the next lower string.
- Octave: two strings and two frets up, or one string and seven frets up.
- Four frets across six strings: 24 positions spanning 28 semitones, not a complete chromatic range.
- Our 49-key range is C2–C6; C4 is key 25.
- Hands and positions follow the phrase. Independent simultaneous guitar voices need separate strings.
