c03.title: Notation of time
c03.text:
Notation orders time in two ways: by note values, which set durations in proportion to each other, and by bars, which divide the durations into equally long sections with a weighting. Both are relative; only the tempo turns them into seconds. This chapter introduces the signs and explains for each example how to count it.

## 4.1 Note values and rests

The duration of a tone is shown by the shape of the note: whole (open head without stem), half (open head with stem), quarter (filled head with stem), eighth (one flag or beam), sixteenth (two), thirty-second (three). Each level halves the previous one. Every value has a rest of the same duration.

[[c03-values]]

The example shows on one tone: quarters; an eighth pair, a quarter and a half; a dotted quarter with an eighth; eighths with eighth rests; four sixteenths; and finally a half tied across the barline to a whole. Counting uses syllables: quarters 1 2 3 4, eighths 1 and 2 and, sixteenths 1 e and a.

[[c03-rests]]

The rests: the whole rest hangs below the fourth line and also denotes an entire empty bar in any meter; the half rest sits on the third line; the quarter rest is the jagged sign; the eighth rest has one flag, the sixteenth rest two. The bass holds through all four bars so that the rests of the upper voice are heard as rests of a voice, not as silence.

## 4.2 Dots and ties

A dot after the note lengthens it by half its value: a dotted half lasts three quarters, a dotted quarter three eighths. A second dot adds a further quarter of the value. A tie joins two notes of the same pitch into one duration; the second is not struck again. It is the only means of carrying a duration across the barline. A slur looks similar but joins different pitches and says nothing about duration, only about legato in performance.

[[c03-dots]]

Bar 1: dotted half and quarter, three plus one. Bar 2: twice dotted quarter and eighth, the rhythm of the long riff. Bars 3 and 4: a quarter, then a dotted half tied across the barline to a whole, seven quarters as one duration. Bars 5 and 6: a half, then a half tied across the barline to a further half, finally a half on G. The tie across the barline is the normal form of the long tones of this music; a tone that holds for two bars is written as two tied wholes.

## 4.3 Bar and meter

The time signature gives the number and note value of units in a measure: 4/4 contains four quarters, 3/4 three, and 12/8 twelve eighths. These units are not always the counted beats. In 12/8, four dotted quarters are usually counted. Metrical weight and performed accent differ: a backbeat can emphasize the metrically weaker beats 2 and 4.

[[c03-meters]]

In three-four time the one carries the weight, and the return of the one after three beats gives the swing of the dance: sarabande, minuet, waltz. The example sets the bass on every one and lets the melody place a half note on the one in bars 2 and 3, so that the weight becomes audible.

Meters with 8 as denominator group eighths: 6/8, 9/8 and 12/8 are compound meters in which the eighths arrange themselves in threes; the felt beat is the dotted quarter, and 12/8 has four such beats.

[[c03-compound]]

The example shows 12/8 in three layers: first the twelve eighths, beamed in four groups of three, then two bars in dotted quarters, four per bar, which one feels as beats, finally two dotted halves that divide the bar into two halves. All three layers are the same bar. 5/8 and 7/8 arrange their eighths unequally, usually 2+3 and 2+2+3 or 3+2+2; the felt beat alternates between quarter and dotted quarter. Chapter 17 treats how these meters sound.

## 4.4 Beams, grouping, syncopation

Beams connect short notes and clarify grouping. Here we group by quarters in 4/4, by groups of three in 12/8, and by the specified divisions in 7/8. Other beaming is possible, including eighths grouped across half a measure. The rhythm must remain clearly readable; a beam extending across a beat is not automatically wrong.

[[c03-sync]]

A syncopation is an accent between the beats: the tone begins on an eighth after the beat and holds across the next beat. Bar 1 shows the straight rhythm, bar 2 the syncopation in its usual spelling, eighth, quarter, quarter, quarter, eighth. Bar 3 writes the same syncopation with ties so that every beat remains visible; strict engravers prefer this form as soon as the rhythm becomes more complicated. Both bars sound the same.

## 4.5 Triplets

A triplet divides a value into three instead of two. The figure 3 above the group indicates it; the three notes together last as long as two of their value.

[[c03-triplet]]

Bar 1 has eight straight eighths, two per beat. Bar 2 has eighth triplets on the first two beats, three per beat. Bar 3 has a quarter triplet: three quarters in the time of two, that is, across the first half of the bar. The triplet is the bridge between 4/4 and 12/8: a 4/4 bar in which every beat is divided in triplets sounds like 12/8 (chapter 17).

## 4.6 Tempo

Tempo is given as the number of beats per minute, together with the note value that is counted: ♩ = 60 means sixty quarters per minute, one quarter per second. In compound meters the dotted quarter is given (♩. = 50), in 5/8 and 7/8 the eighth (♪ = 120). The same number with different note values yields three different speeds. The Italian tempo words (Largo, Adagio, Andante, Allegro, Presto) denote ranges and characters; Vivaldi's movements carry them, the metal albums do not. Chapter 18 treats tempo as a musical device.

## 4.7 Repeat and navigation signs

A section between repeat signs (double bar with two dots) is played twice. If the endings differ they stand under brackets: on the first pass the first ending applies, on the second the second.

[[c03-repeat]]

D.C. (da capo) demands a return to the beginning, D.S. (dal segno) to the sign 𝄋. After the return, "al Fine" leads to the word Fine, "al Coda" to the sign 𝄌 and from there into the coda. On the first pass Fine and the coda jump are ignored.

[[c03-dscoda]]

The example writes the first bar out as a count-in; the melody begins on the fourth beat as an upbeat to the second bar. In printed music an upbeat is usually written short: the first bar contains only the upbeat, and the missing beats are balanced at the end. Both spellings denote the same music.

[[c03-dcfine]]

Here D.C. al Fine leads back to the beginning, and the piece ends on the second pass at the word Fine, not at the last written bar. Navigation signs are the shorthand of form (chapter 27): they save paper and at the same time show which sections are identical.

## 4.8 Signs for performance and technique

An accent (>) demands a stronger attack, a dot above or below the note (staccato) a shortened tone, a line a sustained one. Dynamics are given with letters: pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff; hairpins show growth and decrease. For guitar there are in addition: the curve with an arrow for bending the string (chapter 23), the diamond notehead for harmonics, the slur for hammer-on and pull-off.

[[c03-articulation]]

Bar 1: accents on the first and third beats. Bar 2: staccato, every quarter sounds about half as long. Bar 3: slurs over eighth pairs, played on the guitar as hammer-ons. Bar 4: a bend from D4 up a whole tone to E4, then E4 as a harmonic. These signs say how a tone begins and ends; the note values only say when.

## 4.9 Summary

- Each successive note value halves the duration; each has its rest.
- A dot adds half the value. Ties connect equal pitches without a new attack.
- Time signatures count note units; a perceived beat can comprise several units.
- 6/8, 9/8 and 12/8 normally group three eighths per beat.
- Beams should make the chosen grouping readable.
- Syncopations displace accents; triplets divide the duration of two equal notes into three.
- Tempo specifies a number and note value: ♩ = 60 means one quarter per second.
- Repeat and navigation signs describe the performed form.

c04.title: Intervals
c04.text:
Intervals are the vocabulary from which scales, chords and voice leading are built. This chapter gives them names and sizes, shows inversion, orders them by consonance and anchors each to a sound one knows. Chapter 1 treated the physical side; here the musical one.

## 5.1 Counting and names

An interval is the distance between two tones. Its name counts the natural tones from the lower to the upper tone including both: E–F is a second, E–G a third, E–A a fourth, E–B a fifth, E–C a sixth, E–D a seventh, E–E an octave. The same tone with itself is the unison. The counting ignores accidentals: E–G and E–G♯ are both thirds, but of different sizes.

[[c04-names]]

The example plays the eight intervals from E as melodic steps in E minor: E–E, E–F♯, E–G, E–A, E–B, E–C, E–D, E–E. One counts the letters: for E–B they are E F G A B, five, hence a fifth. Heard melodically an interval is a step or a leap; seconds are steps, everything larger is a leap.

## 5.2 Sizes

The size of an interval is measured in semitones. Seconds, thirds, sixths and sevenths occur in two basic sizes, minor and major; unison, fourth, fifth and octave in one, perfect. Minor second 1 semitone, major second 2, minor third 3, major third 4, perfect fourth 5, perfect fifth 7, minor sixth 8, major sixth 9, minor seventh 10, major seventh 11, octave 12. Between fourth and fifth lies the tritone with 6 semitones.

[[c04-twelve]]

The example lays out the twelve intervals over E4 in rising size, each as a dyad. Heard in succession, the sound opens increasingly from the second to the octave; the small intervals rub, the large ones carry.

[[c04-sizes]]

Minor and major lie a semitone apart: E–G is the minor third, E–G♯ the major; E–C the minor sixth, E–C♯ the major; E–F the minor second, E–F♯ the major; E–D the minor seventh, E–D♯ the major. The semitone decides between minor and major (chapter 6), between suspension and resolution (chapter 14) and how much gain an interval tolerates (chapter 1).

In general: a major or perfect interval enlarged by a semitone is augmented, a minor or perfect one reduced by a semitone is diminished.

[[c04-augdim]]

B3–F4 is a diminished fifth: B C D E F counts five letter names, and MIDI 65 − 59 = 6 semitones. B3–E#4 is an augmented fourth using the same keys but four letter names. C4–D#4 and C4–Eb4 both span three semitones, but are an augmented second and a minor third. D#4–C5 is a diminished seventh; enharmonically, Eb4–C5 is a major sixth. Both span MIDI 72 − 63 = 9 semitones.

## 5.3 Inversion

If the lower tone is moved up an octave, the inversion of the interval results. The numbers add up to nine: a second becomes a seventh, a third a sixth, a fourth a fifth. The sizes swap: minor becomes major, augmented becomes diminished, perfect stays perfect. The semitones add up to twelve: minor third (3) and major sixth (9), perfect fourth (5) and perfect fifth (7).

[[c04-inversion]]

Each bar shows an interval and its inversion: E–G becomes G–E, minor third becomes major sixth; E–A becomes A–E, fourth becomes fifth; E–B becomes B–E, fifth becomes fourth; E–F♯ becomes F♯–E, major second becomes minor seventh. This complementarity is why the guitar strings are tuned in fourths and the bass in fourths although harmony thinks in fifths: a fourth upward reaches the same letter as a fifth downward (chapter 8).

## 5.4 Compound intervals

Intervals beyond the octave are called compound: ninth (second plus octave), tenth (third plus octave), eleventh (fourth plus octave), twelfth (fifth plus octave). For harmony they count like their simple forms; for sound they do not: a tenth is more open than a third.

[[c04-compound]]

The example compares simple intervals with their compound forms. E3–G4 is a minor tenth: a minor third plus an octave, 3 + 12 = 15 semitones. Wider spacing can help separate voices. Whether distortion products are disruptive depends on the signal chain, not solely on the interval name.

## 5.5 Consonance and dissonance

In the classical contrapuntal model, unisons, octaves and fifths are perfect consonances, while thirds and sixths are imperfect consonances. Seconds, sevenths and tritones are treated as dissonances. A fourth above the bass is normally treated as a dissonance, while one between upper voices can be consonant. These categories describe a compositional practice; a rock sus chord need not resolve because of them.

[[c04-consonance]]

The example compares intervals treated as consonant and dissonant in this practice. Dissonances can appear as passing tones, suspensions or independent colors. Preparation and resolution are required in particular contrapuntal models, not in every kind of music.

Under distortion, level and spectrum can alter roughness. No single interval works under all conditions. Classical consonance rules and the sound choices of a distorted arrangement answer different questions.

## 5.6 Intervals on the fingerboard and the keyboard

In P4 tuning, interval shapes retain their relationships when moved to other string pairs, within the available strings and frets. The same interval has multiple shapes. On adjacent strings: same fret = fourth (5 semitones), upper string two frets higher = fifth (5 + 2 = 7), two frets lower = minor third (5 − 2 = 3), one fret lower = major third (5 − 1 = 4). Two strings and two frets higher give the octave (5 + 5 + 2 = 12).

[[c04-shapes]]

The example plays the fifth on all five string pairs with the lower string open: E2–B2, A2–E3, D3–A3, G3–D4, C4–G4. On the P4 guitar this is one and the same shape, second fret of the upper string. In standard tuning the shape changes at the transition to the B string because a semitone is missing there: the fifth above G3 would lie at the third fret. This geometry is the reason for P4 tuning.

On the keyboard one counts keys, black ones included: E–F is one key, E–F♯ two, E–G three. The white keys alone form the natural tones; where two white keys follow each other without a black one (E–F, B–C) lies the semitone.

## 5.7 Hearing intervals

Every interval can be anchored to a familiar sound, best of all to material from one's own repertoire.

[[c04-anchors]]

E–G anchors the minor third in the Em triad, E–B the perfect fifth in a power chord, F–E the minor second in a possible Phrygian closing gesture, and E–C# the major sixth in E Dorian. B7 contains B D# F# A; its tritone is D#–A, six semitones. It can resolve to E–G. B–F is a different tritone and does not belong to B7.

## 5.8 Summary

- The name counts natural tones, the size counts semitones; both belong together.
- Second, third, sixth, seventh are minor or major; unison, fourth, fifth, octave are perfect.
- Augmented is a semitone larger than major or perfect, diminished a semitone smaller than minor or perfect.
- Inversion: numbers add to nine, semitones to twelve, minor becomes major, perfect stays perfect.
- Compound intervals count harmonically like simple ones but sound more open.
- Perfect: unison, fifth, octave. Imperfect: thirds, sixths. Dissonant: seconds, sevenths, tritone.
- In P4 tuning interval shapes retain their relationships when shifted; the fifth lies two frets higher on the next string.
- Every interval needs an anchor in the repertoire.

c05.title: Major, minor and the keys
c05.text:
Scales order the tone stock of a piece, keys give it a centre. This chapter introduces major and the three forms of minor, explains key signatures and the circle of fifths and shows how keys are related. At the end stands the question of what makes a key audible when no cadence confirms it; for the repertoire of this book it is the most important one.

## 6.1 The major scale

A scale is a sequence of tones within an octave, ordered by pitch. The major scale has seven degrees with the intervals whole tone, whole tone, semitone, whole tone, whole tone, whole tone, semitone (2-2-1-2-2-2-1). On C this gives the white keys C D E F G A B C. The semitones lie between the third and fourth and between the seventh and eighth degrees. The seventh degree is called the leading tone because it lies a semitone below the tonic and leads to it.

[[c05-major]]

The example plays the major scale on C and then on E. The pattern of intervals is the same; on E it needs four sharps (F♯ C♯ G♯ D♯) so that the semitones fall in the same places, between G♯ and A and between D♯ and E. On the P4 guitar this is one and the same fingering shifted by four frets; on the keyboard the picture of the black keys changes.

The degrees have names: tonic (1), supertonic (2), mediant (3), subdominant (4), dominant (5), submediant (6), leading tone (7). Tonic, subdominant and dominant are the primary degrees; the harmony of chapter 13 rests on them.

[[c05-degrees]]

In the E minor example, E, A and B represent tonic, subdominant and dominant. In pitch-class terms, A is a fifth below E and B a fifth above. The three lowest open guitar strings are instead E, A and D: the string chain is not the same sequence as the primary scale degrees.

## 6.2 The minor scales

Natural minor has the intervals 2-1-2-2-1-2-2; on A it gives the white keys A B C D E F G A, on E the tones E F♯ G A B C D E. It contains no leading tone: the seventh degree lies a whole tone below the tonic. So that a dominant with a leading tone can arise, the seventh degree is raised by a semitone. That gives harmonic minor: E F♯ G A B C D♯ E. Between the sixth and seventh degrees an augmented second arises (C–D♯, three semitones), which sounds awkward in a melody.

Melodic minor raises the sixth degree as well and smooths the path to the leading tone: E F♯ G A B C♯ D♯ E ascending. Descending, where no leading tone is needed, one traditionally returns to natural minor.

[[c05-minor3]]

The example shows the three forms in turn over an E pedal, then an application: over Am the melody rises with C♯ and D♯ to the dominant B7; after the return to Em it falls with D and C.

[[c05-augsec]]

Measure 1 gives B–C–D#–E with the augmented second C–D#; measure 2 gives B–C#–D#–E as a smoother ascent; measure 3 gives E–D–C–B. These are comparison models. In minor, degrees six and seven can be raised or lowered according to harmony and melodic motion, independently of direction. Counterexample: E–D#–C–B can use harmonic minor while descending. Jazz frequently uses the raised form in both directions as melodic minor.

## 6.3 Key signatures and the circle of fifths

Every major scale except C major needs accidentals. Starting a fifth higher adds a sharp: G major has F♯, D major F♯ and C♯, A major F♯ C♯ G♯, E major four sharps. Starting a fifth lower adds a flat: F major has B♭, B♭ major B♭ and E♭. The sharps appear in the order F C G D A E B, the flats in the order B E A D G C F.

[[c05-circle]]

The example walks the circle as a tone sequence: C, G, D, A, E, B in fifths upward, each step one sharp more; then from C, F, B♭, E♭, A♭ in fourths upward, each step one flat more. Arranging the keys in a circle this way gives the circle of fifths; after twelve steps it closes, F♯ major and G♭ major coinciding enharmonically. Two rules for reading: the last sharp of the signature lies a semitone below the major tonic. The second-to-last flat is the major tonic.

## 6.4 Relative and parallel keys

Every major key has a minor key with the same signature, its relative minor: it begins a minor third lower. G major and E minor share the F♯, C major and A minor have no accidentals, F major and D minor share the B♭.

[[c05-relative]]

Both scales of the example carry one sharp; they consist of the same seven tones and differ only in which tone counts as the centre. A piece in E minor that lingers on G sounds for moments like G major without changing the signature; that is the most common brightening effect in minor and the basis of the mediant harmony in chapter 13.

The parallel key has the same tonic with the other mode: E major and E minor. Three accidentals lie between them because third, sixth and seventh change.

[[c05-parallel]]

The example sets the E major triad, broken and as a chord, beside the E minor triad. One tone, G♯ or G, decides the mode. Chapter 10 treats the triad; here the observation suffices that major and minor on the same root are closer to each other than they are on paper: the Picardy third (chapter 13) uses exactly this closeness.

The three centres of this book, E, A and D, sit next to each other in the circle of fifths: E minor (one sharp), A minor (none), D minor (one flat). Their parallel majors E, A and D have four, three and two sharps. Changes between neighbouring keys are soft because they share almost all tones; changes across several steps are hard. Chapter 15 treats these routes as modulation.

## 6.5 The key as sound

A key is more than its signature. It becomes audible when one tone appears as the centre: through duration, recurrence, low register and closing position. A piece in E minor can linger long on C or D without leaving the key as long as E remains the reference to which everything returns.

[[c05-pedal]]

The example holds E in the bass while the melody moves through E Aeolian. The pedal supports E as the center. One bass note does not establish a key: an E pedal with F, G and C can suggest E Phrygian, for example. Melody, harmony, duration and closure must be heard together.

## 6.6 Summary

- Major: 2–2–1–2–2–2–1; natural minor: 2–1–2–2–1–2–2.
- Harmonic minor raises degree 7; ascending melodic minor also raises degree 6.
- Harmony and melodic motion determine variants in actual music, rather than an automatic ascending/descending rule.
- Sharps: F C G D A E B; flats: B E A D G C F. The penultimate-flat rule does not yet apply to F major with its single flat.
- Relative keys share a signature; parallel keys share a tonic.
- E, A and D minor are neighbors on the circle of fifths. The effect of a change depends on its connection.
- A pedal supports a center; it does not determine the key alone.

c06.title: Modes, pentatonic, chromaticism
c06.text:
This chapter introduces the seven diatonic modes, pentatonic scales and chromaticism. A mode combines a pitch collection with an audible center. Modality and functional harmony can interact within the same piece; a genre label does not determine their use.

## 7.1 The seven modes

The white keys contain seven scales, depending on which tone counts as the root: C Ionian (the major scale), D Dorian, E Phrygian, F Lydian, G Mixolydian, A Aeolian (natural minor), B Locrian. All seven consist of the same tones; they differ in the position of the two semitones relative to the root. The names have a long history; the modern seven-mode ordering is not identical to the medieval system of final and ambitus.

The intervals: Ionian 2-2-1-2-2-2-1, Dorian 2-1-2-2-2-1-2, Phrygian 1-2-2-2-1-2-2, Lydian 2-2-2-1-2-2-1, Mixolydian 2-2-1-2-2-1-2, Aeolian 2-1-2-2-1-2-2, Locrian 1-2-2-1-2-2-2. Every mode can be transposed to any root. Over E: E Ionian is E major with four sharps, E Aeolian is E minor with one, E Phrygian has no accidentals, E Lydian has five sharps.

## 7.2 Characteristic tones and brightness

For a shared tonic, a brightness ordering is possible: lydian, ionian, mixolydian, dorian, aeolian, phrygian, locrian. Each step lowers one pitch. “Bright” and “dark” are comparative images, not guaranteed emotions. Characteristic degrees require a reference mode: lydian has ♯4 against major, mixolydian ♭7 against major, dorian a major 6 against natural minor, phrygian ♭2 against natural minor. The pitch just lowered in the ordering is therefore not automatically the new mode’s characteristic degree.

[[c06-modes7]]

The example compares seven modes on E. Locrian has a diminished rather than a perfect fifth, so its tonic lacks the familiar stability of a major or minor triad. E can nevertheless be established as a Locrian centre through repetition, sustained notes and phrasing; the mode is not restricted to passing passages.

## 7.3 Modality: the audible centre

Since all modes can contain the same tones, it is not the pitch set that decides the mode but the centre.

[[c06-bass]]

The melody stays the same over different bass notes. The full E-Aeolian collection also fits C Lydian, D Mixolydian and A Dorian. A sustained new bass can suggest these centres, but does not force them. A short melody may omit characteristic degrees. Rhythm, resting points, chords and repetition also shape the perceived centre.

[[c06-colours]]

Conversely, over a fixed bass a single tone changes the colour. The example holds E in the bass and changes one melody tone from bar to bar: F makes Phrygian, F♯ Aeolian, C♯ Dorian, G♯ major. The contour stays, the colour moves from dark to bright.

Our examples use Aeolian as a starting point. Phrygian changes degree two and Dorian degree six. The E-Aeolian collection can give C Lydian when C is convincingly established as centre. An F bass under that same collection does not produce complete F Lydian: F Lydian requires F, G, A, B, C, D and E, without F#.

[[c06-closes]]

Four endings over E: F–E reaches the tonic by a semitone from above; C–B ends on the fifth; D–E approaches the tonic by a whole tone; D#–E uses the leading tone. Their sense of closure also depends on rhythm, bass and preceding material. No fixed ranking from open to final applies independently of context.

[[c06-dorian]]

Dorian in the chord: the fourth degree of E minor is Am (A C E) in Aeolian, A (A C♯ E) in Dorian. One tone of the inner voice changes, and the move Em–A sounds brighter and more floating than Em–Am without leaving the base colour of minor.

## 7.4 The pentatonic scale

E minor pentatonic consists of E G A B D: 1, b3, 4, 5, b7. Compared with E Aeolian it omits F# and C, degrees 2 and b6. The remaining pitches have no semitone steps between them. That does not guarantee consonance: D above E is a minor seventh and A above E a fourth. Chord, register and style determine which notes create rest or tension.

[[c06-pentatonic]]

E minor pentatonic and G major pentatonic share E G A B D. G is a minor third above E and the second note of the ascending E-minor-pentatonic sequence. G major pentatonic reads G A B D E. The audible centre matters, not just the first note played. E major pentatonic instead contains E F# G# B C#.

[[c06-melody]]

The example leads a pentatonic melody over a bass that alternates between E and other roots. Five tones demand all the more shaping through rhythm, repetition, rest and target tone, because the pitches alone carry little tension; chapter 21 treats melody as a whole.

## 7.5 Chromaticism

Chromatic tones extend the diatonic collection currently in use. They can be passing tones, neighbours or members of another chord. Spelling follows interval and harmonic function. Sharps ascending and flats descending are a common reading convention for chromatic lines, not a universal rule: in D#–E–D#, the leading tone remains D# on the descent.

[[c06-chromatic]]

Bar 1: E♭ as a passing tone between E and D, written with a flat because it goes downward. Bar 2: D♯ and F as lower and upper neighbours of E, the sharp shows the way upward. Bars 3 and 4: the chromatic scale from E4 to E5, ascending with sharps. It has twelve semitones and is not a mode but the stock from which all modes draw.

## 7.6 Summary

- One collection can support several modes; the audible centre is decisive.
- With a fixed tonic, intervals change: for example 2 to b2 or b6 to 6.
- The bass contributes to the centre but does not determine it alone.
- Locrian has b5 and can still establish its own centre.
- Pentatonic collections without semitone steps are not automatically free of dissonance.
- Closure depends on melody, bass, rhythm and context.
- Chromatic spelling follows function; direction alone is insufficient.

c07.title: Tuning and instrument
c07.text:
The tuning of an instrument is not a side issue of technique but a musical decision: it determines which tones sound open, which fingerings are easy and which intervals lie under the hand. This chapter explains why the low strings are called E A D, what pure-fourths tuning changes, what low tunings enforce and how Biber uses retuning as a compositional device.

## 8.1 The chain of fourths

The four low strings of the guitar and the four strings of the bass are tuned in perfect fourths: E A D G. Fourth and fifth complete each other to the octave, which is why a fourth upward reaches the same letter as a fifth downward.

[[c07-chain]]

E up a fourth reaches A; E down a fifth also reaches A in the lower octave. The actual sequence E2–A2–D3–G3 rises in fourths, and its reversal G3–D3–A2–E2 also descends in fourths. In pitch-class terms the same chain can be read as descending fifths on the circle of fifths. Direction and actual octave placement must be distinguished.

For the harmony of this book the first three tones, E, A and D, are at the same time the three centres. Read in A, D is the subdominant and E the dominant: the cadence axis. Read in E, A is the subdominant and D the seventh degree without a leading tone: the modal axis. Read in D, A is the dominant and E the second degree.

[[c07-axes]]

The example plays the same basses twice. In A major, A, D, E, A give the cadence I–IV–V–I; the E carries a major chord with the leading tone G♯ and presses toward A. In E minor, E, A, D, E give the move i–iv–VII–i; the D carries a major chord without leading tone and returns to E by a whole-tone step. The same three open strings therefore carry a functional and a modal reading (chapter 13).

## 8.2 Standard tuning and pure fourths

Standard tuning E A D G B E breaks the chain of fourths between G and B with a major third. The reason is historical and practical: five fourths across six strings span two octaves and a semitone (E2 to F4), six strings with one third span exactly two octaves (E2 to E4), and the common major and minor shapes fall under four fingers. The price is an irregularity: every interval shape changes by one fret at the transition to the B string.

Pure-fourths tuning E A D G C F keeps the chain. Every interval has a single shape valid on all pairs of strings (chapter 5). Scales lie the same in every position, chord shapes can be moved freely, and the two high strings reach a semitone higher than in standard tuning.

[[c07-shape]]

The example plays one four-tone fingering, frets 0 3 0 2 across two strings, on four string pairs: E G A B on strings 6 and 5, A C D E on 5 and 4, G B♭ C D on 3 and 2, C E♭ F G on 2 and 1. Each time it is the same figure a fourth higher; the intervals within the figure stay the same. In standard tuning the same fingering on strings 3 and 2 would give G B♭ B C♯, because the B string lies a semitone lower: the figure would be a different one.

The price of fourths tuning: the familiar shapes of standard tuning do not apply, open chords in E and A sound different, and the literature for guitar in standard tuning has to be reread. This book writes notation with position marks and not tablature, so that the music stays readable regardless of tuning.

[[c07-harmonics]]

The six open strings of P4 tuning as harmonics over the twelfth fret: they sound an octave above the open string, E3 A3 D4 G4 C5 F5, and form the same chain of fourths.

## 8.3 Low tunings

Type O Negative tune the guitar on *October Rust* to B standard: B E A D F♯ B, all six strings a fourth lower than standard. The shapes stay, every tone sounds a fourth lower; an E shape sounds as B. The lowest string sits at B1 with 61.7 Hz.

[[c07-bstandard]]

The standard-tuning shape A2–E3–A3 on the fifth string sounds E2–B2–E3 in B standard, a fourth lower. Lower tuning changes tension, resonances and available pitches. It does not force a fixed allocation of roles: a five-string bass with B0 can sit below a guitar with B1, for example. Registers, voicings and sounds are chosen for the actual arrangement.

## 8.4 Scordatura

Retuning as a compositional device is old. In the *Harmonia artificioso-ariosa* Biber writes six of the seven partitas for retuned instruments; only the sixth is in normal tuning. The tunings are part of the work and enable chords and resonances unreachable in normal tuning.

[[c07-scordatura]]

Bar 1 shows the open strings of the violin in normal tuning, G3 D4 A4 E5, a chain of fifths. Bar 2 the tuning of both violins in the first partita, A3 E4 A4 D5: fifth, fourth, fourth, with two A's that, as the root of D minor's dominant, reinforce it. Bars 3 and 4 the tuning of the two violas d'amore in the seventh partita, C3 G3 C4 E♭4 G4 C5, a broken C minor chord; beneath lie sympathetic strings that vibrate by themselves. Appendix A lists all the tunings. Scordatura notation shows fingerings, not sounding tones: the player reads as if the instrument were tuned normally, and the instrument produces the sounding pitch.

P4, B standard and Biber's tunings follow the same idea: the tuning chooses which sounds are easily reachable, and thereby the music. An instrument in fourths favours quartal sounds and movable shapes; one tuned to a chord favours that chord and its resonance.

## 8.5 The instruments of this book

[[c07-ranges]]

The P4 guitar starts at sounding E2; its highest open string is F4, and with 24 frets it reaches F6. The keyboard model used here spans C2 to C6; other 49-key instruments can have different base ranges. Both hands can cross or use the same registers. The violin’s open strings are G3 D4 A4 E5, with stopped notes extending higher. A standard four-string bass begins at E1; its upper range depends on fret count and technique.

## 8.6 Summary

- A fourth upwards and a fifth downwards reach the same pitch name in different octaves.
- A–D–E can form a cadential axis; string names do not determine harmony.
- P4 retains equal string intervals. Shapes transpose within available frets; open strings must become fretted.
- Uniform down-tuning transposes the same fret locations. Sound and playability also depend on strings and setup.
- Scordatura means retuning; distinguish historical fingering notation from sounding-pitch notation.
- Open guitar E2–F4, keyboard model C2–C6, open violin G3–E5, standard four-string bass from E1.

c07b.title: Keys and scales in practice
c07b.text:
Chapters 6 and 7 introduced the scales and modes as tone stocks. This chapter orders them by the needs of the repertoire and lays them on the instruments: which keys this book needs, which scales are most frequent, what a scale pattern looks like on the P4 fretboard and why the same pattern holds for E, A and D, and how the keys lie on the keyboard.

## 9.1 The keys of this book

Three centres carry the repertoire: E, A and D, the three low open strings and the tones E2, A2 and D3 of the bass (chapter 8). In minor these are E minor with one sharp, A minor without accidentals and D minor with one flat, three neighbours in the circle of fifths (chapter 6). Their relative keys G major, C major and F major share the signature and appear as brightening within the minor pieces. Their parallel keys E major, A major and D major with four, three and two sharps are the keys of the cadence axis A–D–E and of the Picardy third; Vivaldi's Spring stands in E major.

[[c07b-centres]]

The example shows the three centres with their primary degrees i, iv and v: Em Am Bm, Am Dm Em, Dm Gm Am. The chords of one centre are the centres of the others: Am is the subdominant of E minor and the tonic of A minor; that is the kinship that makes changes between the three soft (chapter 15).

Four further keys occur. B minor with two sharps is the key of the low tuning: what is fingered as E minor in B standard sounds in B minor (chapter 8). G minor with two flats and F minor with four flats are Vivaldi's Summer and Winter; F major is his Autumn. Everything else is rare in this repertoire.

## 9.2 The most frequent scales

This course prioritises natural minor, minor pentatonic, major and harmonic minor, then other modes and melodic minor. This is a teaching sequence, not a measured frequency ranking of the reference albums. Lydian and Mixolydian can also support entire pieces. D# supplies the leading tone in an E-minor dominant cadence; outside that context it is not compulsory.

## 9.3 Scale patterns on the P4 guitar

A scale pattern distributes a pitch collection across particular strings and frets. Three notes per string is one possible organisation, not an intrinsic property of P4 tuning. In P4 a uniform shift preserves intervals as long as all required strings and frets exist. Maps show the locations; scores below show a path through them.

[[c07b-aeolian6]]

E Aeolian from string 6: E F# G at frets 0 2 3; A B C on string 5 also at 0 2 3; D E F# on string 4 at 0 2 4; G A B on string 3 at 0 2 4; C D E on string 2 at 0 2 4; F# G A on string 1 at 1 2 4. E2 to A4 spans 29 semitones: 24 + 5, two octaves and a perfect fourth. Open strings extend the four-fret window.

[[c07b-aeolian5]]

Shift the pattern one string up and it begins on A2 and is A Aeolian: the same frets 0 2 3, 0 2 3, 0 2 4, 0 2 4, 0 2 4 on strings 5 to 1. No fingering changes, only the string.

[[c07b-aeolian4]]

One more string up it is D Aeolian with B♭ instead of B; again the same frets. That is the practical reason for E–A–D as the three centres of this book: on the P4 guitar they are a single fingering on three groups of strings, and every riff, line and chord in E can be carried to A and D without new fingerings. In standard tuning the pattern would break at the B string.

[[c07b-shift]]

The second motion is along the string: the same pattern seven frets higher begins on B2 and is B Aeolian, the key in which the guitar in B standard sounds when it fingers E minor; the example shows one octave on strings 6 to 4 in seventh position, frets 7 9 10, 7 9 10, 7 9, the same distances as 0 2 3, 0 2 3, 0 2. Five frets higher it would be A Aeolian on the same strings as E Aeolian, the same tones as the pattern from string 5 in open position, in a thicker sound. Every key is thus reachable in two ways: one string further or five frets further.

[[c07b-pentatonic]]

E minor pentatonic contains E G A B D. In the written window string 6 uses frets 0 3; strings 5 and 4 use 0 2; string 3 uses 0 2 4; string 2 uses 2 4; string 1 uses 2 4. Here the third string carries three notes. Two-notes-per-string patterns are also possible, but require a different path.

[[c07b-harmonic]]

Harmonic minor changes a single tone in the pattern: D becomes D♯, on the fourth string fret 1 instead of 0 and on the second fret 3 instead of 2. Whoever knows the Aeolian pattern knows this one too; the leading tone is one fingering.

[[c07b-major]]

E major in the same frame: G♯, C♯ and D♯ lie one fret higher each than G, C and D. The frets per string are 0 2 4, 0 2 4, 1 2 4, 1 2 4, 1 3 4, 1 3 4. Major and minor on the same root differ by three fingerings; chapter 6 showed that they are the same three tones, third, sixth and seventh.

## 9.4 Keys on the keyboard

Black keys help locate a pitch collection. C major and A minor use the same white keys but are different keys: their centres differ. E minor/G major have F#, D minor/F major Bb; D major has F# and C#, A major adds G#, and E major adds D#. Accidentals can add further keys. A musical key is more than a set of black keys.

[[c07b-fingering]]

For the single octaves of E minor, E major and D minor shown here, right 1–2–3–1–2–3–4–5 and left 5–4–3–2–1–3–2–1 are starting points. This is not a universal fingering. Key, direction, length and phrase continuation can require different crossings. In particular, left-hand B minor and scales starting on black keys need separate preparation. Finger 1 is the thumb.

[[c07b-blackkeys]]

E major has four black-key pitches per octave and D minor one. In this example the right thumb plays E and A or D and G; the left thumb plays B and E or A and D. White-key thumb positions can ease movement, but black-key thumb positions are not forbidden. Reachable movement and the musical continuation determine the choice.

## 9.5 One pattern, three centres

Compare the E, A and D maps first. A shifted P4 pattern preserves intervals but is truncated at the highest string. A figure using all six strings therefore cannot be shifted fully one string higher. When moving along the neck, open notes become fretted notes. On the keyboard the interval sequence stays the same, while black keys and fingering change with the tonic.

## 9.6 Summary

- This course centres on E, A and D: a selection, not a stylistic boundary.
- A P4 pattern shifts as far as strings and frets allow.
- Three or two notes per string are fingering choices, not tuning rules.
- E2–A4 spans 24 + 5 = 29 semitones: two octaves and a fourth.
- Harmonic minor raises degree seven; major changes the third, sixth and seventh relative to natural minor.
- Black keys identify a collection. Centre and phrasing determine its function.
- Adapt fingering to key, direction and continuation.

c08.title: Triads
c08.text:
The triad is the basic unit of harmony: three tones heard together as one sound. This chapter builds it from thirds, shows its four types, its inversions and spacings, derives the diatonic triads from the scale and assigns them functions. It is the foundation of chapters 11 to 14.

## 10.1 Construction and types

A triad consists of three tones a third apart: root, third and fifth. Four types arise from the sizes of the two thirds. The major triad stacks a major third with a minor one above (4 + 3 semitones, E G♯ B); the minor triad a minor third with a major above (3 + 4, E G B); the diminished triad two minor thirds (3 + 3, E G B♭); the augmented two major (4 + 4, E G♯ B♯). Major and minor have a perfect fifth and are consonant; the diminished has a diminished, the augmented an augmented fifth, and both are dissonant and press onward.

[[c08-types]]

The example plays the four types over the same root E. One hears: major bright and stable, minor dark and stable, diminished tight and pressing, augmented floating and without ground, because its fifth B♯ is enharmonically C and the chord divides the octave into three equal parts.

The difference between major and minor lies solely in the third. Over an E bass, G♯ or G decides whether the sound is bright or dark; the fifth B is common to both.

[[c08-third]]

The bass holds the power chord E–B through all four bars. Without a third (bars 1 and 4) the sound is neither major nor minor; with G♯ above (bar 2) it is E major, with G (bar 3) E minor. A single tone in an upper voice decides the mode of the whole sound; that is why a power chord can be either and is neither (chapter 11).

## 10.2 Inversion and spacing

A triad remains the same chord whichever of its tones lies at the bottom. With the root in the bass it is in root position; with the third in the bass in first inversion (sixth chord); with the fifth in the bass in second inversion (six-four chord). The names come from the intervals above the bass: in first inversion third and sixth lie above the bass, in second inversion fourth and sixth.

[[c08-inversions]]

The example compares Em in root position, first inversion and second inversion. In a classical cadential model, Em/B can act as a cadential six-four before B major. This is not a requirement for every second inversion: it can also be passing, pedal-supported or an independent rock voicing.

Spacing must be distinguished from inversion: the distribution of the tones above the bass. In close position the three tones lie within an octave, in open position with gaps. Em as E2, B3, G4 is the same inversion as E4, G4, B4 but sounds entirely different. Open position with a low root and a high third is the default of this music because the third then stays out of the range of the combination tones (chapter 1).

[[c08-spacing]]

The example compares close and open spacing and inversions. Both instruments can play close and open voicings. Fourths tuning does not force open spacing: E3–G3–B3 at frets 7, 5 and 4 on the A, D and G strings is a close Em triad.

## 10.3 Diatonic triads

On every degree of a scale a triad arises from its tones. In major, degrees I, IV and V are major, II, III and VI minor, VII diminished. In natural minor (Aeolian), i, iv and v are minor, III, VI and VII major, ii diminished. The degrees are labelled with Roman numerals, upper case for major, lower case for minor, with ° for diminished and + for augmented.

[[c08-diatonic]]

E Aeolian: i Em, ii° F♯dim, III G, iv Am, v Bm, VI C, VII D. Three minor, three major, one diminished; the major chords lie on III, VI and VII, and those are the chords that give minor its bright side without leaving it. The example climbs the degrees as chords in close position.

Harmonic minor changes three chords: v becomes major (B), VII becomes diminished (D♯dim), III becomes augmented (G+).

[[c08-harmonic]]

The example precedes each changed chord with its Aeolian form: Bm and B, D and D♯dim, G and G+. In practice the first of these changes usually suffices: the major dominant B is the tonal chord in an otherwise modal surrounding. Melodic minor additionally makes ii minor (F♯m) and IV major (A), which corresponds to Dorian (chapter 7).

## 10.4 Functions

Functional theory gathers the degrees into three groups: tonic (I, with III and VI as substitutes), subdominant (IV, with II as substitute), dominant (V, with VII as substitute). The letters T, S and D denote them in major, t, s and d in minor; an appended P (German Parallele, here R for relative) denotes the relative, the substitute in the other mode.

[[c08-functions]]

In E minor, Em represents t, Am s and B7 D. The tonic’s relative chord tP is G major (G B D). C major (C E G) is the tonic counter-relative tG, not tP. D major is the relative of the minor dominant Bm (dP); the major dominant B has different relationships. Measure 5 replaces Em with C and measure 7 replaces B7 with D. These functions are interpretations in tonal context; scale-degree numerals can be clearer in a modal progression.

## 10.5 Triads on guitar and keyboard

On the keyboard the close triad lies under one hand: 1–3–5 for the right hand in root position, the inversions by shifting one finger. Open spacing arises when the left hand takes the root low and the right hand third and fifth above. On the P4 guitar root, fifth and octave lie on three neighbouring strings in the same shape as the power chord, and the third is added on the next string: the major third one fret below the fourth shape, the minor third two frets below.

[[c08-hands]]

The example sets both voicings side by side: on the keyboard Em and Am close in the right hand over the low root of the left; on the guitar E2 B2 E3 G3 and A2 E3 A3 C4, power-chord shape with the minor third on the fourth string. Both are the same chord in open position. All guitar shapes transfer to every pair of strings and every position; open strings cannot be moved along.

## 10.6 Summary

- A triad has root, third and fifth; it is major, minor, diminished or augmented.
- The third distinguishes major from minor.
- The bass determines inversion; spacing describes the upper voices’ distribution.
- E Aeolian: i ii° III iv v VI VII. Harmonic minor changes v to V, VII to vii° and III to III+.
- In E minor, tP = G, tG = C and dP = D. Determine functions from context.
- Close and open voicings are possible on guitar and keyboard.

c09.title: Chords without thirds: power chord, fourths, suspended chords
c09.text:
Power chords, suspended chords and quartal stacks add thirdless sonorities alongside triads. This chapter covers their notation, P4 shapes and registers. Distortion affects their sound; it does not impose a separate mandatory theory of harmony. Triads and dense voicings can also work musically under gain.

## 11.1 The power chord

A power chord is a root with its fifth, often with the octave above: 1–5 or 1–5–8. It has no third and is therefore neither major nor minor. The symbol writes a 5 after the root: E5, A5, D5. Calling it a chord is generous, since two tones strictly form a dyad; musically, however, the power chord takes on in distorted music the role the triad has in clean writing, and the third is supplied by the context: the voice, the keyboard, the melody, or nobody.

In a just fifth, both tones share many partials and possible combination tones can fit this series. This models its fusion. In equal temperament the fifth is only approximately just. Low thirds are not universally forbidden; their clarity depends on the signal chain and arrangement.

## 11.2 Shapes and registers

On the P4 guitar the fifth lies one string higher and two frets further than the root, the octave two strings higher and two frets further. The third shape is the inverted fifth, i.e. the fourth: fifth below, root above, for example B2–E3. It lies on two neighbouring strings at the same fret and sounds heavier than the fifth shape because the root is on top and the difference tone, the root an octave below the upper tone, replaces the missing bass.

[[c09-power]]

The example shows the three shapes over E and then the power chords on the three open bass strings E, A and D: the chain of fourths from chapter 8 as a riff. All shapes transfer to every position.

[[c09-register]]

The same power chord in three registers: E2–B2 is the riff register, heavy and with the difference tone E1; E3–B3 is the middle register, in which a second guitarist can play above the riff; E4–B4 is high and light, a sound for lines and pads. Finally the fourth shape B2–E3: the same letters as the first, but turned, with the root on top.

## 11.3 The third from the context

[[c09-context]]

The example holds E5 with octave in the bass and places above it once G and once G♯ as a melody tone. The listener hears Em and E major although the guitar plays the same thing both times. That is the division of labour in the references: the distorted guitar carries root and fifth in the low register, thirds appear in the keyboards, the violin, the voice or in high guitar positions with less gain. Whoever plays alone must achieve this distribution on one instrument: power chord low, third high, or power chord and then the third as a melody tone.

[[c09-riff]]

A riff of power chords is a bass line with reinforcement. The example goes E5–A5–B5–E5, i.e. i–iv–v–i without thirds, with muted eighths between the chords; whether the music is major or minor is decided by the other voices. Chords without thirds are not a substitute for harmony but its relocation.

## 11.4 Suspended chords

A suspended chord replaces the third with its neighbour: sus4 with the fourth (Esus4 = E A B), sus2 with the second (Esus2 = E F♯ B). The name comes from the suspension (chapter 20): historically the fourth was a tone held over from the previous chord that then resolved into the third.

[[c09-sus]]

Esus4 and Esus2 are compared with E major and E minor. A then moves to G# as a fourth-to-third resolution. Sus sounds can also stand without resolution. A major second is major, not a perfect interval; it does not make a sus2 chord universally resistant to distortion.

## 11.5 Quartal voicing

Stacking fourths instead of thirds yields sounds such as E–A–D or A–D–G. They contain no third and no fifth to the lowest tone but fourth and minor seventh, and are therefore open: they can be read differently over different basses.

[[c09-stacks]]

On the P4 guitar a quartal stack lies on three strings at the same fret; the open strings themselves are four such sounds: E–A–D, A–D–G, D–G–C, G–C–F. It is the simplest form of the tuning itself, and every fingering that takes three strings at the same fret produces it at another height.

[[c09-quartal]]

The notation shows E–A–D over E, then over A; measure 3 changes the stack to G–C–F over A, and measure 4 returns to E–A–D over E. Over E, E–A–D contains root, fourth and minor seventh but no fifth: E7sus4(no5). Over A, E and D are the fifth and fourth: Asus4, not Asus2. Measure 3 adds minor seventh G, minor third C and minor sixth F above A. Quartal sounds are ambiguous, but can certainly conflict with some bass notes.

## 11.6 Summary

- Power chord: 1–5 or 1–5–8; without a third it initially specifies neither major nor minor.
- Fifth, fifth-octave and fourth shapes distribute the same pitch classes differently.
- Register changes sound; available frets limit transposition.
- Other voices can supply the third.
- sus2 contains a major second, sus4 a perfect fourth; judge their behavior under gain by listening.
- Quartal stacks allow multiple interpretations, but not every bass fits equally well.

c10.title: Seventh chords and chord symbols
c10.text:
With the seventh, harmony begins to have direction. This chapter builds the four-note chords, orders the symbol notation that names them, and shows two older scripts for the same thing: Roman numerals with inversion figures and the thoroughbass in which Vivaldi and Biber write their accompaniment. Whoever can read all three can read every score and every lead sheet.

## 12.1 Seventh chords

A seventh chord stacks another third above a triad: root, third, fifth and seventh. In classical voice leading, the chordal seventh frequently descends by step. In other contexts it can remain or move differently. The following five types are common.

[[c10-types]]

The dominant seventh (major with minor seventh, E7 = E G♯ B D) is the chord of the dominant. The major seventh chord (major with major seventh, Emaj7 = E G♯ B D♯) is soft and usually stands on I and IV. The minor seventh chord (minor with minor seventh, Em7 = E G B D) is the default on ii, iii, vi in major and on i, iv, v in minor. The half-diminished seventh (diminished with minor seventh, Em7♭5 = E G B♭ D) stands on ii in minor. The diminished seventh (diminished with diminished seventh, Edim7 = E G B♭ D♭) stands on vii in harmonic minor; chapter 15 treats its ambiguity. The example builds all five over E so that the differences become audible one tone per step.

[[c10-diatonic]]

Diatonic seventh chords in E Aeolian: Em7, F♯m7♭5, Gmaj7, Am7, Bm7, Cmaj7, D7. In harmonic minor Bm7 becomes B7 and D7 becomes D♯dim7. The minor chord with major seventh (Em(maj7) = E G B D♯) arises from harmonic minor on the first degree and sounds tense.

[[c10-resolve]]

What the seventh does: in B7–Em, A, the seventh, falls to G, the third of the tonic, while D♯ rises to E and B stays. In Cmaj7–Em7 the major seventh B stays as a common tone; it is not a dissonance that pushes but a colour that rests. That is the difference between the dominant seventh, which has direction, and the major seventh chord, which needs none.

## 12.2 Sixth, add and ninth chords

A sixth chord in the sense of symbol notation adds the major sixth to the triad: E6 = E G♯ B C♯, Em6 = E G B C♯. An add chord adds a tone without the seventh: Eadd9 = E G♯ B F♯, Emadd9 = E G B F♯. If the chord contains the seventh, the extensions are called 9, 11 and 13: E9 = E G♯ B D F♯, Em9 = E G B D F♯, Emaj9 = E G♯ B D♯ F♯. With 11 the third is usually omitted because it rubs against the eleventh; with 13 the eleventh is omitted. Alterations stand in brackets or appended: B7♭9 = B D♯ F♯ A C, B7♯9, B7♭5, Cmaj7♯11.

[[c10-added]]

Four colours over E: Emadd9 with the ninth F♯ and without seventh, soft and without direction; Em6 with the Dorian C♯; Em9 with seventh and ninth, denser; Em(maj7) with D♯, tense. For the references two of them matter: madd9 as a pad without direction, as Anathema use it in clean guitars and keyboards, and maj7 on VI (Cmaj7 in E minor), which turns the Aeolian C into a resting sound. Dominant sevenths appear constantly in Vivaldi and Biber and rarely in the metal references, because they create direction.

## 12.3 The system of symbols

A chord symbol is read from left to right: root; quality (nothing for major, m for minor, dim or ° for diminished, aug or + for augmented); seventh (7 for the minor, maj7 or Δ for the major); extensions (9, 11, 13); alterations (♭5, ♯5, ♭9, ♯9, ♯11, ♭13); additions (add); omissions (no3, no5); bass tone after a slash. The symbol fixes the tones, not their spacing, doubling or duration. Two players with the same symbol play different voicings. Appendix D lists all symbols with their tones over E, A and D.

[[c10-symbols]]

The example shows eight symbols in specific voicings. G B E over C gives the same pitch classes as Cmaj7. Em/C also describes the written notes exactly: Em in the upper voices, C in the bass. Which name is analytically more useful depends on voice leading and context.

[[c10-slash]]

A slash symbol X/Y means chord X with bass note Y. Em/G and Em/B are inversions. Em/C remains a valid spelling even though Cmaj7 names the same pitch collection. D/E contains E D F# A and can be interpreted as E9sus4(no5); fifth B is absent. The bass note is not automatically the chord root.

## 12.4 Thoroughbass

Vivaldi and Biber notate their accompaniment as thoroughbass: a bass line with figures giving the intervals above the bass. No figure means a triad in root position, 6 the sixth chord, 6/4 the six-four chord, 7 the seventh chord, 4–3 a suspension of the fourth resolving into the third. A sharp or flat beside a figure alters that tone, a lone accidental the third.

[[c10-figured]]

The example shows a figured bass line and above it a realisation: E without figure is Em; C with 6 is a sixth chord, i.e. Am/C; B with 4–3 is the dominant with a suspended fourth, E resolving to D♯; E without figure is Em again. The harpsichordist or organist realises the chords from this by the rules of voice leading (chapter 14). The chord symbols of rock are the direct descendant of this practice: both give the player the harmony and leave the voicing to them.

## 12.5 Roman numerals with inversions

Roman-numeral analysis marks inversions with appended figures taken from thoroughbass: triad in first inversion 6, in second 6/4; seventh chord in root position 7, in first inversion 6/5, in second 4/3, in third 4/2.

[[c10-roman]]

Am/C is iv6 in E minor and B7/D# is V6/5. The example gives i–iv6–V6/5–i over E–C–D#–E. E–C is a third leap; the bass then rises by step. A slash between scale-degree numerals instead names a target: V7/iv is the dominant of the subdominant (chapter 15).

## 12.6 Summary

- A seventh chord has root, third, fifth and seventh.
- Common types: 7, maj7, m7, m7b5, dim7.
- The seventh frequently descends by step in classical writing; context determines its continuation.
- add supplements without an implied seventh; 9, 11 and 13 normally include one.
- Symbols specify a pitch collection; actual voicings can omit tones.
- X/Y means chord X above bass Y; a non-chord bass is permissible.
- Figured bass names intervals above the bass; chord symbols refer to a chord root.

c11.title: Cadence and function
c11.text:
The cadence is the harmonic close, and whether and how a section closes decides its form of time. This chapter explains the dominant from two tones, introduces the cadence types and draws the line between tonal music, which creates expectation, and modal music, which strings colours. For the repertoire of this book the refusal of the cadence is as important as the cadence itself.

## 13.1 The dominant

In major-minor tonality the dominant lies on degree five. In E minor, B major supplies leading tone D#; B7 adds seventh A. D# can rise to E while A falls to G, resolving the tritone D#–A into E–G. These are typical voice-leading motions, not physical forces imposed by notation. A dominant triad needs no seventh to function as a dominant.

[[c11-tritone]]

Bars 1–2 isolate D#–A and its resolution E–G. Bars 3–4 add B7–Em. B major without a seventh can also be a strong dominant. B minor lacks the leading tone; depending on style, minor v can still serve a dominant function or participate in a modal progression.

The subdominant prepares the dominant. Am contains the C that falls to B, and the A that stays and becomes the seventh of B7.

[[c11-full]]

Am–B7–Em demonstrates preparation, tension and resolution: iv–V7–i. A is the root of Am; on moving to B7, that same pitch becomes its minor seventh and can then fall to G. E descends a semitone to D# and then rises back to E. The written voicing determines which voice takes each path.

## 13.2 The cadence types

A harmonic close is called a cadence. The authentic cadence leads from dominant to tonic (V–I); it is perfect when both chords are in root position and the melody ends on the root, otherwise imperfect. The plagal cadence leads from subdominant to tonic (IV–I); it has no leading tone and feels soft, like the amen at the end of a hymn. The half cadence ends on the dominant (I–V or IV–V) and leaves the phrase open. The deceptive cadence leads the dominant not to the tonic but to the sixth degree (V–VI, in E minor B7–C); the leading tone resolves upward, the bass moves a step instead of a fourth, and the expected arrival is postponed.

[[c11-types]]

The example compares authentic, plagal, half and deceptive cadences. A plagal cadence can fully close a piece too. A half cadence usually suggests continuation in major-minor tonality; a deceptive cadence redirects an expected tonic arrival. Rhythm and form also affect their impact.

## 13.3 The Phrygian cadence

A special half cadence of the Baroque is the Phrygian cadence: the subdominant in first inversion to the dominant, iv6–V, in E minor Am/C–B. The bass falls a semitone (C–B), the top voice rises a whole tone (A–B), and the close stays open on the dominant. Vivaldi ends slow movements and transitions with it.

[[c11-phrygian]]

Bars 1 and 2 show the Baroque form with contrary motion of the outer voices. Bars 3 and 4 show the same bass motion as power chords: C5–B5, the ending of countless riffs, with an open continuation. The same bass motion, the same openness; only the third is missing.

## 13.4 Modal and tonal

Tonal music creates expectation: every dominant promises the tonic. Modal music strings chords as colours over a centre without a leading tone pushing.

[[c11-axis]]

The fourth-related chain can acquire different functions. In A major, D is subdominant and E with G# is dominant; in an E-Dorian context, A is major IV, D is bVII, and Em is the centre. The bass path alone is insufficient. Read the actual thirds, melody pitches and endings together.

[[c11-criterion]]

A leading tone alone does not reliably distinguish tonal and modal music. A plagal cadence can omit it in clearly tonal music; a chromatic leading tone can occur in an otherwise modal passage. Compare whole phrases: which pitch acts as centre, which chords prepare others, and how are endings established? Em–C–D–Em and Em–C–B7–Em offer different closing models; either can form a complete phrase.

The following models distinguish functional dominant progressions from modal returns. These terms describe specific passages. Classifying entire albums by genre does not replace analysis; both approaches may occur within one piece. Sequences can also be diatonic without forming a chain of major dominants.

## 13.5 Refusing the cadence

Expectation also arises without a dominant cadence: through repetition, rhythmic patterns, bass direction and density. Three possible section endings are a return to the tonic without a leading tone, an open ending on another chord, and a cut-off. The strength of closure depends on the preceding course of the music.

[[c11-refusal]]

The same riff receives three endings: return without a leading tone, D followed by silence, and B7 to a major tonic. A composition may contain many cadences or avoid them entirely. Its form determines which endings articulate sections and which provides the strongest closure.

[[c11-picardy]]

A major tonic ending a minor-key piece is called a Picardy third. Am–B7–Em and Am–B7–E differ at the end through G versus G#. This is a historical closing convention and an available colour choice. Its use is not explained by an inherent acoustic superiority or longer decay of major thirds.

## 13.6 Summary

- Both dominant triads and dominant sevenths can lead to the tonic.
- In B7–Em, D# often rises to E and A falls to G.
- Am–B7–Em joins preparation, dominant and tonic.
- Authentic and plagal cadences can close; half and deceptive cadences often suggest continuation.
- Phrygian half cadence: iv6–V, such as Am/C–B.
- Determine tonality and modality from context, not a single leading tone.
- Picardy third: a major tonic at the end of a minor-key piece.

c12.title: Voice leading
c12.text:
Voice leading describes the paths of individual voices between sonorities. This chapter compares common tones, small steps, contrary motion and deliberate parallels. These serve different goals; chord changes and good melodies need not obey one rule. A pedal is a particular form of oblique motion.

## 14.1 Chords as voices

Four-part writing, in which voice leading is taught, distributes every chord among bass, tenor, alto and soprano; every voice has a line of its own that must be singable by itself. That is the criterion by which every voicing can be measured, whether on the keyboard, in Type O Negative's organ or in Vivaldi's continuo: can every voice be sung on its own?

## 14.2 The basic rules

Common tones and small movements are useful starting points for economical voice leading. In classical cadences, leading tones and chordal sevenths normally resolve upward and downward respectively. These are compositional conventions. Melodic goals, voice exchange, register changes or intentionally parallel writing can require other paths. The bass can also move by step.

[[c12-common]]

Em to C: E and G stay, B moves to C. Em to Am: E stays, G to A, B to C. Em to B7: B stays, E to D♯, G to F♯. Em to D: no common tone, everything shifts a step downward. In all four bars the bass leaps and the upper voices move by at most a whole tone; that is the division of labour in part writing.

[[c12-eight]]

The example leads eight chords in three upper voices over a leaping bass. The top voice stays on E until D forces it; the largest moves lie where two chords share no tone.

Fifth, from classical writing: two voices should not move in parallel octaves or perfect fifths when they are meant to be heard as independent, because the parallel fuses the two voices into one.

[[c12-parallels]]

Bar 1 moves E–B to F#–C#: parallel fifths. Bar 2 reaches F#–A by contrary motion. Bar 3 uses parallel fifths as a power-chord riff. Parallels can emphasise a shared contour, yet register, rhythm, articulation and timbre may still distinguish the voices. Prohibiting parallel fifths belongs to particular historical counterpoint exercises; it is not a universal judgement of quality.

## 14.3 Top voice and inner voices

The highest voice often attracts attention, but a melody can also lie in the bass or an inner voice. Loudness, articulation and rhythmic activity affect which line stands out. A still upper voice with moving inner voices is one possible accompaniment model.

[[c12-top]]

From D7 to G, D stays on top, F♯ rises to G, C falls to B. In Type O Negative the organ carries this kind of writing, in Anathema the keyboard pad; in both the bass makes the motion, on top one tone changes.

## 14.4 Pedal point

A pedal point is a bass tone that stays while the harmony above it changes. On the tonic it rests; on the dominant it tenses, because every chord above the sustained B pushes toward Em.

[[c12-pedal]]

Measures 1–4 hold E beneath Em, C, Am and B7. C over E is C/E, not Cmaj7/E: the written E G C contains no B. Measures 5–7 hold B beneath Em, Am and B7; these are not all dominant chords. The pedal can support a dominant region while the upper voices form different harmonies. A repeated chaconne bass pattern is an ostinato; it is only a pedal if the same pitch is sustained or reiterated.

## 14.5 Voice leading on the instruments

On the keyboard voice leading means not shifting the hand but single fingers.

[[c12-hands]]

Fingering follows the actual written voicings. A common tone may be retained if the same key or string remains reachable; it may also be rearticulated. P4 guitar permits close and open voicings. Keyboard chord changes need not retain a fixed thumb position. Follow each pitch path, then assess the complete hand movement.

## 14.6 Summary

- Read and hear voices as individual lines.
- Common tones and short paths support economical voice leading.
- Leading tones and sevenths have typical resolutions in classical cadences.
- Strict counterpoint avoids parallel fifths and octaves; riffs can use them deliberately.
- Melody can lie above, inside or in the bass.
- A pedal stays on one pitch; it can create harmonic friction and need not be an open string.

c13.title: Extended harmony
c13.text:
Extended harmony adds tones to the key from outside: leading tones to secondary degrees, the lowered second, the symmetrical diminished seventh chord, and finally the change of the centre itself. This chapter shows the Baroque formulas that shape these devices and their path into metal, where they usually appear reduced to their bass.

## 15.1 Secondary dominants

A major or minor chord can temporarily become the target of its own dominant. A secondary dominant is a major chord, often with a minor seventh, rooted a fifth above its target. In E minor, examples include E7–Am, A7–D, D7–G, G7–C and F#7–B. Analysis writes V7/iv, V7/VII and so on; the slash names the target. A secondary dominant need not include a seventh.

[[c13-secondary]]

The example strings three secondary dominants and closes with the real dominant. Without the seventh chords the same root sequence would stay modal; every secondary dominant adds a direction. Vivaldi strings them in falling fifths, each chord the dominant of the next (chapter 16).

[[c13-v7iv]]

The E7–Am example temporarily raises G to G# and adds D, making Am the target of a secondary dominant. Such moves remain available in doom and gothic. Power chords alone omit the third; a melody or another voice can supply G#. Suitability depends on the actual phrase, not the genre label.

## 15.2 The Neapolitan

The Neapolitan sixth chord is the major chord on the lowered second degree, usually in first inversion: in E minor F major with A in the bass, F/A. It stands before the dominant and replaces the subdominant: F/A–B7–Em. The semitone step F–E in the top voice is the same as in Phrygian, but here as a cadence.

[[c13-neapolitan]]

The cadence F/A–B7–Em shows a Neapolitan in E minor. F descends to D#, a diminished third spanning two semitones, then moves to E. The following power chords F5–E5 instead show a bII–i root motion. Without the full chords and preparation of the dominant, this is not a Neapolitan cadence.

[[c13-formulas]]

The example compares a Phrygian half cadence, a Neapolitan and a dominant pedal. Their chord tones and voice leading distinguish them. Reducing them to bass notes or power chords can show similarities but does not automatically preserve their harmonic functions.

## 15.3 The diminished seventh chord

D♯dim7 = D♯ F♯ A C consists of three minor thirds and divides the octave into four equal parts.

[[c13-symmetry]]

In equal temperament, all four intervals including the octave completion span three semitones. The inversions remain inversions of D#dim7. New roots require new spellings: F#dim7 = F# A C Eb, Adim7 = A C Eb Gb, Cdim7 = C Eb Gb Bbb. The three distinct symmetrical pitch-class sets follow from 12 / 4 = 3; this does not mean that only three musically distinct chord functions exist.

[[c13-dim7]]

Each of the four tones can be a leading tone and resolve a semitone upward: D♯ to E, F♯ to G, A to B♭, C to D♭. A single chord therefore leads into four keys, each a minor third apart. As a dominant substitute, D♯dim7 before Em corresponds to a B7♭9 without root; the sound is sharper than B7 because the tritone is present twice. Vivaldi uses the diminished seventh for storm and terror, often as tremolo; in slow metal it appears in passing (E–D♯–D in the bass) and in organ pads as church sound. The leading-tone dim7 (D♯dim7 to Em) must be distinguished from the dim7 over its own root (Edim7 = E G B♭ D♭), which is a colour over E and not a dominant.

## 15.4 Modulation

Modulation establishes a new centre. A common chord can mediate the move and a cadence can confirm it. Both are possible, neither is necessary: repetition, a pedal, melody or a direct cut can also establish a centre. Diatonic collections a fifth apart share six of their seven pitches.

[[c13-pivot]]

From E minor to A minor: Am is iv in E minor and i in A minor, the pivot; E7 is the new dominant, with G♯, which does not occur in E minor; Am is the arrival. After the third bar E minor has been left without any jolt being heard. Vivaldi modulates in every fast movement to the dominant or the relative key and back; Biber closes the first part of a dance movement in the dominant or relative and comes home in the second.

Third-related keys lie a third apart and share fewer tones; the change is a jolt. E to C (major third down) opens, E to G (relative) is soft, E to C♯ or E♭ is hard. The chromatic mediant changes between keys of the same mode a third apart, E minor to C minor, with two foreign tones and a cinematic sound.

[[c13-modulation]]

[[c13-shift]]

The example transposes a riff from E minor to G minor without a connecting chord. If G is established as the new center, this is a direct modulation. A brief transposition without stable confirmation can instead be a tonicization or sequence. A pivot is not a necessary condition for modulation.

## 15.5 Summary

- Secondary dominant: a major chord, often with a minor seventh, a fifth above its target.
- E7 can temporarily confirm Am.
- Neapolitan in E minor: F/A preparing the dominant; F5–E5 alone is insufficient.
- In equal temperament, dim7 has three symmetrical pitch-class sets; spelling and function can change.
- Modulation establishes a new center, with or without a pivot.
- A transposed riff can create a direct modulation.
