c14.title: Bass models and sequences
c14.text:
A bass model is a fixed bass sequence over which the upper voices move freely; a sequence is the transposition of a pattern to other degrees. Both are the engines of Baroque harmony and, often unrecognised, the building forms of the riff. This chapter presents the most important models: lamento, circle of fifths, chain of sevenths, falling thirds and the ostinato of the ciacona.

## 16.1 The lamento bass

The oldest model in this book is the descending tetrachord from root to fifth, the lamento bass: diatonic E–D–C–B or chromatic E–E♭–D–D♭–C–B. In the 17th century it was the formula of lament; Vivaldi uses it in slow movements, Biber in variations. It works because every step is small, the direction unambiguous and the goal, the dominant, the point of greatest expectation. Over every bass tone a different chord can be built: Em, D (or Bm/D), C, B.

[[c14-lamento]]

The example shows both versions and the arrival on Em. In the chromatic one the upper voices fall in parallel sixths, and every bass step carries a chord of its own.

[[c14-riff]]

Slow metal did not quote the lamento bass but rediscovered it; Em–D–C–B is the progression of countless riffs, mostly in power chords. The example plays it as E5–D5–C5–B5 with a line above that stands in thirds and sixths to the bass and at the end brings on D♯ the leading tone that the power chord B5 itself lacks.

[[c14-ascending]]

The ascending tetrachord B–C–D–E is the reverse of the model and the arrival after the descent: B, C, D, Em, every step a chord, and the last one the tonic. Descent and ascent together form an eight-bar shape that does without a cadence and still arrives.

## 16.2 The circle of fifths

The diatonic descending-fifths sequence in E minor follows E–A–D–G–C–F#–B–E. C–F# is not a descending perfect fifth but a diminished fifth, or an ascending augmented fourth. Em–Am–D–G–C–F#dim–Bm–Em stays diatonic; B major adds the leading tone for the return. Bass motion alone does not make each chord a functional dominant of the next.

[[c14-fifths]]

The upper voice of the example is itself a sequence: the same three-tone motif is transposed along with the bass. Where the scale has semitones the motif changes its spacing; that is the diatonic sequence which chapter 26 treats as a formal device.

## 16.3 The chain of sevenths

Giving every chord of the circle of fifths a seventh makes it fall into the third of the next chord: D, the seventh of Em7, becomes C, the third of Am7; G, the seventh of Am7, becomes F♯, the third of D7. Two voices alternate, one holds, one falls. That is the engine of the Baroque sequence and the basis of every modulation in Vivaldi.

[[c14-sevenths]]

The seventh-chord chain is a voice-leading model that can also be used outside Baroque music. Seventh chords can convey direction or sustained color; genre and chord name alone do not determine their effect.

## 16.4 Other sequence models

Falling thirds (E–C–A–F♯) are soft because every chord shares two tones with the next; the sequence floats and suits a riff without a goal. Rising fifths (E–B–F♯) are the reverse of falling fifths and build rather than release. Falling seconds are the lamento.

[[c14-thirds]]

Bars 1 to 4 show the falling thirds: from Em to C, E and G stay, from C to Am, C and E stay, from Am to F♯m7♭5, A, C and E stay; the upper voices hardly stir, and the progression could continue in any direction. Bars 5 to 8 show the rising fifths Em–Bm–F♯dim: every step moves away from the centre, and the diminished chord on F♯ forces the return.

Diatonic sequences follow the degrees of the current scale and can change their semitone distances. Real sequences preserve semitone distances. A real sequence can introduce foreign notes without establishing a new center, so it is not automatically a modulation.

[[c14-sequence]]

Bars 1 to 4 transpose a motif diatonically downward: the letters shift, the spacings follow the key, and the sequence stays in E minor. Bars 5 to 8 transpose the same motif really, each time exactly a whole tone lower with the same semitone spacings; after three steps, with F, E♭, D♭ and B♭, the key has been left. The diatonic sequence is the rule; the real one is a means of modulation and in the Baroque a sign of intensification.

## 16.5 Ostinato: ciacona and passacaglia

An ostinato is a bass model that repeats unchanged while everything above it changes. The Baroque ciacona (also chaconne) and passacaglia are variation sets over a four- or eight-bar bass in triple meter; Biber closes the third partita of the *Harmonia artificioso-ariosa* with a ciacona and the fifth with a passacaglia. After the second pass the listener knows the bass and hears only what is new above it.

[[c14-ciacona]]

The example lays out a four-bar bass model E–B–C–B in quarters and brings an upper voice with leading tone on the second pass. The model can be repeated any number of times; every pass needs only a new upper voice, and after the last one an ending must stand, otherwise the piece stops instead of ending.

[[c14-layers]]

The riff is the same principle: a bass model repeats, and voice, violin or lead guitar vary above it. The example shows three layers over Em–C–Am–B7: the bass, a figure in eighths that fills it out, and a melody that moves freely above. Chapter 22 treats the layered texture, chapter 27 repetition as form.

## 16.6 Summary

- Lament bass: a descending tetrachord such as E–D–C–B, also possible chromatically.
- B–C–D–E reverses the model’s direction.
- A diatonic fifths sequence can contain a diminished fifth; function does not follow solely from bass interval.
- A seventh-chord chain links chords through descending sevenths.
- Descending thirds, ascending fifths and descending seconds are different sequence paths.
- Diatonic follows the scale; real preserves semitone distances. Modulation requires a new center.
- An ostinato repeats a pattern; a chaconne is a historical variation model.

c15.title: Meter and subdivision
c15.text:
Rhythm is the ordering of time into beats and their weighting, meter the grouping of those beats. This chapter leads from the pulse through subdivision to the deviations that make rhythm interesting: syncopation, polyrhythm, hemiola, odd meters, swing. Each of these deviations presupposes that the pulse stays audible; without reference no deviation can be heard.

## 17.1 Pulse and accent

Music orders time into even beats, the pulse, and the pulse orders itself into groups with an accented first beat, the meter. The bar is the notation of meter (chapter 4). There are two basic meters: duple with groups of two or four beats and triple with groups of three. Within a 4/4 bar the first beat is heaviest, the third second heaviest, the second and fourth light.

[[c15-accents]]

Accent arises through loudness, length, harmonic change and bass entry. Bars 1 and 2 make it audible with accent marks; bars 3 and 4 achieve the same without accents, merely because the bass changes on 1 and 3 while the melody stays on one tone. The ear hears the harmonic change as weight. The drums make the same weighting audible with kick and snare (chapter 19).

## 17.2 Binary and ternary

Every beat can be divided in two or in three. Duple division (eighths in 4/4) is the straight, walking feel; triple division (triplets in 4/4 or eighths in 12/8) the rocking one. All further subdivisions are combinations: sixteenths are 2 × 2, sextuplets 2 × 3 or 3 × 2.

[[c15-binary]]

The bass retains quarter pulses while the upper subdivision changes from two to three. Three triplet eighths last as long as two straight eighths. 12/8 can directly show four large pulses with triple subdivision; 6/8 two, 9/8 three. Extended triplet passages in 4/4 are also valid. Meter and beams should make grouping readable; compound-meter tempo usually names the dotted quarter.

[[c15-compound]]

The example in 12/8 is counted 1-2-3 2-2-3 3-2-3 4-2-3. The bass holds two big pulses per bar. The same tone sequence in 4/4 as straight eighths would walk instead of rock; the subdivision is not a detail but the basic posture of a piece. Vivaldi writes the Danza pastorale, the third movement of Spring, in 12/8; Type O Negative have pieces in triple meter and in 6/8; My Dying Bride alternate within a piece between straight and triplet riffs.

## 17.3 Syncopation

A syncopation shifts the accent to a light beat or between the beats.

[[c15-sync]]

It arises in three ways: through an entry on the "and" that is held across the next strong beat (bar 1); through a rest on the strong beat so that the first tone comes on the light one (bar 2); through an accent on the light beat in an otherwise straight rhythm (bar 3). The first form is written with a tie so that the beat played across remains visible (chapter 4). The syncopation works only while the pulse stays audible; that is why the bass holds the whole note in every bar. Without reference it is just another rhythm.

## 17.4 Polyrhythm and hemiola

In polyrhythm two voices divide the same span differently: three against two, four against three. The shared span is divided into the least common multiple, for 3:2 into six; the triple voice enters on 1, 3 and 5, the duple voice on 1 and 4. Both share only the beginning.

[[c15-poly]]

A hemiola places groups of three and two within the same time span against each other or in succession. In 6/8, six eighths can be regrouped from 3+3 into 2+2+2. Across two bars of 3/4, six quarters can be weighted as 2+2+2 instead of 3+3. Both change perceived grouping without changing total duration.

[[c15-hemiola]]

[[c15-332]]

3+3+2 in 4/4 divides eight eighths into unequal groups. This is asymmetrical accent grouping, not a classical 3:2 hemiola. Quarter notes can continue unchanged beneath it. Compare accents and quarters in the grid: some attacks coincide and others fall between beats.

## 17.5 Odd meters

An odd meter is a chain of groups of two and three that does not split into equal halves: 5/8 as 2+3 or 3+2, 7/8 as 2+2+3, 3+2+2 or 2+3+2, 5/4 as 3+2 or 2+3 in quarters. The grouping is part of the composition, not of the notation; 2+3 and 3+2 are different rhythms.

[[c15-odd]]

[[c15-five]]

Odd meters may organise an entire section or appear as a single extension or contraction. The example’s 2+2+3 grouping makes three unequal steps audible. A riff may instead require 3+2+2 or another grouping. Singing, clapping and playing can clarify it; difficulty singing a rhythm does not automatically make it wrong.

## 17.6 Swing and shuffle

Swing shifts the second eighth of every beat backward. Straight eighths are written with the indication swing or shuffle, and long–short is played. The ratio varies: 2:1 corresponds to the triplet, 3:1 to dotting, 3:2 lies between; at slow tempo it becomes more extreme, at fast tempo straighter. Drum machines give it as a percentage of the first eighth: 50 straight, 67 triplet, 75 dotted (appendix C). The French Baroque practice of unequal notes (notes inégales) likewise plays written equal eighths unequally; whether a Vivaldi recording does so is a decision of the ensemble. Unequal eighths have been a question of performance, not of notation, for three hundred years.

[[c15-swing]]

The riff uses ordinary eighths with a swing instruction; preview uses 2:1 as a learning model. Actual swing timing depends on tempo, style and interpretation. Ternary accompaniment is available in original doom, gothic and progressive pieces too; the references do not restrict the choice.

## 17.7 Summary

- Pulse, meter, bar: beats, their grouping, their notation. In 4/4, 1 is heavy, 3 medium, 2 and 4 light.
- Weight arises through accent, length, harmonic change and bass.
- Binary walks, ternary rocks; lasting triple division is written as 12/8, 6/8, 9/8.
- Syncopation: entry on "and", rest on the beat, accent on the light beat; it needs the audible pulse.
- Polyrhythm divides simultaneously, hemiola in succession; 3+3+2 is the hemiola of 4/4.
- Odd meters are chains of 2 and 3; the grouping must be singable.
- Swing is long–short with straight notation; a device, not a trait of the references.

c16.title: Tempo and the shaping of time
c16.text:
Tempo is more than a number: it decides how long a tone sounds, how a bar feels and where the boundaries of a piece lie. This chapter treats tempo as a decision about decay, the half-time feel, the freedoms of rubato and fermata, the small shifts of agogics and the relations between two tempi.

## 18.1 Tempo and decay

Tempo is the speed of the pulse, measured in beats per minute (chapter 4).

[[c16-seconds]]

At ♩ = 60, 60/60 = 1 second per quarter. A half lasts 2 seconds and a whole 4. The example compares these prescribed durations. Audible decay time is a different quantity: it depends on instrument, attack, damping, sound and hearing threshold. Fixed clean and distorted sustain times cannot be inferred from it.

[[c16-decay]]

Three tied whole notes at ♩ = 60 last 3 × 4 × 1 = 12 seconds. A note can occupy time after its audible decay; this does not make it a rest. At ♩ = 140 an eighth lasts 60/140/2 ≈ 0.214 seconds. Two seconds of reverberation at ♩ = 60 correspond to two quarters, not half a beat. Reverberation follows a decaying room response and does not extend every note by an exact fixed amount.

## 18.2 Half-time

The same tempo can feel twice as fast or half as fast depending on where the accent lies.

[[c16-halftime]]

The example writes a drum pattern on the pitched staves (chapter 19): the hi-hat as eighths on top, the snare as an accent in the middle, the kick at the bottom. In bars 1 and 2 the snare lies on 2 and 4; the bar feels in quarters. In bars 3 and 4 it lies only on 3; the bar feels in halves, the half-time feel, although tempo and hi-hat are unchanged. The hi-hat keeps the grid, the snare defines the felt speed.

At ♩ = 60, a quarter pulse lasts 1 second. If the half note becomes the felt pulse, pulses are 2 seconds apart: 60/2 = 30 half notes per minute. A backbeat change can alter the feel without changing the written tempo. This is half-time or double-time; metric modulation actually changes the tempo reference or pulse through a shared ratio.

## 18.3 Rubato, ritardando, fermata

Rubato means flexible shaping of time. It can displace individual voices against a steady accompaniment or change the common tempo. Not every stretch must be mathematically repaid. Ritardando slows, accelerando speeds up, and a fermata extends a note or rest according to musical judgment. These devices are also possible with responsive drums.

[[c16-rubato]]

The example uses fixed note values; the preview performs neither rubato nor fermatas. Time shaping belongs to the performance. A static accompaniment loop allows less freedom than a responsive ensemble. Stretches and pauses follow the phrase; consecutive fermatas are not forbidden.

## 18.4 Agogics

Agogics means expression through temporal weighting, such as slightly extending a target note. Microtiming is a related but distinct idea: an onset falls slightly before or after a shared grid. The same displacement can have different effects depending on tempo, articulation and ensemble timing. The preview uses a fixed grid and does not demonstrate these offsets.

[[c16-agogic]]

If all voices enter at a constant offset from the grid, the whole performance is displaced in time, not automatically slower. It becomes slower only when the intervals between onsets increase. A click or an unchanged voice provides a reference for comparison.

## 18.5 Tempo relations

Two sections can stand in simple ratios: double (♩ = 60 to ♩ = 120), half, or linked through a shared subdivision.

[[c16-ratio]]

A triplet quarter at ♩ = 60 lasts 1 × 2/3 ≈ 0.667 seconds. If it becomes the new quarter, 60/0.667 ≈ 90 BPM: a factor of 3/2. The preview changes from ♩ = 60 to ♩ = 90 at measure 3. Triplet quarters before the boundary and quarters afterwards therefore have equal duration. The bass also follows the new tempo.

## 18.6 Summary

- At ♩ = 60, a quarter lasts 1 second and a whole 4.
- Notated duration and audible decay time are different quantities.
- Half-time changes the pulse feel while written tempo remains constant.
- Rubato, ritardando and fermatas shape time; an ensemble can follow together.
- A constant overall offset is not a tempo change.
- Metric modulation links pulses through a shared note value, such as a factor of 3/2.

c17.title: The drums
c17.text:
Drums can shape pulse, subdivision, weight and form, or act as an independent line. This chapter covers notation, common pattern roles, attack weighting and transitions. Its grid examples can be programmed on suitable drum machines or performed by hand.

## 19.1 Notation

Common percussion notation assigns lines and spaces to instruments rather than pitches; the assignment can require a legend. This book uses B4 for hi-hat, E4 for snare and E2 for kick as a rhythm model. The preview plays these as piano pitches, not actual percussion sounds. Course accompaniment instead uses MIDI percussion notes on channel 10.

## 19.2 The grammar of a pattern

A pattern has three levels. The hi-hat (or ride) gives the subdivision: quarters, eighths or sixteenths. It is the grid on which everything else hangs; closed it sounds dry, open it is an accent with decay. The snare gives the backbeat: in 4/4 on 2 and 4 or, in half-time, only on 3. The kick gives the foundation and links with the bass: on 1 and 3, or on 1 alone, plus syncopations doubling the rhythm of the bass voice.

[[c17-patterns]]

The example places both basic patterns side by side. The tempo is the same; the snare on 3 halves the felt speed (chapter 18).

[[c17-weight]]

The accents mark the weighting: the kick on 1 is louder than the one on 3, the hi-hat on the beats louder than between them, the snare loudest. Bar 1 plays the pattern without this weighting, bar 2 with it. Without weighting every pattern sounds like a machine; with it even a programmed one sounds played.

[[c17-compound]]

A slow pulse allows large gaps between attacks, but can also carry dense hi-hat, kick or tom figures. At ♩ = 60 a quarter lasts one second; an attack every two quarters is two seconds apart. Half-time is a possible treatment, not a tempo requirement. The kick can double the bass, answer it or provide a different accent.

## 19.3 The drums in slow metal

At tempi between fifty and eighty the drums are less an engine than an architect. The rests are long; one hit every two seconds is normal, and every hit therefore has to sit. Half-time is the default, the kick follows the bass rhythm, toms replace the snare at transitions, the ride replaces the hi-hat in open sections, and the crash rings out long.

[[c17-tremolo]]

The following notes transfer a percussive function to a repeated bass pitch. Sixteenths can animate a quarter pulse while chords hold. This is an original analogy to tremolo and tutti weight; it does not imply that all continuo parts function identically or that every baroque ensemble lacked percussion.

## 19.4 Fills and form signals

A fill, crash, pattern change or dropout can mark a formal boundary. Melody, harmony, register or articulation can also make the boundary audible while drums continue unchanged. Choose a signal when it supports the actual phrase.

[[c17-fills]]

Two or three tom attacks may suffice for a fill. A dense roll over a slow pulse is also possible; it does not automatically accelerate the tempo. The destination downbeat must remain in place regardless of fill density.

[[c17-signals]]

Two further signals: in bar 3 the drums drop out, and the silence is louder than any fill; bar 4 re-enters with the crash on the one, and the new section is marked. Both signals cost nothing and work more strongly at slow tempo than at fast, because the pause is longer.

## 19.5 Patterns as grids

A sequencer may use sixteen steps per 4/4 bar for sixteenths and twelve per 12/8 bar for eighths. Hi-hat, snare and kick have individual attacks and velocities. Counting from 1, a 4/4 half-time snare falls on step 9 and a straight backbeat on 5 and 13. Fills, swing and timing offsets are further choices. Some sequencers provide other resolutions, unquantised recording or separate track lengths; a rigid grid is not a universal property.

## 19.6 Summary

- Hi-hat, snare and kick can supply subdivision, backbeat and foundation; roles may change.
- Velocities and note endings shape weight; uniformity is also a deliberate choice.
- Half-time and straight backbeats work at different tempos.
- Tremolo and tutti can have percussive impact; the examples are original analogies.
- Fills, crashes, changes and dropouts are possible formal signals.
- Patterns contain attacks, durations and velocities; resolution and timing depend on the system.

c18.title: Two-part writing
c18.text:
Two voices already allow distinct contours, rhythms and timbral roles. This chapter covers motion types, selected historical dissonance treatments, suspensions, parallel thirds and sixths, imitation and canon. Bass and melody are a useful framework, not the only possible two-voice texture.

## 20.1 Types of motion

Two voices can move in four ways relative to each other. Parallel motion: same direction, same interval, such as thirds or sixths. Similar motion: same direction, changing interval. Oblique motion: one voice holds, the other moves; that is the pedal with melody from chapter 14. Contrary motion: opposite directions.

[[c18-motion]]

Changing motion types can create contrast. Continuous parallels can connect voices; oblique motion can support a drone. Either can form a complete texture. With two violins, as in Biber's partitas, the types of motion change within a few bars; with two guitars, as My Dying Bride lead them, parallels in thirds and sixths over the riff dominate, and the violin adds a third voice above.

## 20.2 Consonance and dissonance in part writing

Between two voices, octave, fifth, third and sixth are consonances; second, seventh and tritone dissonances. The fourth is a dissonance against the bass because the bass is heard as the root and the fourth above it sounds like a suspension before the third; between two upper voices over a bass it is a consonance. In strict writing consonances stand on the accented beats; dissonances appear on light beats as passing or neighbour tones reached and left by step, or on heavy beats as suspensions.

[[c18-passing]]

Bar 1 approaches and leaves F# over C stepwise as a passing tone; bar 2 decorates G with F# over E as a neighbour. Bar 3 leaps between consonances. These examples follow a limited convention. Other valid figures include the leaping approach of an appoggiatura and the leaping departure of an escape tone; chordal dissonances and modal friction can receive other treatments. A dissonant leap is not a universal compositional error.

## 20.3 The suspension

A suspension is a tone held over from the previous chord that becomes dissonant in the new one and then resolves downward by step. It has three phases: preparation (the tone is consonant), dissonance (on the heavy beat), resolution (on the light one). The most common suspensions are 4–3 (fourth resolving into third), 7–6 (seventh into sixth) and 9–8 (ninth into octave), named after the intervals above the bass.

[[c18-suspensions]]

The example shows all three in the same form: one bar of preparation, in which the tone lies consonant over its bass, then the bass change that makes the held tone dissonant, then the resolution by a step downward. A over A is the octave; over E it becomes the fourth and resolves to G. B over D is the sixth; over C it becomes the seventh and resolves to A. C over A is the third; over B it becomes the ninth and resolves to B. Vivaldi's Largo movements consist over long stretches of chains of such suspensions; the tension arises not through new chords but through delayed voices. Slow metal does the same when the violin or a keyboard tone holds across a chord change and becomes dissonant for a bar. The first example of this chapter likewise ends with a suspension: A held over E as a fourth resolving to G.

## 20.4 Parallel thirds and sixths

Two voices a third apart through a scale alternate between major and minor thirds: in E Aeolian E–G, F♯–A, A–C and B–D are minor, G–B, C–E and D–F♯ major. Sixths are the inversions: the minor third becomes a major sixth. Thirds sound dense, sixths open; both are the standard parallels of the Baroque between first and second violin, and both are the standard parallels of two guitars.

[[c18-thirds]]

[[c18-sixths]]

Parallel thirds and sixths can connect lines. Register and distortion affect their clarity; neither implies a fixed register boundary or gain rule. The example changes from parallel sixths to contrary motion. This creates contrast but is not required after a fixed number of measures.

## 20.5 Imitation and canon

Imitation means one voice repeating what another played shortly before. In a canon this happens strictly: the second voice (the comes) follows the first (the dux) at a fixed distance and fixed interval, usually the octave or fifth, and the melody must be built so that it stays consonant against itself. Biber's partitas contain canons for two violins; the *Harmonia artificioso-ariosa* is over long stretches a textbook of two-part writing.

[[c18-canon]]

The following voice takes up the descending line one measure later and an octave lower. With a delay of two half notes, the voices form mostly sixths, including major and minor sixths. At the end the following voice changes: F# rises to G rather than strictly following the leader to E. The example is therefore an octave canon with a free ending, not a strict canon throughout.

## 20.6 Bass and melody as two-part writing

On a guitar alone or in two hands every piece with bass and melody is two-part writing.

[[c18-bassmelody]]

Bars 1–2 use oblique motion; bars 3–4 contrast E–D–C–B in the bass with G–A–B–D# above; bar 5 arrives. Here the particular progression creates the peak. Contrary motion is not inherently a climax, and consonance on every strong beat is not required in every piece.

## 20.7 Summary

- Motion types: parallel, similar, oblique and contrary.
- Passing and neighbour tones are possible dissonance treatments; other figures permit leaps.
- A classical suspension combines preparation, tied dissonance and usually stepwise downward resolution.
- Thirds and sixths can move in parallel; register and timbre shape their effect.
- Canon follows an imitation rule; its dissonance treatment depends on style.
- Bass and melody can remain independent without a fixed climax formula.

c19.title: Melody and bass
c19.text:
Melody and bass are the two outer voices a listener perceives first. This chapter treats melody as contour, phrase and goal, its relation to power chords, and the bass in its three roles and its register. What lies between, the layers and pads, is treated in chapter 22.

## 21.1 Motif and contour

A melody is a sequence of tones with its own contour, rhythm and goal. Its smallest building block is the motif: two to five tones with a rhythm, recognised as a unit. The contour is the outline of the motion, rising, falling, arched, static; it is recognised even when the pitches change, and is therefore what links a sequence or a variation to the original (chapter 26).

[[c19-contour]]

Four bars from the same tones of the Em triad: rising, falling, as an arch, and as a leap with stepwise return. Steps (seconds) hold the line together, leaps (a third and larger) open it; after a large leap a good melody usually returns by step in the opposite direction, as in bar 4 after the leap E–B.

## 21.2 Target tone and phrase

Every phrase has a tone toward which it runs: the target tone, usually at the end, often the root or the fifth, in modal music also the characteristic tone. What the target is, is decided by duration, accent and position at the phrase end.

[[c19-target]]

The melody ends over B with D#4–F#4. This is a minor third: MIDI 66 − 63 = 3 semitones, not a semitone. F# is the fifth of the B major chord, so the phrase ends on a dominant sound. A subsequent return to Em would provide a different closing model.

[[c19-phrases]]

Between two phrases the melody breathes: a rest or a long tone separates them. The example has two two-bar phrases, each with a rest at the end, and a target tone in the fifth bar on which both arrive. Slow metal has long phrases with few tones; the rests are often longer than the phrases. The violin in My Dying Bride and the voice in Anathema lead such lines over the riffs; Vivaldi's solo violin has shorter phrases with more tones, but the same principle: motion to the goal, then breath.

## 21.3 Melody over power chords

Over fifths without thirds the melody determines the mode of the chord.

[[c19-overpower]]

G above E5 supplies the minor third and G# the major third. E minor pentatonic contains E G A B D. Above E, A and D form a fourth and minor seventh; above B5, G can form a minor sixth. This collection therefore guarantees neither consonance nor a suitable target over every power chord. Chord, duration and accent also matter.

[[c19-characteristic]]

F# and C extend E minor pentatonic to the Aeolian collection; F instead of F# can add Phrygian color. Whether a mode becomes audible depends on more than one note. The example compares different additions above E; “correct” or “better” does not follow solely from the scale’s name.

## 21.4 The three roles of the bass

The bass has three possible jobs. As doubling it plays the guitar riff an octave lower: pressure and unity, no new information; that is the default in doom. As foundation it plays roots in long values under chords or figures: calm and room for the motion above; that is the default in Anathema and in every continuo. As countervoice it has a line of its own with passing tones, leaps and rhythm: two-part writing and density; Type O Negative often let the bass carry the actual melody under the voice.

[[c19-roles]]

[[c19-continuo]]

A continuo bass can connect roots, chord tones and passing tones. The example gives Em–Am–B7–Em with motion between downbeats. The bass may move more frequently than the melody: a walking bass beneath a sustained upper voice is a counterexample to the opposite rule. Clear function and controlled balance are what matter.

## 21.5 Bass register

E1 is approximately 41.2 Hz and B3 approximately 246.9 Hz: f = 440 × 2^((n − 69)/12). These are fundamental frequencies, not exclusive frequency territories of an instrument. Bass, guitar and kick have overtones and overlapping spectra. Loudness, articulation, voicing and sound processing determine how clearly they can be distinguished.

[[c19-register]]

The example shifts the guitar fifth an octave relative to the bass, changing their overlap. Simultaneous low notes are not automatically wrong; the same pitch can be doubled intentionally. Minor thirds have no universal lower boundary at C3 either. The voice intended for the foreground must remain audible in the actual mix.

## 21.6 Summary

- Motive and contour make a line recognizable.
- Steps and leaps are compositional tools, not guarantees of quality.
- Duration, accent and position can emphasize a target.
- Melody can supply thirds over power chords; pentatonic scales do not guarantee consonance.
- Bass roles: doubling, foundation and counterline.
- The bass may change more frequently than the melody; overlapping registers are possible.

c20.title: Layered writing
c20.text:
Bass and melody can form a complete texture. Additional figures, pads and inner voices change density and roles; each added layer needs its rhythm and register. This chapter treats the three layers, the arpeggio figure, the distribution by register, density as a controllable quantity, the frequency spaces of the sounds and the question of what happens in an instrumental piece with the register of the voice.

## 22.1 Three layers

One possible three-layer model assigns bass as reference, an inner voice or figure as movement, and melody as a recognisable line. Different rhythms make the layers easier to distinguish. A complete piece can also be monophonic; two voices or homorhythmic chords do not need a third layer to be musically complete.

[[c20-three]]

The example gives bass, figure and melody different rhythms. Simultaneous attacks do not automatically merge voices into one: in homorhythmic writing several voices share a rhythm while retaining independent pitch paths.

## 22.2 The arpeggio figure

An arpeggio distributes the tones of a chord in time. As a middle layer it supplies motion without melody; the figure stays the same while the bass changes, and only the tones that do not fit the new chord move a step. So the texture stays calm although it moves. On *Eternity* Anathema build long sections from clean arpeggio figures over keyboard pads; Vivaldi's accompanying voices break chords into even motion in a similar way.

[[c20-arpeggio]]

Common tones can connect chord changes in an arpeggio figure. The chords determine which notes remain: E belongs to Em, C and Am, but is not a chord tone of B7. There E can act as a suspension or move to D#. Bass changes, melody rests and density follow the phrase, not a fixed minimum duration.

## 22.3 Register and layering

Register separation is a tool, not a set of fixed boundaries. Our 49-key synthesizer supplies C2–C6; the P4 guitar starts at E2. Bass, chords and melody may overlap in register. Different articulation, level, rhythmic activity and timbre help maintain clarity. The following voicings demonstrate one such distribution.

[[c20-registers]]

The example stacks a low fifth, high chord tones and a line between them. Instruments generated separately and then mixed do not automatically pass through the same distortion stage. A low keyboard third therefore does not inherently create intermodulation in a separately distorted guitar signal. Masking in the common mix and distortion within a sound source are different processes.

## 22.4 Density

Density has four dimensions: the number of voices, the number of attacks per bar, the width of the register and the sonic density through gain, reverb and chorus. Each can be controlled separately. A section with one voice, many attacks, narrow register and heavy gain is dense in a different way from one with four voices, few attacks, wide register and a clean sound. Across a piece density can be drawn as a curve; typically in slow metal voices and register grow until the last quarter while attacks stay low, with a drop in the middle. Vivaldi's ritornello form yields a zigzag: tutti dense, solo thin, with rising peaks.

[[c20-density]]

[[c20-terrace]]

A thin texture can make the following full texture seem stronger. Terrace dynamics describes stepped contrasts in level; a crescendo can also arise through stronger attack, breath or bow pressure, controller movement and added voices. Form determines where the maximum and minimum belong. A quiet ending or loud opening is not an error.

## 22.5 Frequency spaces

Register and frequency spectrum differ: high notes can have many upper partials, and so can low notes. Masking depends on level, spectrum and temporal overlap. A high-pass filter can remove unwanted lows and a low-pass can soften sharp highs. There is no requirement to high-pass every voice except the bass. Listen in context and filter only as far as the intended result requires.

[[c20-stack]]

The example distributes bass, fifth, pad and line across different registers. The preview demonstrates the written notes, not high-pass processing. Whether a filter improves clarity must be assessed in the complete sound; register alone does not establish masking.

## 22.6 The gap of the voice

Three of the five references are albums with vocals; the Vivaldi and Biber collections serve here as instrumental references. An instrumental arrangement can add a singing line, place chords in that register, or leave space deliberately. These different voices do not imply one fixed vocal range.

[[c20-gap]]

The opening bars leave space between bass and a high pad; a line then fills the gap. Chords in the middle register can also be effective. The key questions are which voice should receive attention and whether its contour remains audible amid the other notes.

## 22.7 Summary

- Bass, figure and melody are one possible model, not a mandatory ensemble.
- Shared rhythms can connect several independent voices.
- Register, articulation and level help distinguish them.
- Density changes through voice count, attacks, register and sound.
- Contrast can strengthen an entry; form determines where peaks belong.
- Apply filtering according to the audible result. A high-pass filter cannot replace voice leading.

c21.title: Guitar and amplifier
c21.text:
Guitar, amplifier and effects work together as a signal chain. Distortion changes how clearly voices are heard but imposes no universal rules of part writing. This chapter covers distortion, signal flow, sustain, modulation effects, harmonics, bending and string tension. Tempo remains a musical decision; long releases can also work in fast music.

## 23.1 Types of distortion

Distortion changes the waveform nonlinearly; clipping is one common process. Overdrive, distortion and fuzz describe overlapping sound and circuit categories. Soft or hard limiting, asymmetric transfer curves, filtering and level shape the result. Even heavily distorted sounds can respond to attack. Multiple tones produce additional intermodulation products; how they interfere or colour the sound depends on register, spectrum and circuit.

[[c21-gain]]

The example compares a triad with a power chord. The preview demonstrates the pitch collections with the same sound, not changing distortion settings. Compare different gain levels on the instrument, using matched loudness and the same notes.

[[c21-intervals]]

More distortion can make complex chords rougher; wider voicings, fewer notes and separate sound sources may help. This does not prohibit thirds through fuzz or assign intervals rigidly to gain levels. Compare the same phrase at matched loudness. SoundFont preview demonstrates notes, not distortion.

## 23.2 Gain staging

One possible chain is pickup → distortion → modulation → delay/reverb → amplification/speaker. Other orders are possible: delay before distortion treats repeats differently from delay after it. An effects loop exists only on amplifiers equipped for one. Compression before and after distortion serves different purposes. Match levels to each input and distinguish intentional distortion from unintended overload.

## 23.3 Sustain

Sustain depends on string, instrument, attack, damping, amplification and audibility threshold. Fixed decay times for E2 or E4 require specific measurements. Clean notes can also sustain for a long time; distortion can raise the quieter part of the decay without automatically creating unlimited sustain.

[[c21-sustain]]

The example compares written durations at ♩ = 60: two tied wholes last 2 × 4 × 1 = 8 seconds and a half lasts 2 seconds. These are compositional values, not measured properties of clean or distorted sounds. A line may still occupy time after its audible decay. Tempo, articulation and intended rests are chosen together.

## 23.4 Chorus, flanger, phaser

Chorus and flanger mix time-delayed, modulated signals with the original. Flanging typically uses shorter delays and often feedback; the mixture produces moving comb-filter notches. A phaser uses all-pass filters and phase-dependent cancellation. It is not merely another short delay stage. Rate, depth, feedback and mix determine the movement.

[[c21-modfx]]

One starting point is slow chorus after distortion with a low wet mix. A high-pass in the effect path can keep the low end steadier if that routing is available. Chorus before distortion or without high-pass produces other usable sounds. The phrases should remain intelligible with the chosen effect.

## 23.5 Harmonics and bending

A natural harmonic arises when the string is touched at a node and plucked: above the twelfth fret the second partial sounds (the octave), above the seventh the third (octave plus fifth), above the fifth the fourth (two octaves), above the fourth the fifth (two octaves plus major third). The diamond notehead denotes the sounding tone.

[[c21-harmonics]]

Above E2, partials 2–5 give E3, B3, E4 and approximately G#4; above A2 they give A3, E4, A4 and approximately C#5. A harmonic can contain further partials and is not a pure sine. The preview plays tempered pitches without reproducing harmonic timbre.

Bending pulls the fretted string sideways and raises the pitch continuously, usually by a semitone or whole tone to a heard target tone. The arrow in the notation names the target. Vibrato is a small, repeated bend; it raises the pitch and returns, it does not swing symmetrically around the fretted tone.

[[c21-bending]]

The intonation of a bend is checked against the target tone, which is heard fretted beforehand; in the example A4 is the fretted tone and B4 the target.

## 23.6 Low tuning and strings

With string and scale length fixed, tension is proportional to frequency squared. Tuning down a fourth gives a frequency factor of 2^(−5/12); squared, this is 2^(−10/12) ≈ 0.561, about 56 percent of the original tension. A semitone higher gives 2^(2/12) ≈ 1.122, about 12 percent more. Gauge, construction and setup determine suitable strings for a tuning. P4 raises the two highest strings by one semitone relative to standard tuning.

## 23.7 Summary

- Distortion changes spectrum and dynamics; overdrive, distortion and fuzz are not sharply bounded technical classes.
- Chord clarity depends on sound, voicing and arrangement.
- Effect order changes the result and is a compositional choice.
- Measure or listen to sustain; pitch and gain alone do not imply a fixed duration.
- Chorus and flanger use modulated delays; phaser uses all-pass filters.
- Harmonics near frets 12, 7, 5 and 4 give partials 2, 3, 4 and 5.
- With string and scale length fixed, tension changes with frequency squared.

c22.title: Synthesizers
c22.text:
Synthesizers can provide pads, organ, choir and bell colours, bass, melody or rhythmic chords. These roles are not exclusive; a distorted guitar can also play thirds and dense voicings. This chapter explains sources, filters, envelopes and modulation, and how different decays affect texture.

## 24.1 Subtractive synthesis

A subtractive synthesizer shapes a source signal through filters and an amplifier. An ideal sawtooth contains all integer harmonics; an ideal square wave at 50 percent duty cycle contains only odd harmonics. A triangle also has odd harmonics with rapidly falling amplitudes, while a sine contains one partial. Detuning can create beating, but pads can also use one oscillator, samples, wavetable or FM.

A low-pass filter attenuates high frequencies beyond its transition region rather than cutting them off abruptly. 24 dB/octave describes a steeper asymptotic slope than 12 dB/octave, not an automatically warmer sound. Resonance emphasises the cutoff region. High-pass and band-pass filters offer other spectral shapes. Whether low frequencies should be removed depends on the arrangement.

The envelope shapes the course: attack is the time to the maximum, decay the time to the sustain level, sustain the held level, release the time to silence after the key is let go. An envelope on the amplifier shapes loudness, one on the filter the timbral course. A pad has an attack around one second and a release around two; an organ attack zero, full sustain and short release; a bass attack zero and short decay.

[[c22-waveforms]]

The example shows the same chord as it is conceived with four sounds: a sawtooth with open filter, a square, a triangle, and two detuned sawtooths with slow envelope and high-pass as a pad. The SoundFont preview plays the tones; the sounds arise at the instrument.

## 24.2 Wavetable and FM

A wavetable oscillator has, instead of a fixed waveform, a table of many waveforms; one parameter selects the current one, and if it is modulated by envelope or LFO the sound travels through the table. This gives spectral motion that a filter alone cannot supply: metallic, glassy, vowel-like. For pads that change over seconds this is the sound of wavetable synthesis.

In FM one signal modulates another signal’s frequency, producing sidebands around the carrier. Frequency ratio and modulation depth determine their placement and strength. Integer ratios often yield harmonic spectra; rational noninteger ratios can also share a fundamental. Irrational ratios such as 1 to √2 have no common harmonic fundamental in the ideal model. Bell-like sounds are one application, not evidence of how a particular recording was produced.

[[c22-wavetable]]

## 24.3 Modulation

Sound design is largely the choice of connections between sources and destinations: velocity to the filter (hitting harder makes brighter), modulation wheel to the wave position, LFO to the pulse width, envelope to the filter (opens on attack and closes), key position to the filter (high notes brighter). Synthesizers lead these connections either in a modulation matrix, a list of source, destination and amount, or as a morph, in which wheel, velocity or pedal move almost every knob between two stored settings; the names change from instrument to instrument, the principle does not.

## 24.4 The three keyboard roles

Three useful roles are organ, pad and choir-like colour. An organ-like sound can start from added sine waves or other harmonically rich sources: short attack, high sustain level and short release. It can hold chord tones or carry independent lines. This is a design option for the following score, not a reconstruction of a particular album sound.

[[c22-organ]]

The example shows the organ's writing over power chords: the guitar plays E5, C5, A5, B5 without thirds, the organ lies above from G4 and supplies the thirds G, E, C and D♯; from chord to chord it changes one tone. So the sound stays clean below and complete above (chapters 11 and 14).

A possible string pad combines detuned sources, slow attack, longer release and chorus. Choose filter frequencies for the actual sound and arrangement; two kilohertz or 150 hertz are not universally suitable cutoffs. Choir colours may use formant filters, wavetables, samples or other sources across different registers. The following notes show voicings, not synthesis parameters.

[[c22-pad]]

The example compares low and high voicings. An octave shift changes the fundamentals and all partials; a high-pass filter attenuates spectral components below its cutoff. These are not equivalent operations. The preview plays the voicings without this filtering.

[[c22-roles]]

Begin with one sound per section when assessing voice balance. Multiple sounds and overlapping registers are possible; they require deliberate levels and note endings. The example supplies a starting distribution. Sound and density may change with the form.

## 24.5 Synthesizers in the texture

A synthesizer can sustain a suitable sound without natural decay. Sampled or plucked patches may instead decay while the key remains held. Piano energy decays after the attack, but fingers and pedal still control the note ending.

[[c22-hold]]

A written rest requires a deliberate note ending even on piano: a decaying note is not yet a rest. On a synthesizer the release phase contributes to the ending after key-up. Long tails can work at fast or slow tempos; attack spacing, register and intended overlap matter. A high-pass filter can create space but does not replace suitable voice distribution.

## 24.6 Summary

- Signal path: source → filter → amplifier; modulation controls its parameters.
- Ideal waveforms have different spectra. Pulse width changes harmonic content.
- Filter slope is measured in dB/octave, not in warmth.
- Attack, decay and release are time stages; sustain is a level.
- Wavetable changes waveforms; FM produces sidebands.
- Organ, pad and choir colours are possible roles, not fixed register laws.
- Written rests require controlled note endings on every instrument.

c23.title: Delay and reverb
c23.text:
Delay and reverb are the time effects: they repeat and lengthen what was played, and thereby change the writing, not only the sound. This chapter treats the four parameters of delay, the delay time in the bar, the three delay types, the parameters of reverb and the question of which register reverb belongs to.

## 25.1 The four parameters of delay

A delay reproduces a signal later in time. Important parameters include delay time, feedback, mix, filtering and modulation. Short times can produce doubling or comb-filter effects; longer times can be heard as separate echoes. The boundary also depends on signal and level. Feedback controls recirculation and therefore the number and decay of repeats. Modulating delay time also changes the delayed signal’s instantaneous pitch.

## 25.2 Delay in time

With quarter-note BPM, 60000/BPM gives the quarter duration in milliseconds. At ♩ = 60: 60000/60 = 1000 ms; eighth = 1000/2 = 500 ms, dotted eighth = 1000 × 3/4 = 750 ms, eighth triplet = 1000/3 ≈ 333 ms. Appendix C contains the table. A dotted-eighth delay shifts the first repeat by three sixteenths. Over continuous eighths, echoes therefore fall between later attacks. A quarter delay with exactly one repeat adds an attack halfway between half-note attacks. An eighth-triplet delay over straight eighths does not automatically produce shuffle: original and echo use different subdivisions.

[[c23-time]]

The notation compares rhythmic density schematically. It is not a complete transcription of a delay output. The following diagram shows the timing offset between original attacks and their first repeats more precisely.

[[c23-fill]]

The example places four attacks on the first eighth of each quarter. An eighth delay with exactly one repeat fills the second eighth: four original attacks + four echoes = eight onsets per bar. Distortion does not rule out delay; mix, filtering and rests help determine whether repeats remain distinct.

## 25.3 Tape, BBD, digital

Tape echo, bucket-brigade delay (BBD) and digital delay differ in how they produce the delay. Their names alone do not fully specify modulation, filtering, saturation or maximum delay time. For a listening comparison, change those properties individually while keeping the played motif the same.

[[c23-types]]

Tape and BBD delays may exhibit noise, saturation and altered high frequencies; digital algorithms can repeat cleanly or model those properties. Built-in modulation is not essential to every BBD delay. Matching parameter names do not guarantee identical circuits or sound. Comparing repeats trains listening rather than reliably identifying a device.

## 25.4 Reverb

Reverberation arises from many reflections or their technical simulation. Pre-delay shifts the reverb onset relative to the direct signal. RT60 is the time for a 60 dB level drop, not absolute silence. Damping changes frequency-dependent decay; diffusion changes reflection density. Room, hall, plate and spring name model families whose specific properties vary. Filtering the reverb path can create space.

[[c23-tail]]

At ♩ = 60, two seconds equal a half note. The example represents sonic overlap schematically with notes. In ordinary notation a staccato note is still a new, shortened attack; it does not mean “reverb only, do not play”. SoundFont preview attacks written notes and does not simulate a room response. For an original piece, describe the played voice and intended effect separately in sound directions.

## 25.5 Reverb as a register decision

Reverb distributes energy over time. On low voices it can blur the foundation or create an intended sense of space. Short rooms can preserve rhythmic contours; long tails can connect them. Register, damping and mix also matter. This does not imply a blanket ban on bass reverb or a fixed tempo dictated by decay.

[[c23-room]]

The example compares a riff and a high line with rests. A short room can preserve riff contours; longer reverb can partially fill rests. Whether that connection is desirable depends on the piece. In solo playing reverb can add a spatial layer, but it is neither necessary nor confined to high registers.

## 25.6 Summary

- Delay time, feedback, filtering, modulation and mix shape repetitions.
- With quarter-note BPM: 60000/BPM = quarter duration in milliseconds.
- A dotted eighth lasts three quarters of a quarter note: 750 ms at ♩ = 60.
- Tape, BBD and digital models differ through their specific circuits and algorithms.
- RT60 denotes a 60 dB level decrease, not absolute silence.
- Choose reverb on low or high voices according to sound and form.
- Notes mark played attacks; effect tails need separate sound directions.

c24-retrograde.title: Two further treatments: retrograde and diminution

c24-period.title: An eight-bar period: antecedent with half cadence, consequent with full close

c24.title: Motif, phrase, period
c24.text:
Form begins in the small: with the motif that is recognised, with the phrase that breathes, and with the period in which two phrases answer each other. This chapter introduces the treatments by which long pieces arise from few motifs, and shows the two basic forms of the phrase, period and sentence, plus the measure of the eight-bar unit and the riff as motif with bass.

## 26.1 The motif

The motif is the smallest unit recognised as an idea: a few tones with a rhythm. It is defined not by its pitches but by the union of contour and rhythm; that is why it stays recognisable when transposed, mirrored or stretched. A piece needs few motifs. What makes it long is their treatment.

[[c24-motif]]

The example repeats a motive and then changes its rhythm or final note. Isolating one change makes comparison easier during learning. Musical variation may change several properties simultaneously and remain recognizable: a motive can be rhythmically augmented and transposed at the same time, for example.

## 26.2 Treatment

The sequence transposes the motif to another degree, usually a step lower or higher, and keeps contour and rhythm; led diatonically the semitone spacings change in the process (chapter 16). Inversion mirrors the contour: up becomes down. Augmentation doubles the note values.

[[c24-treatments]]

The example leads a three-tone motif through sequence, inversion and augmentation over an E pedal. The references work with the same means: Vivaldi's episodes are sequences of the ritornello motif, Biber's variations are diminutions and embellishments of the aria, and a riff that sounds longer the second time is an augmentation.

[[c24-retrograde]]

Retrograde reads the motif backwards; it is hard to recognise by ear and more a device of writing than of listening. Diminution halves the note values and is the counterpart of augmentation; it turns a motif in quarters into a figure in eighths that fits twice into the bar.

## 26.3 Phrase and period

A phrase is a musically coherent unit, often with a cadence or resting point. A classical period joins antecedent and consequent: a basic idea and contrasting material lead to a weaker cadence; the consequent returns to the basic idea and closes more strongly. Eight measures are a common model, not a definition. Any two answering phrases do not automatically form a classical period.

[[c24-period]]

The period is the basic form of the tonal melody; Vivaldi's themes and Biber's dance movements are built from periods. A related form is the sentence: a two-bar motif, its repetition or sequence, then four bars of continuation to the cadence, likewise eight bars, but with acceleration instead of answer.

[[c24-sentence]]

The example shows the sentence: the basic idea over Em, the same idea a fourth higher over Am, then the continuation, in which the motif is shortened to its first two tones and driven over C and B7, finally the cadence. The period answers, the sentence presses; both are eight bars long.

## 26.4 Eight-bar units and riff lengths

Four- and eight-measure groups are common expectations established by style and preceding material. Three, five or irregular measure counts can also form complete phrases. A fifth measure only sounds like an extension if an earlier return was expected.

[[c24-lengths]]

Deviations are devices: the example plays a four-bar riff twice and on the second pass appends a fifth bar on D5 before E5 returns. The listener who expects the return after four bars is held back by a bar; the return weighs more afterwards. Vivaldi's odd phrase lengths in the solo passages and the riff lengthened by a bar are the same technique.

## 26.5 The motif in the riff

A riff is a recurring rhythmic or melodic figure, often in an accompaniment part. It requires neither an additional bass voice nor a fixed length. Sequence, augmentation, diminution and variation can develop it. Form determines whether this happens slowly or quickly.

[[c24-riff]]

The example plays a one-bar riff in quarters twice and then its augmentation in halves across two bars; the guitar fifth above lies still. What carries a riff is its repetition; what develops it is treatment by the rules of this chapter.

## 26.6 Summary

- A motive is a recognizable musical unit; pitch, rhythm and contour can contribute.
- An isolated change aids comparison in learning; variation can change multiple properties.
- Sequence transposes, inversion mirrors, retrograde reverses; augmentation and diminution change durations.
- A period joins weaker and stronger closure; a sentence joins presentation and continuation.
- Eight measures are a model, not a requirement.
- A riff is a recurring figure and needs no separate bass part.

c25-repeat.title: Repeat signs as form notation: A twice, then B

c25.title: Repetition as form
c25.text:
Form arises from return and contrast. This chapter orders the three kinds of return, ostinato, ritornello and chorus, sets song form against riff form, explains Vivaldi's ritornello form, names the tools of long form and treats the edges of a piece: intro, outro, transition.

## 27.1 Three kinds of return

An ostinato is a recurring rhythmic or melodic pattern, not necessarily a bass model. A ritornello returns between episodes and may be changed on its return. A refrain is a recurring section and can be instrumental. These terms describe different functions of repetition; they imply no fixed repetition counts.

## 27.2 Song form and riff form

Song form orders sections by function: verse (open, narrating), chorus (closed, repeated, denser), bridge (contrast, once), framed by intro and outro. Riff form orders sections as riffs: riff 1 four times, riff 2 four times, riff 1 shortened, riff 3 at a new tempo, riff 2 as the ending. No chorus, but return; the form lives on the contrast between riffs and on the length of the repetitions. *October Rust* is a song album with long intros and outros; *Turn Loose the Swans* builds pieces of seven to twelve minutes from few riffs, each long enough to become a state; *Eternity* mixes both, song form with riff lengths.

[[c25-song]]

The example contrasts sections A and B. A refrain is established through its role and return across the whole piece, not simply through a higher register or closing note. Instrumental music can use song forms, riff chains, ritornello forms or other designs. The letter sequence makes the chosen order visible.

[[c25-repeat]]

The repeat signs from chapter 4 are the notation of this form: A stands once on paper and is played twice, then B follows. In the score of a riff piece there are as few bars as there are riffs, and the form stands in the signs.

## 27.3 Ritornello form

A common Baroque concerto model begins with a tutti ritornello and then alternates with solo episodes. Returns may be shortened, reordered or moved to other keys. A return to the tonic often supports closure. The number, length and completeness of ritornellos must be established from the particular movement; they are not a fixed template.

[[c25-ritornello]]

For original riffs, the principle can be adapted: a recognisable section returns between contrasting episodes. How much each return changes is a compositional choice. This is a working model, not a claim about every piece by a reference band.

## 27.4 Long forms

Long forms need understandable relationships between sections. Returns, contrasts, shortened motifs, transitions, texture changes and rests can establish them. There is no minimum number of riff repetitions, fixed riff count or mandatory late climax. A form diagram shows when material returns and where something new begins.

[[c25-long]]

Sections gain function through context: a contrast can prepare, surprise or strengthen a return. Through-composed music without literal repetition is still a piece. When comparing two orders, listen for direction, proportion and transitions; interchangeability alone does not prove a section redundant.

## 27.5 Contrast and density arc

Contrast is heard through context. A thin passage can highlight the next full entry; a returning motif can feel especially familiar after a contrasting section. Peaks, minima and silence can be marked in a form diagram. Their order is flexible and should support the intended course.

## 27.6 Intro, outro, transition

An intro can establish pitch space, pulse, sound and expectation or deliberately leave them open. An outro can close through a cadence, thinning texture, return, cut-off or fade-out. A fade-out is a recording technique with formal effect; live it needs a playable equivalent, such as coordinated diminuendo or a separate ending.

[[c25-commontone]]

Transitions can use fills, rests, sustained voices, common tones or a change of pulse feel. The example holds B as Em changes to G. Half-time changes the feel without automatically being metric modulation. An abrupt transition can also be deliberate and successful.

[[c25-frame]]

## 27.7 Summary

- Ostinato: recurring pattern; ritornello: return between episodes; refrain: recurring section, also possible instrumentally.
- Letters name recognisable material. A′ denotes a variant.
- Four bars can carry A–B–A–C; longer lettered sections build larger forms.
- Return, contrast, proportion and transitions connect a form.
- Through-composed forms without literal repetition are also possible.
- Intro and outro frame the piece; fade-out and cut-off are different closing devices.

c26.title: Suite, variation, programme
c26.text:
The large forms of the Baroque, suite, variation and concerto, and programme music are the models for pieces longer than a song. This chapter presents them through Biber's partitas and Vivaldi's Seasons, shows the dance movements as shapes of time, variation as treatment of a whole theme and the programme as a formal aid, and ends with the album and the concert programme as a suite on a higher level.

## 28.1 The suite

A suite is a sequence of dance movements in one key. Biber's *Harmonia artificioso-ariosa* consists of seven such partitas. Each begins with a free movement, praeludium, sonata or intrada, and then strings dances: allamande, sarabande, gigue, aria, balletto, trezza, canario, amener, plus as finales a ciacona in the third and a passacaglia in the fifth partita; the sixth partita is an aria with thirteen variations, the seventh for two violas d'amore ends with a varied arietta. Every movement type has a fixed character through meter, tempo and rhythm.

[[c26-allemande]]

The allamande stands in duple meter, moderate, with an upbeat and running eighths; the example writes the upbeat as two eighths at the end of an otherwise empty first bar.

[[c26-sarabande]]

The sarabande stands in triple meter, slow, with weight on the second beat: the second beat is long, and there the weight lies. The same eight bars as a gigue in 12/8 at double tempo would be another movement without a single tone changing.

[[c26-gigue]]

The gigue stands in a fast compound meter with dotted rhythms, quarter and eighth within every group of three. The principle of the suite is contrast by type, not by material: one key, many shapes of time. Slow metal does the reverse, one shape of time over many harmonies.

## 28.2 Variation

A variation set presents a theme, the aria, and repeats it with one new treatment each time: the melody embellished in smaller values, the rhythm dotted, the harmony kept or changed, the register changed, the voices swapped. The bass or the harmony remains the constant against which the variation is measured; in the ciacona it is the bass alone (chapter 16), in the aria with variations harmony and phrase structure. Biber's sixth partita shows the set in thirteen stages.

[[c26-aria]]

The example varies an aria over the same bass through eighth-note embellishment and dotted rhythm. Here the contour remains recognizable; in other variations, harmony, bass or phrase structure can preserve the relationship instead. Not every variation must retain the original contour.

[[c26-variations]]

Two further stages: the third variation moves the aria up an octave without changing a tone; the fourth swaps the voices, the aria goes into the bass, and the upper voice holds what was previously the bass. Transferred to the riff: the bass stays, the texture changes from power chords to arpeggios to single voices, and the form arises from the succession of these versions.

## 28.3 Programme

Vivaldi attached sonnets to the *Four Seasons* and wrote their lines at the corresponding places in the score: birdsong, the murmuring brook, the summer thunderstorm, the autumn hunt, the chattering of teeth in the icy wind of winter.

[[c26-programme]]

Figures can suggest images: trills for birds, repetitions for cold, tremolo for a storm. Vivaldi’s sonnets establish an explicit relationship. Lyrics do not automatically make a piece program music. An imagined scenario can help composition, but does not force a particular loudness or duration.

## 28.4 The concerto

A Vivaldi concerto has three movements, fast, slow, fast, and the Seasons stand in E major, G minor, F major and F minor. The fast movements are ritornello forms (chapter 27), the slow movements are lines over a sustained accompaniment: in Winter a solo violin over plucked strings, an image of rain on the window. The same three-part shape carries many long pieces of slow metal: a fast or dense frame, a slow, thin middle section, the return. It is the simplest large form with contrast and return.

## 28.5 Album and set as suite

An album or set orders pieces into a larger course. Contrast, transitions and recurrence are possible tools; a late maximum is not required. Key distance alone does not determine whether a change feels smooth or abrupt. Add the durations: six pieces of six minutes plus four minutes of transitions give 6 × 6 + 4 = 40 minutes. Other numbers of pieces are equally possible.

## 28.6 Summary

- A suite joins several movements, often dances, usually around a common key.
- Allemande, sarabande and gigue are historical dance types with different rhythmic models.
- Variation can change melody, rhythm, harmony, bass, register or voice distribution.
- A program establishes an extramusical relationship; lyrics alone do not suffice.
- The Four Seasons use the concerto succession fast–slow–fast.
- A set plans relationships and actual durations; neither a late maximum nor a fixed piece count is required.

c27.title: The five references
c27.text:
The five references of this book are two metal albums from England, one from New York and two Baroque collections from Venice and Salzburg. This chapter describes each with the documented facts of its line-up, tuning and form, shows its texture in one short example each in the style of this book, and names at the end what they share and what they do not. The examples are not quotations but models: they show the mechanism, not the passage.

## 29.1 My Dying Bride, *Turn Loose the Swans* (1993)

The second album of the band from Halifax was released in October 1993 on Peaceville. Line-up: Aaron Stainthorpe (vocals), Andrew Craighan and Calvin Robertshaw (guitars), Adrian Jackson (bass), Rick Miah (drums), Martin Powell (violin and keyboards). Seven pieces, together almost an hour; the longest, *The Crown of Sympathy*, lasts over twelve minutes, three others between nine and ten. The first and the last piece dispense with the band line-up: *Sear Me MCMXCIII* consists of voice, keyboard and violin, *Black God* of keyboard, violin and two voices. On this album the violin is fully integrated into the band's sound, and the vocals combine guttural voice, speech and clear melody.

[[c27-mdb]]

The original example combines a low power-chord riff, thirds in higher voices and an additional line. It is a working model connecting chapters 11, 19 and 20. It does not establish specific registers, gain settings or chord progressions on the album. Such claims require identified passages and a transcription.

## 29.2 Type O Negative, *October Rust* (1996)

The fourth album of the band from Brooklyn was released in August 1996 on Roadrunner. Line-up: Peter Steele (vocals, bass), Kenny Hickey (guitar, vocals), Josh Silver (keyboards, programming, vocals), Johnny Kelly (drums, on the album as drum machine); the drum tracks are programmed, and Josh Silver, who produced the album with Steele, programmed them. The guitar stands in B standard, a fourth below normal tuning (chapter 8). The album is a song album with ballads, long intros and outros, a cover of Neil Young's *Cinnamon Girl* and two short joke pieces at the beginning.

[[c27-ton]]

The original example distributes fifths, chord tones and a line across several registers and ends on a major tonic. These choices serve the course; they do not prove a general register scheme or a Picardy third in particular album tracks. Programmed drums can support an arrangement; their effect depends on the entire pattern and texture.

## 29.3 Anathema, *Eternity* (1996)

The third album of the band from Liverpool was released in November 1996 on Peaceville. Line-up: Vincent Cavanagh (vocals, guitar), Daniel Cavanagh (guitar, keyboards), Duncan Patterson (bass), John Douglas (drums), plus guests with vocals, keyboards and, on the cover of Roy Harper's *Hope*, Harper himself with spoken word. The album moves away from the death-doom of the first two albums, with markedly more keyboards and mostly clean vocals.

[[c27-anathema]]

The original example holds E and B as common tones above Emadd9 and Cmaj9 while an arpeggio figure moves over them. It shows one way to combine a figure and a pad. The chord names describe these notes, not a verified passage from Eternity. The preview does not recreate album production or a delay chain.

## 29.4 Vivaldi, *Le quattro stagioni* (1725)

The four concertos for violin, strings and continuo were published in 1725 in Amsterdam as the first four of the twelve concertos *Il cimento dell'armonia e dell'inventione*, opus 8. Spring stands in E major, Summer in G minor, Autumn in F major, Winter in F minor; each has three movements, fast, slow, fast, and each is accompanied by a sonnet whose lines stand at the corresponding places in the score. The fast movements are ritornello forms, the slow ones lines over a sustained accompaniment. The accompaniment is written as thoroughbass.

[[c27-vivaldi]]

The original E major example uses broken triads and an IV–V–I cadence. Useful questions for analyzing The Four Seasons include ritornello returns, solo episodes, sequences and relationships to passages of the sonnets. Not every phrase must end in a cadence; the original example does not replace analysis of the score.

## 29.5 Biber, *Harmonia artificioso-ariosa* (1696)

The collection of seven partitas was published in 1696. Five are for two violins and continuo, the fourth for violin and viola, the seventh for two violas d'amore; six of the seven demand scordatura, only the sixth in D major stands in normal tuning (chapter 8, appendix A). Every partita begins with a free movement and then strings dances; the third ends with a ciacona, the fifth with a passacaglia, the sixth consists of an aria with thirteen variations and finale, the seventh ends with a varied arietta.

[[c27-biber]]

What the book has learned from it: two-part writing with imitation, parallels and contrary motion (chapter 20), the ostinato of ciacona and passacaglia (chapter 16), variation as form (chapter 28), the suite as a sequence of shapes of time in one key (chapter 28), and tuning as a compositional device (chapter 8). The example lets a second violin follow the first one bar later, an octave lower, over a bass that prepares the leading tone C♯ on the dominant.

## 29.6 What the five share and what they do not

The five references do not form one unified compositional system. Recurrence, contrast, bass writing and distribution of voices can be compared across them, but their execution differs. Spring in E major and Autumn in F major already contradict a shared minor-key basis. There is neither a shared number of climaxes nor fixed rules for their placement, register or tempo.

[[c27-common]]

The eight-measure example combines choices made in this course: a minor pitch collection, motivic return, a sustained inner voice and a closing cadence. It is an original texture, not evidence of traits shared by all references.

Three references are albums with vocals; Vivaldi’s concertos and Biber’s partias are instrumental works. Form, keys, tempo and use of cadences must be examined per piece or movement. An audible resemblance does not prove an identical technique or production chain. The book’s models are choices for original writing, not an exhaustive statistical account of the references.

## 29.7 Summary

- Three reference albums combine voices and instruments; two Baroque collections are instrumental.
- Personnel, publication and scordatura are verifiable work data.
- Registers, chord progressions and production methods need specific evidence.
- The original examples are models, not quotations or album analyses.
- Determine similarities and differences in each actual piece.
