c28.title: Listening, analysing, writing
c28.text:
Theory is the ability to hear with names. This last chapter applies the book: how to listen to a piece so that one knows what happens in it; how to analyse it so that one can write it down; and how to write, document and, over years, collect one's own pieces into a repertoire with the same terms. It is not a section of exercises but a description of the practice in which the terms of the previous chapters have their place.

## 30.1 Listening

One possible listening order starts with pulse and subdivision, then follows bass, harmony and melody separately before combining the observations. Other passes can begin with the most prominent line. No listening order turns a listener into the author; the finished sound does not reveal the composition process. Record unclear notes or measure boundaries as hypotheses and listen again.

Two questions help analysis: how is the centre confirmed across the whole phrase, and how do individual voices move? A leading tone alone does not prove tonality, nor does its absence prove modality. Singability helps make a voice understandable; wide leaps or chord blocks do not rule out coherent writing.

## 30.2 Analysing

An analysis is a notation of what was heard with the signs of this book. Four levels suffice: the form as a chain of letters with bar counts (A 8, B 8, A′ 8, break 4, A 16); the bass as a tone sequence with durations; the harmony as degrees above the bass, Roman for triads, with 5 for power chords; the layers with their registers and rhythms. In addition, where it applies, the cadence types at section endings, the refusals (chapter 13), the form signals of the drums (chapter 19) and the density arc (chapter 22).

[[c28-analysis]]

The example shows such an analysis on an eight-bar riff: form letters above the bars, degrees above the chords. The second pass is A′ because a single chord is different, the F5 on ♭II, the Phrygian move that carries the close. An analysis is finished when it answers what returns, what changes and why the piece ends where it ends.

The references offer different material for analysis. Where a score is available, compare recording and notation. Where no reliable score is available, make a transcription with explicit uncertainties. This does not imply that no other transcriptions or editions exist.

## 30.3 Writing: the working path

One possible workflow has seven stages: motive, foundation, form plan, two-voice sketch, inner voices and textures, sound, score and recording. Each stage makes a decision assessable. The order can change: sound, rhythm or a chord can also be the starting point. The bass alone need not already form a complete piece.

[[c28-workflow]]

The example presents the same motif with growing forces: alone, with bass, with a sustained inner voice and with moving texture. This order makes the decisions traceable. Other workflows may begin with sound or a chord progression. What matters is evaluating the audible result and revising earlier decisions accordingly.

The proposed workflow is a method for original pieces. A finished recording does not reliably reveal the actual order of its creators’ compositional decisions. A familiar form can support planning but does not replace decisions about the particular musical course.

## 30.4 Roles from one hand

Whoever works alone has two paths: solo playing, in which one instrument carries foundation, inner voice and line, or layered recording, in which every role is recorded separately. The second needs planning because one layer cannot adapt to the next. Order: first drums or click, the grid; then the bass, the foundation; then the rhythm guitar, which listens to the bass; then the pad, which fills the registers; finally the line, which listens to everything.

[[c28-roles]]

In the example the bass sustains, guitar articulates chords, a pad connects, and the line phrases. Other assignments are possible. Voices sharing a rhythm remain distinct voices, and a continuous pad can have a deliberate function. In layered recordings, revise earlier tracks when necessary so that timing and note endings fit together.

## 30.5 Rules of one's own

A personal style emerges from recurring decisions. Instruments, references and listening supply ideas; they do not restrict available keys, rhythms and forms. Choose a few concrete working decisions for a piece and revise them when the music improves. Technical difficulty calls for practice or deliberate arrangement, not an unjustified exclusion of a musical possibility.

[[c28-rules]]

The example deliberately limits bass rhythm, register, rests, retained notes and an interruption. These choices describe this model. Another version may change faster, contain lower thirds or avoid phrase rests. Compare the audible result; the number of personal rules is not a measure of quality.

## 30.6 Documenting

A recording is not the piece; it is a performance. The piece is the score plus the sound documentation. Reproducible means: playable the same way in a year with the same means, and approximable for someone else with theirs. Five parts: the score with clef, key signature, meter, tempo unit, all voices, form signs and position marks (chapters 2 and 4); the sound sheet, per role instrument, sound parameters in general terms, effects with the four delay parameters and the reverb type, gain level, frequency plan (chapters 23 to 25); the drum grid with steps, velocities, swing and nudge (chapter 19); the recording log with date, order of layers, tempo and reference take; the deviations, where the recording departs from the score and why.

[[c28-document]]

The example documents key, tempo, chords and Fine. A recording preserves a particular interpretation; a sound sheet adds settings and timbral intentions. Readable notation and accessible source files help future work. Score, recording and project file document different aspects of the same piece.

## 30.7 Repertoire and set

A repertoire is a set of pieces one can play at any time, not those one once could. Every piece has a state: new, active, resting, archived; a resting piece is active again after a day of practice. A piece exists in versions: solo, layered, shortened, in another key, say moved from E to A; every version is a decision of its own about what the piece is at its core.

[[c28-set]]

The example orders four contrasting sections E–A–C–E. Their effect comes from connection, duration, sound and material, not solely from key distance. A set can start with its loudest piece or end quietly. Add the pieces and transitions to calculate duration; this implies no fixed number of pieces.

## 30.8 A practice without a market

Whoever pursues this music without income pursues a practice with a public. Three components: the work, the pieces and their documents; the rhythm, when something gets finished; the public, who hears it. The deadline is the device amateurs usually lack and that costs nothing: one piece per quarter, documented and recorded, regardless of whether it is the best; one set per year, played through. Public means: a recording that someone hears is published. A page with recordings and scores, a performance for two people, a piece sent to someone who understands it. The feedback of a few who listen is worth more than any reach.

Revision has no fixed calendar. Play older pieces again, listen to recordings and identify concrete improvements: clearer phrasing, a stronger hook, more suitable accompaniment or better fingering. A new tool is useful when it solves a musical task. References may change with your taste.

## 30.9 Summary

- Listen: follow pulse, pitch space, bass, harmony and melody separately, then judge them together.
- Analyse: record form letters with bar counts, bass, chords and voices.
- Compose: develop and revise motif, form, texture and sound in an appropriate order.
- Determine tonality, modality and closure from context.
- Treat personal style rules as revisable decisions.
- Document: notation, sound directions, rhythm grids and recordings preserve different aspects.
- A repertoire grows through repeated playing and focused revision.

cA.title: Acoustics and tuning
cA.text:
This appendix collects the numbers behind chapters 1, 8 and 23: frequencies, cents, overtones, fret distances, string tension and the tunings of all instruments of this book.

## A.1 Frequency from MIDI number

f = 440 · 2^((n − 69) / 12). A4 = MIDI 69 = 440 Hz. C4 = 60. Every octave doubles; every semitone multiplies by 2^(1/12) ≈ 1.05946.

## A.2 Frequency table (equal temperament, A4 = 440 Hz), rounded

- E1 41.2 · A1 55.0 · D2 73.4 · G2 98.0 · C3 130.8 · F3 174.6
- E2 82.4 · A2 110.0 · D3 146.8 · G3 196.0 · C4 261.6 · F4 349.2
- E3 164.8 · A3 220.0 · D4 293.7 · G4 392.0 · C5 523.3 · F5 698.5
- E4 329.6 · A4 440.0 · D5 587.3 · G5 784.0 · C6 1046.5 · F6 1396.9
- E5 659.3 · A5 880.0 · D6 1174.7 · B0 30.9 · B1 61.7 · B2 123.5
- B3 246.9 · B4 493.9 · B5 987.8 · F#2 92.5 · F#3 185.0 · F#4 370.0
- G#2 103.8 · G#3 207.7 · G#4 415.3 · C#3 138.6 · C#4 277.2 · C#5 554.4
- D#3 155.6 · D#4 311.1 · D#5 622.3 · Eb2 77.8 · Db3 138.6 · Bb2 116.5

## A.3 Cents

1 cent = 1/100 semitone. Distance between two frequencies in cents: c = 1200 · log2(f2 / f1). Pure fifth 3:2 = 701.96 cents, tempered 700 (2 cents too small). Pure major third 5:4 = 386.3, tempered 400 (14 cents too wide). Pure minor third 6:5 = 315.6, tempered 300 (16 cents too narrow). Seventh partial 7:4 = 968.8, tempered minor seventh 1000 (31 cents difference). Pitch discrimination threshold about 5 cents; beating audible from about 1 Hz difference.

## A.4 Overtone series

Partial n has frequency n · f. Over E2 (82.4 Hz): 1 E2 · 2 E3 · 3 B3 · 4 E4 · 5 G#4 (−14 cents) · 6 B4 · 7 D5 (−31 cents) · 8 E5 · 9 F#5 · 10 G#5 · 11 between A5 and A#5 · 12 B5. Harmonic over fret 12 = partial 2, fret 7 (and 19) = partial 3, fret 5 (and 24) = partial 4, fret 4 (and 9, 16) = partial 5, fret 3.2 = partial 6.

## A.5 Fret calculation

With scale length L (nut to bridge) fret n sits at d = L · (1 − 2^(−n/12)) from the nut. For L = 648 mm (25.5 in): fret 1 36.4 · fret 2 70.7 · fret 3 103.1 · fret 4 133.7 · fret 5 162.5 · fret 7 215.5 · fret 9 262.7 · fret 12 324.0 · fret 24 486.0 mm. Fret 12 halves the string. The distance between frets shrinks by a factor of 0.9439 per fret.

## A.6 Intonation

Pressing down stretches the string and raises the pitch; therefore the saddle is set slightly longer than the calculated scale (compensation, 1–4 mm, more for thicker strings). Control: harmonic above fret 12 against the fretted tone at fret 12; if the fretted tone is sharp, the string is lengthened at the saddle.

## A.7 String tension

The ideal string model gives T = 4 × L² × f² × μ, with scale length L and mass per unit length μ. A fourth downward multiplies f by 2^(−5/12) ≈ 0.749 and T by 2^(−10/12) ≈ 0.561. Equal tension would require multiplying μ by 1/0.561 ≈ 1.78. Only solid strings of equal density imply a diameter factor of √1.78 ≈ 1.33. This gives no reliable .046→.061 recommendation for wound strings. One semitone upward gives 2^(2/12) ≈ 1.122, about 12% greater tension. String construction and instrument setup determine the appropriate gauges.

## A.8 Tunings

Standard E2 A2 D3 G3 B3 E4 (intervals 5-5-5-4-5 semitones). P4 E2 A2 D3 G3 C4 F4 (5-5-5-5-5). Type O Negative B1 E2 A2 D3 F#3 B3: standard a fourth lower, Kenny Hickey consistently in B standard. Bass E1 A1 D2 G2. Violin G3 D4 A4 E5 (fifths). Biber, *Harmonia artificioso-ariosa*, scordaturas per IMSLP: Partia I (D minor) both violins A3 E4 A4 D5; II (B minor) B3 F#4 B4 D5; III (A major) A3 E4 A4 E5; IV (E-flat major) violin Bb3 Eb4 Bb4 Eb5, viola Eb3 Bb3 Eb4 Bb4; V (G minor) G3 D4 A4 D5; VI (D major) normal tuning; VII (C minor) two violas d'amore C3 G3 C4 Eb4 G4 C5. The notation shows fingerings, not sounding pitches. Partia I is a fifth-fourth-fourth chain, the violas d'amore a broken C minor chord: the tuning is the chord.

## A.9 Sustain measurement

Measure decay under specified conditions: the same attack, sound, level and register, with a chosen threshold such as 40 dB below the initial level. The result applies to that setup and threshold. It does not necessarily determine the longest notated duration or slowest tempo.

cB.title: Distortion and intermodulation
cB.text:
This appendix calculates possible intermodulation frequencies. Their presence and level depend on the transfer curve and input spectrum; the table establishes no universal register prohibitions.

## B.1 Clipping

Clipping limits signal peaks. Symmetrical transfer curves generate only odd harmonics from a sine; asymmetrical curves can add even harmonics. Soft and hard clipping differ in the strength of high spectral components. Tube or diode alone determines neither symmetry nor a fixed sound category.

## B.2 Intermodulation

For two sine tones, possible products are |mf1 ± nf2|. The transfer curve determines which orders occur. Ideal symmetrical distortion lacks even orders, including f2 − f1; products such as 2f1 − f2 can remain. A combination tone generated in hearing need not be present in the measured output signal.

## B.3 Table over E3 (164.8 Hz)

Interval · upper pitch · difference product f2 − f1 · nearest equal-tempered pitch · third-order product |2f1 − f2| · nearest equal-tempered pitch. All cent offsets appear in parentheses; 2 + 1 = 3 gives the order of the second product.

- Octave E4 329.63 Hz · f2−f1: 164.81 Hz ≈ E3 (+0.0 Cent) · |2f1−f2|: 0 Hz (DC)
- Fifth B3 246.94 Hz · f2−f1: 82.13 Hz ≈ E2 (-5.9 Cent) · |2f1−f2|: 82.69 Hz ≈ E2 (+5.9 Cent)
- Fourth A3 220.00 Hz · f2−f1: 55.19 Hz ≈ A1 (+5.9 Cent) · |2f1−f2|: 109.63 Hz ≈ A2 (-5.9 Cent)
- Major third G#3 207.65 Hz · f2−f1: 42.84 Hz ≈ F1 (-32.6 Cent) · |2f1−f2|: 121.98 Hz ≈ B2 (-21.1 Cent)
- Minor third G3 196.00 Hz · f2−f1: 31.18 Hz ≈ B0 (+17.6 Cent) · |2f1−f2|: 133.63 Hz ≈ C3 (+36.9 Cent)
- Major second F#3 185.00 Hz · f2−f1: 20.18 Hz ≈ E0 (-35.5 Cent) · |2f1−f2|: 144.63 Hz ≈ D3 (-26.2 Cent)
- Minor second F3 174.61 Hz · f2−f1: 9.80 Hz ≈ D#-1 (+13.8 Cent) · |2f1−f2|: 155.01 Hz ≈ D#3 (-6.1 Cent)
- Tritone A#3 233.08 Hz · f2−f1: 68.27 Hz ≈ C#2 (-25.9 Cent) · |2f1−f2|: 96.55 Hz ≈ G2 (-25.9 Cent)
- Minor sixth C4 261.63 Hz · f2−f1: 96.81 Hz ≈ G2 (-21.1 Cent) · |2f1−f2|: 68.00 Hz ≈ C#2 (-32.6 Cent)
- Major sixth C#4 277.18 Hz · f2−f1: 112.37 Hz ≈ A2 (+36.9 Cent) · |2f1−f2|: 52.44 Hz ≈ G#1 (+17.6 Cent)

## B.4 Reading

The table lists frequencies, not levels. B and C both belong to E minor; “outside the Em triad” differs from “outside E minor.” Products of tempered fifths and fourths match tempered pitches only approximately. Whether they sound rough, supportive or inaudible depends on spectrum and playback level.

## B.5 Over E2 (82.4 Hz)

Above E2, the table’s frequencies halve for the same intervals: the fifth’s possible difference tone is about 41 Hz and the minor third’s about 15.6 Hz; the minor third’s 2f1 − f2 is about 66.8 Hz. Halved frequency does not imply greater level or automatically audible modulation.

## B.6 Rules

Register, note count, gain and balance are adjustable variables. A low-pass before distortion changes the spectral components entering the nonlinearity; EQ afterwards processes the resulting signal. Two separately distorted instruments produce no shared intermodulation unless their sum is processed nonlinearly again. Compare using the actual signal path.

cC.title: Delay arithmetic and time values
cC.text:
This appendix holds the calculations for chapters 17, 18 and 25: note values in milliseconds, delay times, numbers of repeats, swing percentages, room sizes and micro timing.

## C.1 Basic formula

Quarter in ms = 60000 / BPM (BPM in quarters). Eighth = quarter / 2. Sixteenth = quarter / 4. Dotted eighth = quarter · 0.75. Eighth triplet = quarter / 3. Quarter triplet = quarter · 2/3. Half = quarter · 2. Whole = quarter · 4. In 12/8 with tempo ♩. = BPM: dotted quarter = 60000 / BPM, eighth = one third of it.

## C.2 Table (quarter · eighth · dotted eighth · eighth triplet · half), ms:

- 50: 1200 · 600 · 900 · 400 · 2400
- 55: 1091 · 545 · 818 · 364 · 2182
- 60: 1000 · 500 · 750 · 333 · 2000
- 65: 923 · 462 · 692 · 308 · 1846
- 70: 857 · 429 · 643 · 286 · 1714
- 72: 833 · 417 · 625 · 278 · 1667
- 75: 800 · 400 · 600 · 267 · 1600
- 80: 750 · 375 · 563 · 250 · 1500
- 85: 706 · 353 · 529 · 235 · 1412
- 90: 667 · 333 · 500 · 222 · 1333
- 95: 632 · 316 · 474 · 211 · 1263
- 100: 600 · 300 · 450 · 200 · 1200
- 120: 500 · 250 · 375 · 167 · 1000
- 140: 429 · 214 · 321 · 143 · 857

## C.3 Rhythmic delays

With a dotted-eighth delay, the original and first repeat share a sixteenth-note grid, but not every later repeat remains between original onsets. A quarter-note delay fills half notes into a continuous quarter pattern only with exactly one repeat and no further feedback. A triplet-eighth delay over straight eighths does not automatically produce shuffle: the onsets lie on different subdivisions.

## C.4 Feedback and number of repeats

In the ideal model, echo n has relative amplitude g^n, with feedback factor 0 < g < 1. A −40 dB threshold corresponds to 10^(−40/20) = 0.01. Echoes meeting this definition satisfy g^n ≥ 0.01, so n ≤ log(0.01)/log(g). Rounding down gives at most 3, 6, 12 and 43 repeats for 30%, 50%, 70% and 90% feedback. For 50%: 0.5^6 = 0.015625 is above the threshold, while 0.5^7 = 0.0078125 is below. Filtering and real listening conditions alter the threshold, not by a fixed factor.

## C.5 Swing percentage

Share of the first eighth in the quarter: 50 % straight, 58 % light, 62 % medium, 67 % triplet (2:1), 75 % dotted (3:1). For sixteenth swing the same at eighth level. Drum machines give swing either as a percentage, usually between 50 and 80, or as a shift of the offbeats in grid steps; in the second case the shift is converted into the percentage: shift divided by the length of a beat, plus 50.

## C.6 Pre-delay and room

With sound speed c ≈ 343 m/s, additional path length is ΔL = c × Δt: 1 ms → 0.343 m, 10 ms → 3.43 m, 30 ms → 10.29 m. This is a path difference, not room size. Artificial pre-delay can be chosen freely. RT60 measures a 60 dB level decrease; geometry, absorption and frequency determine decay time, not merely the label “hall” or “church.”

## C.7 Haas effect

The precedence effect can shift localisation toward the earlier signal. Fusion and echo perception depend on material, level, direction and delay; 30–40 ms is not a fixed boundary. A short stereo delay can widen the image but colours a mono sum through interference.

## C.8 Microtiming

At ♩ = 60 a sixteenth lasts 250 ms; laid-back sits at 10–40 ms, i.e. 4–16 % of a sixteenth. Drum machines offer the shift as nudge or micro timing per hit, in milliseconds or in fractions of the grid; a grid of 1/384 bar corresponds at ♩ = 60 to a step of 10.4 ms, 1/96 bar to a step of 41.7 ms. Devices without nudge reach the same only through recording with quantisation switched off.

cE.title: Chord symbol reference
cE.text:
This appendix lists all chord symbols from chapter 12 with their tones over the three centres E, A and D, plus the degree chords of the three keys.

## D.1 Reading order

Root · type (nothing = major, m, dim/°, aug/+) · seventh (7 minor, maj7/Δ major) · extension (9, 11, 13) · alteration (b5, #5, b9, #9, #11, b13) · addition (add) · omission (no3, no5) · bass (/X). The symbol fixes tones, not spacing, doubling or duration.

## D.2 Table: symbol · over E · over A · over D

- 5 (power chord) · E B · A E · D A
- major · E G# B · A C# E · D F# A
- m · E G B · A C E · D F A
- dim / ° · E G Bb · A C Eb · D F Ab
- aug / + · E G# B# · A C# E# · D F# A#
- sus2 · E F# B · A B E · D E A
- sus4 · E A B · A D E · D G A
- 6 · E G# B C# · A C# E F# · D F# A B
- m6 · E G B C# · A C E F# · D F A B
- 7 · E G# B D · A C# E G · D F# A C
- maj7 / Δ · E G# B D# · A C# E G# · D F# A C#
- m7 · E G B D · A C E G · D F A C
- m(maj7) · E G B D# · A C E G# · D F A C#
- dim7 / °7 · E G Bb Db · A C Eb Gb · D F Ab Cb
- m7b5 / ø · E G Bb D · A C Eb G · D F Ab C
- 7sus4 · E A B D · A D E G · D G A C
- add9 · E G# B F# · A C# E B · D F# A E
- madd9 · E G B F# · A C E B · D F A E
- 9 · E G# B D F# · A C# E G B · D F# A C E
- maj9 · E G# B D# F# · A C# E G# B · D F# A C# E
- m9 · E G B D F# · A C E G B · D F A C E
- 11 (third usually omitted) · E B D F# A · A E G B D · D A C E G
- m11 · E G B D F# A · A C E G B D · D F A C E G
- 13 · E G# B D F# C# · A C# E G B F# · D F# A C E B
- 7b9 · E G# B D F · A C# E G Bb · D F# A C Eb
- 7#9 · E G# B D G (F##) · A C# E G C (B#) · D F# A C F (E#)
- 7#11 · E G# B D A# · A C# E G D# · D F# A C G#
- 7b5 · E G# Bb D · A C# Eb G · D F# Ab C
- maj7#11 · E G# B D# A# · A C# E G# D# · D F# A C# G#
- m6/9 · E G B C# F# · A C E F# B · D F A B E

## D.3 Slash chords

X/Y means chord X with bass note Y. Em/G and Em/B are inversions. Em/C is a valid description of Em over C and has the same pitch classes as Cmaj7. Em/D contains the tones of Em7 in third inversion. D/E contains E D F# A and corresponds to E9sus4(no5). A bass determines inversion but does not automatically determine the chord root.

## D.4 Degrees in E Aeolian (triads · seventh chords)

E Aeolian: i Em/Em7, ii° F#dim/F#m7b5, III G/Gmaj7, iv Am/Am7, v Bm/Bm7, VI C/Cmaj7, VII D/D7. Harmonic minor: i Em/Em(maj7), ii° F#dim/F#m7b5, III+ G+/Gmaj7#5, iv Am/Am7, V B/B7, VI C/Cmaj7, vii° D#dim/D#dim7. Melodic minor with raised 6 and 7: i Em/Em(maj7), ii F#m/F#m7, III+ G+/Gmaj7#5, IV A/A7, V B/B7, vi° C#dim/C#m7b5, vii° D#dim/D#m7b5. In particular, the seventh of vii changes from diminished to minor.

## D.5 Degrees in A Aeolian

Am, Bdim, C, Dm, Em, F, G; harmonic: E, G#dim. **In D Aeolian.** Dm, Edim, F, Gm, Am, Bb, C; harmonic: A, C#dim.

## D.6 Common symbols in this book

Power chords with 5 for the distorted guitar (chapter 11). Plain triads Em, C, D, Am, G, B for modal harmony (chapter 13). madd9 and maj7 as pads without direction (chapter 12). Dominant sevenths, dim7 and the Picardy third at cadences (chapters 13 and 15). sus4 → 3 as suspension (chapter 20).

## D.7 Notation of one's own pieces

Symbols above the notes are commentary; the notes are binding. For power chords write the symbol with 5, not the triad name, so that the missing third is documented.

cG.title: Glossary
cG.text:
This glossary sums up the terms of the book in one sentence each and names the chapter in which they are introduced. It does not replace the explanation but helps in finding it again.

## E.1 Terms A to Z

- **Agogics** — temporal weighting of notes and phrases (chapter 18)
- **Agogics** — small deviation from the time grid at constant tempo; one element behind the beat sounds heavy (chapter 18)
- **Arpeggio** — the tones of a chord in succession; as a figure the middle layer of the texture (chapter 22)
- **Augmentation** — treatment of a motif with doubled note values (chapter 26)
- **Authentic cadence** — close from dominant to tonic, V–I (chapter 13)
- **Bass model** — fixed bass sequence over which the upper voices move freely: lamento, falling fifths, ostinato (chapter 16)
- **Bending** — continuous pulling of the string to a heard target tone (chapter 23)
- **Binary and ternary** — division of the beat in two or in three (chapter 17)
- **Cadence** — harmonic close: authentic, plagal, half, deceptive, Phrygian (chapter 13)
- **Canon** — a melody that follows itself at a fixed distance (chapter 20)
- **Cent** — hundredth of a semitone; measure of tuning deviations (chapter 1)
- **Chromaticism** — notes outside the diatonic collection; spelling follows interval and function (chapter 7)
- **Chromaticism** — tones outside the scale as passing, neighbour or chord tones; spelled by direction (chapter 7)
- **Ciacona** — Baroque variation set over a repeated bass in triple meter (chapter 16)
- **Circle of fifths** — arrangement of the keys by fifths; neighbours share almost all tones (chapter 6)
- **Consonance** — interval that may stand freely; perfect: unison, fifth, octave; imperfect: thirds, sixths (chapter 5)
- **Difference tone** — a possible combination tone at |f2 − f1|, in a nonlinear signal or in hearing (chapter 1)
- **Contour** — outline of the melodic motion; stays recognisable in sequence and variation (chapter 21)
- **Dominant** — function on degree five; its major third supplies the leading tone and a seventh can be added (chapter 13)
- **Deceptive cadence** — dominant to the sixth degree instead of the tonic, V–VI (chapter 13)
- **Delay** — delay of the signal; parameters time, feedback, filter, modulation (chapter 25)
- **Density** — number of voices, attacks, register width and sonic density of a section (chapter 22)
- **Enharmonicism** — different note names for the same equal-tempered pitch; function determines spelling (chapter 2)
- **Diminution** — treatment of a motif with halved note values (chapter 26)
- **Dominant** — chord of the fifth degree; works through leading tone and seventh (chapter 13)
- **Dorian** — minor mode with major sixth; the subdominant turns major (chapter 7)
- **Enharmonics** — same key, different name; the spelling shows the direction (chapter 2)
- **Falling fifths** — sequence of roots in falling fifths; every chord the dominant of the next (chapter 16)
- **Function** — role of a chord as tonic, subdominant or dominant (chapter 10)
- **Half cadence** — phrase ending on the dominant (chapter 13)
- **Half-time** — snare only on 3; halves the felt speed (chapter 18)
- **Harmonic minor** — minor with raised seventh degree; supplies the major dominant (chapter 6)
- **Hemiola** — regrouping of 3+3 into 2+2+2 or the reverse, usually before the cadence (chapter 17)
- **Imitation** — one voice repeats what another played shortly before; strictly as canon (chapter 20)
- **Intermodulation** — origin of combination tones from two tones under distortion (chapter 1)
- **Interval** — distance between two tones; name by natural tones, size by semitones (chapter 5)
- **Consonance** — an interval treated as stable within a given compositional model, not a context-free guarantee of sound (chapter 5)
- **Inversion (interval)** — lower tone moved up an octave; numbers add up to nine (chapter 5)
- **Inversion (motif)** — mirroring of the contour (chapter 26)
- **Key** — centre plus tone stock; audible through duration, return, register and closing position (chapter 6)
- **Lamento bass** — descending tetrachord from root to fifth, diatonic or chromatic (chapter 16)
- **Locrian** — a mode with minor second and diminished fifth that can establish its own center (chapter 7)
- **Locrian** — mode without a perfect fifth; usable only in passing (chapter 7)
- **Melodic minor** — minor with raised degrees 6 and 7; the classical scale exercise descends naturally, while actual use depends on context (chapter 6)
- **Melodic minor** — minor with raised sixth and seventh degrees ascending (chapter 6)
- **Meter** — grouping of the pulse with an accented first beat (chapter 17)
- **Modal and tonal** — overlapping organizations of center, pitch collection and harmony, not determined by one leading tone (chapter 13)
- **Modal and tonal** — colours over a centre without leading tone versus expectation through dominant and leading tone (chapter 13)
- **Mode** — the interval organization of a pitch collection relative to a center (chapter 7)
- **Modulation** — confirmation of a new centre, usually via pivot and new dominant (chapter 15)
- **Motif** — smallest unit recognisable as an idea: a few tones with rhythm (chapter 26)
- **Neapolitan** — major chord on ♭II, usually in first inversion before the dominant (chapter 15)
- **Pedal point** — a sustained or reiterated tone beneath changing harmonies (chapter 14)
- **Ostinato** — a recurring rhythmic or melodic pattern, not restricted to the bass (chapter 16)
- **Overtone series** — integer multiples of the fundamental; octave, fifth, fourth, thirds (chapter 1)
- **Parallel (voice leading)** — two voices at the same distance; octaves and fifths fuse (chapter 14)
- **Pentatonic** — a five-note collection; major/minor pentatonic scales without semitone steps are not automatically consonant (chapter 7)
- **Period** — antecedent and consequent with weaker and stronger closure; eight measures are a model (chapter 26)
- **Pentatonic** — five tones without semitone steps; always consonant over the root (chapter 7)
- **Period** — eight-bar phrase form: antecedent with half cadence, consequent with full close (chapter 26)
- **Phrase** — musical clause with its own breath and target tone (chapter 21)
- **Phrygian** — minor mode with minor second; close F–E (chapter 7)
- **Picardy third** — major tonic at the end of a minor piece (chapter 13)
- **Plagal cadence** — close from subdominant to tonic, IV–I (chapter 13)
- **Polyrhythm** — two voices divide the same span differently, say three against two (chapter 17)
- **Power chord** — root and fifth without third; symbol 5 (chapter 11)
- **Descending-fifths sequence** — a sequence of descending diatonic or perfect fifths; not every chord is a functional dominant (chapter 16)
- **Register** — a voice’s pitch range; registers of several roles can overlap (chapter 22)
- **Riff** — a recurring rhythmic or melodic figure without a fixed length or compulsory bass part (chapter 26)
- **Retrograde** — treatment of a motif backwards (chapter 26)
- **Rubato** — flexible shaping of individual voices’ timing or the common tempo (chapter 18)
- **Riff** — motif with bass that repeats; one to four bars (chapter 26)
- **Ritornello** — section that returns between episodes; Vivaldi's form (chapter 27)
- **Rubato** — stolen time within a phrase (chapter 18)
- **Scordatura** — retuning of an instrument as a compositional device; notation shows fingerings (chapter 8)
- **Slash chord** — chord X over specified bass Y; X/Y can indicate an inversion or a non-chord bass note (chapter 12)
- **Sentence (form)** — eight-bar phrase form: basic idea, repetition or sequence, continuation, cadence (chapter 26)
- **Sustain** — the held level of an ADSR envelope or the audible persistence of an instrumental tone; not a general tempo limit (chapters 23 and 24)
- **Seventh chord** — triad plus third; types 7, maj7, m7, m7♭5, dim7 (chapter 12)
- **Slash chord** — chord with a stated bass tone: inversion or another chord (chapter 12)
- **Suite** — sequence of dance movements in one key (chapter 28)
- **Suspension** — held tone that becomes dissonant and resolves downward by step: 4–3, 7–6, 9–8 (chapter 20)
- **Sustain** — duration for which a tone carries audibly; determines the slowest tempo (chapter 23)
- **Swing** — second eighth of every beat shifted backward; written straight (chapter 17)
- **Syncopation** — accent on a light beat or between the beats (chapter 17)
- **Tempo** — beats per minute with the counted note value (chapter 4)
- **Thoroughbass** — bass line with figures for the intervals above it (chapter 12)
- **Triad** — three tones a third apart: major, minor, diminished, augmented (chapter 10)
- **Tritone** — interval of six semitones; core of the dominant (chapter 5)
- **Upbeat** — beginning of a phrase before the first beat of the bar (chapter 4)
- **Secondary dominant** — a major chord, often with a minor seventh, preparing a chord other than the main tonic (chapter 15)

c05-relative-visual-1.text: Numbers identify intervals from the tonic: 1 = tonic, b3 = minor third. The undimmed area shows one octave; the same pitch collection continues outside it.

c07b-centres-visual-1.title: E Aeolian · interval map
c07b-centres-visual-1.text: Orange = 1. Compare 1–2–b3 on neighbouring string groups. This shows the full pitch collection in the window; the following scores select a particular playing path.

c07b-centres-visual-2.title: A Aeolian · interval map
c07b-centres-visual-2.text: Orange = 1. Compare 1–2–b3 on neighbouring string groups. This shows the full pitch collection in the window; the following scores select a particular playing path.

c07b-centres-visual-3.title: D Aeolian · interval map
c07b-centres-visual-3.text: Orange = 1. Compare 1–2–b3 on neighbouring string groups. This shows the full pitch collection in the window; the following scores select a particular playing path.

c06-colours-visual-1.title: E Aeolian: 1–2–b3–4–5–b6–b7
c06-colours-visual-1.text: Same tonic, different semitone spacing. Compare the marked degrees with the other two maps; E remains the reference.

c06-colours-visual-2.title: E Phrygian: b2 instead of 2
c06-colours-visual-2.text: Same tonic, different semitone spacing. Compare the marked degrees with the other two maps; E remains the reference.

c06-colours-visual-3.title: E Dorian: 6 instead of b6
c06-colours-visual-3.text: Same tonic, different semitone spacing. Compare the marked degrees with the other two maps; E remains the reference.

c06-pentatonic-visual-1.title: Five pitch classes, many positions
c06-pentatonic-visual-1.text: E–G–A–B–D: 1–b3–4–5–b7. A collection without semitone steps is not automatically consonant: A over E is a fourth and D over E a minor seventh.

c08-third-visual-1.title: Em: see the minor third
c08-third-visual-1.text: Compare key distances; the score below supplies duration and musical context. The highlighted keys form the named voicing.

c08-third-visual-2.title: E: only the third moves
c08-third-visual-2.text: Compare key distances; the score below supplies duration and musical context. The highlighted keys form the named voicing.

c10-added-visual-1.title: Em6: C# added to the minor triad
c10-added-visual-1.text: Compare key distances; the score below supplies duration and musical context. The highlighted keys form the named voicing.

c15-poly-visual-1.title: Three against two: six shared subdivisions
c15-poly-visual-1.text: One span = two quarters. Three attacks divide it into 3 × 2 subdivisions; two divide it into 2 × 3. Both meet again at the next beginning.

c15-compound-visual-1.title: 12/8: four large beats
c15-compound-visual-1.text: 12 eighths = 4 × 3 eighths. One large beat lasts a dotted quarter. Each of two dotted halves in the bass spans two beats.

c15-332-visual-1.title: 3+3+2 in 4/4
c15-332-visual-1.text: Three groups fill the same bar: 3 + 3 + 2 = 8 eighths. This is asymmetrical accent grouping; a classical hemiola uses a 3:2 relationship.

c15-odd-visual-1.text: The last group is one eighth longer: 2 + 2 + 3 = 7. Beams in the score show the same groups.

c24-motif-visual-1.title: Four bars: return creates form
c24-motif-visual-1.text: The example shows a motif, its exact repetition and two variants. An original four-bar piece can use A–B–A–C: motif, answer, return and a distinct ending.

c24-period-visual-1.title: Period: four plus four bars
c24-period-visual-1.text: The second four-bar phrase answers the first. Return and a stronger ending connect the halves; eight bars alone do not make a period.

c22-waveforms-visual-1.title: Subtractive synthesis signal path
c22-waveforms-visual-1.text: Envelopes and LFOs control parameters along the signal path. SoundFont preview demonstrates the notes; it does not simulate waveforms or filter settings.

c23-time-visual-1.title: Delay: a second attack after a fixed time
c23-time-visual-1.text: At ♩ = 60, a quarter lasts 60000/60 = 1000 ms. A dotted eighth lasts 3/4 of that: 750 ms. Feedback routes part of the echo into the delay again.

c22-hold-visual-1.title: ADSR: distinguish time and level
c22-hold-visual-1.text: Attack, decay and release are time stages. Sustain is a level that can persist while a key is held. Release begins at key-up; the linear curve is schematic.
